#6822. Designers Say These Are the 10 Best Antiques to Find at Estate Sales

Thrift stores and flea markets are popular spots for finding unusual vintage pieces, but they’re not the only options. Estate sales let you browse antiques in the very homes where they’ve been used and collected over the years. And since many items haven’t passed through a dealer, they may cost less than similar finds at an antique shop.

That combination makes estate sales a favorite among interior designers. They’re a source of characterful pieces for both client projects and personal collections. Krystal Reinhard, founder and principal designer of Old Soul Design Studio, likes being able to see items in the settings where they’ve long belonged. “It makes it easier to spot quality, scale, and patina,” she says.

For Valerie Helgeson, founder and lead designer at Design Directions, the appeal of estate sales is the fast-paced nature of the hunt. “There’s an immediacy to them that I like. You have to make a decision and trust your instincts,” she shares.

Whether you’re after a bargain, an authentic antique, or the fun of finding an unexpected treasure, estate sales are worth exploring. Ahead, interior designers reveal the 10 antiques they always look for—and explain why each belongs on your estate sale wish list.

Paige Loperfido, founder and principal designer of Decor & More Design Studio, is always game to grab hand-painted porcelain, midcentury ceramics, and antique glassware, like ice buckets and goblets.

“These collectibles bring color, pattern, and personality to kitchens and dining rooms,” she says. “Beyond their practical use, they easily transition into art, with vintage plates mounted on walls for a dynamic display, or grouped on open shelves. In dining spaces, glassware and tableware act as statement pieces, highlighting one-of-a-kind treasures that feel timeless, sophisticated, and thoughtfully curated, adding both charm and character to special gatherings.”

Reinhard calls antique candlestick holders “an instant layer,” with their warmth, height, and “a little romance with a surprisingly big impact for a small spend.” She adds that she often styles them as matched pairs on mantels and consoles, or as loose trios at varying heights on dining tables and coffee tables.

Going into estate sales with an open mind, Helgeson typically finds herself buying something she “could have never imagined looking for.” But frequently, one item tops her wish list, and that’s copper kitchenware. She displays these antique pieces in kitchens alongside other estate sale–found items, such as turned-wood bowls, old cutting boards, and bread bowls.

Pottery is a designer darling, since these pieces add texture and even imperfection (in a good way) to spaces, as Reinhard puts it. She tracks down pottery at estate sales, then showcases it on open shelving, sideboards, and tablescapes. She prefers to pair pottery with “something refined,” like brass, stone, or glass, to keep the mix elevated.

Loperfido’s favorite estate sale gems are what she calls “culturally rich pieces” that have been collected by homeowners from around the world. Think: Chinese antiques like foo dogs and ginger jars, and vintage ceramics such as majolica fish candlesticks, figurative pieces, or midcentury glazed pottery.

Oftentimes, she says that these particular pieces “showcase incredible craftsmanship and character,” adding that they’re perfect to layer on surfaces throughout the house, from bookshelves to nightstands to end tables.

At estate sales, Helgeson is scanning the spaces for “furniture with a strong silhouette.” Acting as anchors in rooms, Helgeson believes in accessorizing the rest of these spaces with vintage finds, which she says makes even new pieces appear like collected treasures.

“Vintage rugs bring color, pattern, and age instantly,” Reinhard remarks. She decorates with them “everywhere”: in powder rooms, mudrooms, and under seating areas to anchor the furniture and add depth.

“Original art can feel inaccessible at gallery pricing, but estate sales are one of the best places to find something truly special for a fraction of the cost,” Reinhard points out. She goes for single statement pieces, small collected clusters, or creates a full gallery wall that combines vintage art with modern pieces and personal photos.

Continually on the lookout for leather-bound collections and cocktail books, Reinhard snaps up antique books at estate sales.

“They’re one of the easiest ways to add personality and story—especially art, history, and travel titles that feel timeless and intentional,” she says. “I use them everywhere—stacked on coffee tables, tucked onto consoles, layered into shelves, or used as risers for objects to create height and visual rhythm.”

Loperfido says that these “finely detailed etched artworks” are often overlooked at estate sales, but they can instantly add sophistication and historical texture to any space.

“Small but rich in visual storytelling, they work beautifully against neutral or patterned backgrounds,” she notes.

#6821. 6 Safety Razors That’ll Make You Swear Off Multiblade and Electric Shaving

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

One blade gives you a smoother shave and is better for your skin.

If you shave your face with any sort of frequency (daily, every other day, weekly), chances are you use a multiblade cartridge razor—a Gillette razor is what smart money would bet on. It’s the most common option for a reason. Cartridge razors are cheap, readily available, and easy to pick up new blades for (which frequently aren’t as cheap). But if you’ve often found yourself suffering from razor bumps, ingrown hairs, or razor burn—all issues that come readily to those with coarse or thick hair—you might need a course correction. That is because multiblade razors tend to cut too close. Or, well ... it’s not that they cut too close; they cut too much. By the time three to five blades track over a hair follicle, it’s underneath the outer layer of the skin. At that point, it’s simple mathematics that some of these hairs will not grow back perfectly straight out of your skin. They get stuck underneath your epidermis and cause those big, fat ingrown pimples.

Out in the world of shaving, there are single-blade razors, safety razors, multiblade cartridge razors, hell, even electric razors. In the past decade or so, traditional single-blade razors, aka safety razors, have enjoyed a bit of a renaissance. These blades are particularly good for men with sensitive skin or that thick, coarse hair. Safety razors, since they have only one blade, are able to shave close to the skin without going overboard. That comes with some risk. It is easier to cut yourself with, since the blade is sharp and unprotected by some of the features—like moisturizing bars—that you find in cartridge razors. There’s also a pretty steep learning curve associated with them, particularly if you come from the cartridge-razor world.

For those who put in the work and get the hang of it, many say a safety razor gives a far superior shave. And they do save you money in the long run. What else are you waiting for? Oh, for me to tell you what the best ones are. Easy enough. For my money, these six are the best safety razors you can buy.

Some might say Bevel was responsible for the safety-razor renaissance of the past decade with the release of this razor (one of its very first products). The thought behind this design, and the reason many people prefer safety razors, is that they don’t cut as close to the skin as multiblade razors, which helps prevent razor bumps and ingrown hairs. That’s a great thing for men with coarse and/or curly hair, which tends to form ingrowns more easily—and it’s also great for anyone with sensitive skin.

This handy razor is on the weighty side at over four ounces, which can be a good thing for a safety razor, and the sleek design is easy to understand and use. The double-edged blades are easy to replace using the screw top. Whether you’re a safety-razor beginner or expert, this is always going to be a good pick.

If you’re new to safety razors, investing in an expensive one might not be your top priority. This budget-friendly razor is all you need in order to get the hang of safety-razor shaving. It has a traditional screw-top design that uses the same double-edged blades as some of the more expensive handles on this list. The handle has a good heft to it that, combined with an easy-to-grip handle, helps you get used to shaving at a 30-degree angle. The closed-comb design is ideal for beginners and pros alike and delivers a smooth, close shave with minimal risk of nicks and cuts. If you’re a beginner, it’s a great option to learn with. If you’re a pro, it’s a great travel option so you can leave your pricier tool at home.

If you’re starting shaving with a safety razor from scratch, there are a few things to know. The two key elements are the weight of the razor and the angle of the blade. You want a handle that is hefty and feels heavy in your hand, not so light that you’re tempted to move it too quickly over the surface of your skin. The right weight lets the blade do most of the work and allows you to shave your hair with minimal strokes and less risk of nicks. The blade angle should always be about 30 degrees, not perpendicular to your skin, so you usually want to hold the razor at a slight angle.

This well-designed razor from pubic grooming giants Manscaped takes both of those into account. The weight is perfectly hefty, and the blade is actually already designed to sit at a 30 degree angle, so you don’t need to worry as much about how you’re holding it. Both of those things make this razor a perfect jumping off point for those who are coming from the multiblade side.

Safety razors are good for a lot of things, but if you’ve ever used one to try to tackle a few days’ worth of stubble, you know it’s not always great at powering through a lot of growth—at least not with the risk of nicking or cutting yourself going up exponentially. That’s where this safety razor shines. There are six different adjustable settings that subtly widen the space between the razor and the comb, allowing for thicker and coarser hair to be shaved more easily. If you shave every day, you’ll likely want to keep it on the lowest (zero gap) setting, which is basically your classic safety-razor setting, but if you tend to go a few days between shaves, change the setting to allow you to shave your stubble more easily with fewer strokes.

Sometimes you gotta go with a classic. Merkur has been making razors in Germany for over 125 years, and you can’t argue with that pedigree. This traditional safety razor has a traditional screw-top design and a weighted head that allows you to get a silky-smooth shave pretty much immediately. There aren’t any newfangled features in this thing, but that’s kind of the point. The nonslip coating and the perfectly weighted head, as well as the closed-comb design, make this the ideal short handle traditional razor.

Up until this point, I’ve been talking about closed comb razors. The difference, as you can see, is the exposed teeth of the blade on this style, making it sharper but also more of a risky proposition. Knowing your safety razor basics is a must, but if you have the technique down, this is a way to tackle longer or coarser beards.

Don’t get me wrong, this is an expert move. For those of us who grow facial hair faster and can never get a shave as close as we want before it starts growing back, the open comb razor is one way to achieve this. The cleanest shave of your life won’t just feel great, many say it will make your hair grow back slower.

Whether or not you’re experienced with safety razors, there are a few things to take into account when choosing the right one for you.

Weight: You’ll notice that most safety razors are way heavier than the drugstore cartridge razors you may be used to, and it’s not just because they’re made of metal. That’s by design. Safety razors tend to concentrate their weight in the head, which allows them to use gravity to give you a smooth shave without applying too much pressure (which can lead to nicks and cuts). Not all safety razors are the same weight, though. Ultimately you want to find a razor that is heavy enough to give you a good, close shave but not so heavy that your hand gets tired halfway through the process.

Blades: Most safety razors will use a traditional double-edged blade. This allows you to use both sides of the blade to get a little more usage out of it. Some razors will use a single-edged blade, usually called an injector blade, which is often thicker and more durable than its double-edged counterparts. Double-edged blades are preferable, but whichever you choose, make sure refills are readily available, as you’ll need to change the blade every few uses. (Most safety razors, especially those that use double-edged blades, can be refilled with any brand of blade.)

Razor Head Type: Speaking of changing the blades, safety razors typically come with two types of head. The most common is screw-off, where you unscrew the head of the razor in order to change the blade. The downfall of these is that while they’re easy in theory, it means the head comes in multiple parts that must be unscrewed and then screwed back together, making for a somewhat complicated experience, especially for beginners. The other kind, butterfly, pops up in the middle and allows you to drop in the blade.

Open Comb vs. Closed Comb: In this case, “comb” refers to how much distance there is between the razor head and the blade itself. The more open the comb, the more aggressive the shave. Closed comb razors are especially ideal for beginners because they help cut down on the risk of nicks and cuts (as there is no space for skin to get caught). Open-comb razors are ideal for people with thicker beards or longer stubble, as they allow more hair to reach the blade at once, but they carry a higher risk for nicks and cuts.

Adjustable Settings: Some razors will allow you to adjust the settings to take it between a closed and an open comb. Usually this involves different inserts that push space between the blade and the razor head. While not always necessary for everyone, this is ideal if you like to allow time between shaves and sometimes shave with a few days’ worth of stubble or more.

#6819. These 7 Storage Solutions for Small Spaces Look Too Good to Hide

Display-worthy baskets, glass-fronted cabinets, and colorful tins can make organization part of your decor.

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

From a Brooklyn studio to a narrow Baltimore rowhouse, two decades of small-space living have taught me how to make every square foot count. Add in my Type A Virgo tendencies and an appreciation for good design, and I have strong opinions about storage: Namely, it should be as good-looking as it is hard-working. My first stop when hunting for products that deliver just that is always IKEA. The Swedish retailer has an unmatched selection of storage furniture and decor. Here are seven pieces that offer both function and form.

I have never known the pleasure of a linen closet, but I’ve gotten so many compliments on this metal-and-glass cabinet in my bathroom that I no longer mind. The reeded glass offers an unexpected texture while obscuring what’s inside to reduce visual clutter, and each interior shelf is roomy enough to hold a stack of towels, plus a small bin for toiletries and medicine bottles. I like to use the bamboo UPPDATERA boxes for material contrast; the larger style works great on the lower shelves to tame my mess of serums, makeup, lotions, and the like.

There is no such thing as too many bins or baskets when you live in a small space. They are the unsung organizational heroes, giving you a way to stash all the miscellaneous things that would typically be tucked away in a closet, attic, basement, or even a spare room in a larger home. IKEA sells a huge variety, but the woven styles like this one are particularly lovely to keep on display. I use them on my EKET living room shelves for games, in my bedroom for scarves and bags, and in the kitchen for tea towels and napkins.

When square footage is at a premium, closets tend to get eliminated. A free-standing wardrobe is the solution to creating clothes storage in a small bedroom. This chic new design features sliding doors—a space-saver itself since you won’t need to account for door clearance—adjustable shelves, and two drawers.

If your front door, like mine, opens directly into your living space, you need to fake a foyer as best you can. The key to that is shoe storage—otherwise, guests will be staring at muddy boots the minute they walk into your home. This cabinet hides 14 pairs behind a traditional design, and sticks out from the wall less than a foot. Two drawers make space for keys and sunglasses while four hooks give bags and dog leashes a home.

All kitchens can benefit from more storage, but it’s the small cook spaces where you really need to get creative. A mobile cart offers that utility, and this one features three shelves for anything from spices and baking supplies to serveware or a coffee bar.

Another simple small kitchen storage idea: Keep your dry goods in stackable containers, like the BETTHAJ tins, to maximize your pantry shelf space. They’re far easier to handle than flimsy paper containers or plastic bags, plus, they look great on a countertop or open shelving. They come in five different sizes, from 19 oz. to 3.3 qt., so you can mix and match to suit your needs.

Why choose between extra seating or more storage when you can have both? This sturdy little pouf hides a compartment that I use for an extra throw blanket, but it could also fit a few games, your knitting supplies, or remote controls. The cushioned top is taut enough that it can also function as a side table, making this a small space triple threat.

Head to IKEA to find storage that maximizes space without sacrificing style.

#6816. Ben Ahlers Teases Jack and Bridget’s “Tangible, Objective Obstacle” in The Gilded Age Season 4

Does entering his gentleman era mean leaving her behind?

The rise of Jack Trotter—or as the internet calls him, “Clock Twink”—has been one of The Gilded Age’s most rewarding storylines. He started as a humble footman in the Van Rhijn household and got rich practically overnight after inventing an affordable alarm clock—all while somehow avoiding becoming a terrible person. He is one of the easiest characters on the show to root for. Jack could do practically anything onscreen and I would be thrilled.

His will-they-won’t-they relationship with Bridget, one of the Van Rhijn household’s maids, is part of that. Fans have been hoping for these two to get together for multiple seasons now. But after a close call last season, they seem further apart than ever. The actor behind Jack, Ben Ahlers, chatted with Cosmopolitan about what season 4 has in store for this maybe-couple and whether Jack will be able to stay true to himself as he climbs the social ladder.

What's so interesting about this whole world is the public and private self, and Jack has become a master of that. He has a private self downstairs in the Van Rhijn household as the trickster, the one who can poke at Armstrong or keep the vibe going when everybody's having a long day. My accent would change between the two, upstairs and downstairs, over the last few seasons. But now he's in a completely different scenario where he doesn't have that family. He doesn't have the private self. As he's stepping into these new worlds with inherently manipulative, distrustful, power-hungry people, there's a level of caution.

You don't become a gentleman overnight. You don't make 300 grand and just become a swaggy dude. There's an acclimating that has to happen, and I really enjoyed playing with that tension. A lot of what you see of him over this season is him trying to find the people and the places where he can reconnect with that beautiful, loving private self.

I think he has an opportunity to more so than anybody because he is carving his own path. He was an orphan who grew up in servitude and then elevated into the upper class. There's no one else who has that track. He has the money and the skill set to provide a life for himself. But he doesn't have the support of Banister patting him on the back to tell him to keep going. It’s going to be a challenge. This isolation and new beginning is a really incredible curriculum for the type of man that I know he can be.

Jack and Bridget have one of the most foundational relationships in his life. It's been a bit nebulous. They were kind of romantic, and then they were friends, and then there are glimmers of maybe something happening at the end of season 3. It's a really unique but relatable challenge that when you're in an interpersonal relationship with that much love, how do you foster change in one another, necessary growth when that doesn't always align? Now they're in two separate classes, and that's going to create a tangible, objective obstacle. And I'm really hopeful for them to find that sense of intimacy and connection, regardless of the sort of stations of their lives.

It's so fun to play in that tension, especially with a great scene partner, because you get to try out different tactics and you get to try it at a different event or a party, and sometimes you connect and then it breaks away again. That's what makes people gravitate towards stories like this, because that expansion contraction internally and interpersonally is the whole bag that all of us are going through every day of our lives.

#6813. How One Mistake Unleashed a Horde of Night of the Living Dead Bootlegs

A simple copyright error allowed George A. Romero’s zombie classic to enter the public domain. For years, the filmmakers fought to get the rights back.

would you rather accidentally set your arm on fire with spilled gasoline or spend decades grappling with a paperwork mistake? Gary Streiner, who personally experienced both while making 1968’s Night of the Living Dead, says there’s no contest: “Oh, believe me, I would take the burn again.”

Streiner was the sound man on George A. Romero’s classic indie zombie flick, but since everyone on the makeshift Pittsburgh project did multiple jobs, he also helped create visual effects, like the fireball on a porch chair that would later engulf his limb. His brother, Russ Streiner, was another multitasker, playing the taunting brother Johnny in the movie’s opening, and serving as jack-of-all-trades co-producer. Both were loyal Romero confidantes who helped him found Image Ten, the production company that created the apocalyptic undead tale.

So both were among those bitten in the ass when Night of the Living Dead accidentally ended up in the public domain due to a copyright mistake that was anything but simple to fix. Even today, it hasn’t entirely been resolved, which is why there is a right way and a wrong way to watch the movie (at least, if you care about seeing it in the best possible format, while also not picking the pocket of the people who made it.)

Today, Romero is gone, and his debut feature is considered an all-time American classic. Stephen King himself calls it the scariest movie he’s ever seen. But the independent film garnered such success partly because it was so widely and freely shared. The friends and colleagues who helped Romero make Night of the Living Dead have finally figured out a way to pull the movie back into their legal possession. But the freebie versions are still out there, so they are hoping fans will be honest and honorable about the version of the film they choose to play this Halloween.

Don’t worry, they aren’t “coming to get you, Barbara,” as Russ intones in the iconic opening of the movie. They are just, once again, asking nicely.

Basically, look for the Criterion Collection logo. The beloved cinema preservation group helped the Streiners restore the original black-and-white negative for the Museum of Modern Art, and by refining the moody imagery as Romero originally intended, they technically created a “new” work that Image Ten could officially claim as their own. You can find it on the Criterion streaming service, but also HBO Max is among those that license their version of the movie.

“All of it’s licensed now. Now we get paid for it. That’s the point, every time it’s screened on any of those platforms,” Gary says.

“There are other streaming channels that aren’t,” adds Russ. If you don’t spot that big, silver C when Night of the Living Dead starts playing, you’re probably watching a bootleg.

The average joe might not care much whether these aging producers or Romero’s estate get their share, but keep in mind that these were average joes too, not Hollywood big shots. They were working stiffs who had a dream, made something immortal (in many senses of the word), and then got stiffed for real.

“To be honest with you,” Russ begins. “George—and I want to measure my words pretty carefully …”

“He was not a great businessman,” Gary cuts in, not measuring his words at all.

“None of us were great businessmen,” Russ adds with a sigh.

The Streiner brothers were toiling away on local Western Pennsylvania commercials when they helped Romero bring his feature film dream together, and their collective work inspired generations of other nobodies to max out their credit cards, load up on cameras and lights, and make a crazy movie with their friends. “It’s fair to say that without George A. Romero, I would not have the career I have now,” Shaun of the Dead and Hot Fuzz filmmaker Edgar Wright wrote when Romero died in July 2017. “A lot of people owe George a huge debt of gratitude for the inspiration. I am just one of many.”

It’s easy enough to find the right version of Night of the Living Dead, and it happens to be the one that looks the best too. Many of the bootlegs are copies of copies of copies. When the Streiners got MoMA and Criterion to revive a new version of the movie, they went back to the original negatives, part of which they possessed, and some of which belonged to Romero’s cowriter. “We gathered up all of the elements from Russ’s basement and John Russo’s garage, and we trekked out to their facility, and we were all quite amazed at the good condition that everything was still in, not having been kept in absolute ideal conditions,” Gary says.

Now it looks as good as it did when the very first prints were sent out into the world. That also happened to be the moment everything went wrong.

You know how old movies have a noticeable copyright tag in their opening credits, usually right under the title? Today, that’s an affectation, used by filmmakers like Quentin Tarantino and Rian Johnson to conjure a feeling of nostalgia. But once upon a time in real Hollywood, that was actually a legal requirement to establish ownership of a film.

Romero and his team understood this, and had it on their initial cut of the movie. The mix-up happened when they were negotiating to get the zombie picture into theaters and struck an agreement with the indie distribution company the Walter Reade Organization. “That was the beginning of our nightmare,” Russ says. “The movie at that time was called Night of the Flesh-Eaters. They didn’t like the title. They said, ‘We’ve got to come up with something new.’ ”

The executives had a point: Night of the Living Dead has a certain ring to it, so Romero and the Streiners agreed. They left the print in Walter Reade’s hands. “They were in charge of changing the title, but when the title got changed, the copyright was left off,” Russ says. “It became their responsibility to deal with their lab, and the copyright notice for Night of the Living Dead went by the wayside.”

No one realized the mistake until the prints were shipped out, and by that point it was too late. “Not that ownership was ever denied,” Gary says. “There’s never been any, ‘Well, no, you didn’t make Night of the Living Dead.’ We made it.”

Under the United States’ 1909 copyright law, this technical mistake just meant no one was legally obligated to account for tickets or pay them a portion of the sale. “That was the start of it, and we’ve been spending tons of money legally to get this thing on its right feet,” Gary adds.

If that seems both unbelievable and unfair, then welcome to the copyright law revision of the mid-1970s that eliminated this requirement. “It’s totally different now,” says Russ. “As a matter of fact, Night of the Living Dead was one of the reasons that the language for the copyright office changed, because it was preposterous.”

But it was too late for the zombie film and the team behind Image Ten, until the new restoration came about from MoMA and the Criterion Collection. The Streiners learned this lesson the hard way, but they were used to that.

Who could have guessed that a simple line of text could cause so much trouble? Well … who could have guessed that when you pour gasoline on a chair for a zombie attack scene that it could somehow also go wrong.

“George didn’t like the way it was looking, and it took about a half hour for him to reset and get the shot that he wanted,” Russ recalls of the infamous incident. “So the chair was put out, and when it came time to do another take in the new camera position, I had been all over that thing diligently making sure that there were no embers or whatever.”

He didn’t think about what was below the surface. “There was no fire on the chair itself, but the interior workings of the chair, the springs and the metal framework, were still hot,” Russ adds. “And when Gary started dousing it with gasoline—BOOM!—it was like an explosion that set him on fire.”

“I’m literally pouring gasoline out of a plastic jug, and the flame shot right up,” Gary says, mimicking the motion.

Spilled gas on his sleeve meant his whole arm was engulfed. “Fortunately, Bill Hinzman, who was a cemetery ghoul, was actually a volunteer fireman, and he had enough common sense to just tackle me and roll me to the ground,” Gary says.

It was over in seconds, with only relatively minor burns that eventually healed. The copyright conflagration took a lot longer to resolve, but now, finally, they don’t feel so scorched by it anymore.

#6809. Is the Fitbit Edge Worth Buying?

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

The future form of the wearable tech is here.

It’s been a pretty big year for Fitbit. In May, the Fitbit Air joined the ever-growing list of no-screen fitness trackers alongside Whoop, and now, not even six months later, I have on my wrist the brand-new Fitbit Edge. It is, as the name suggests, a slimmer fitness tracker. It feels slightly like a step forward, slightly like a step back—a return to form. Let’s say. It’s new, but it’s also a throwback to the slim shape of the (not so) old Fitbit devices like the Charge and Inspire. Importantly, despite being Google’s latest wearable with a screen, it is not trying to be a Pixel Watch. Far from it. Some might complain about what it can’t do, but I’d argue the pared-back nature of the Fitbit Edge is its greatest strength.

At its core, this is the state-of-the-art Fitbit bringing a smooth, responsive modern touchscreen experience to a wearable focused on health tracking. It certainly does more than count your steps, monitor heart rate, and detect REM cycles; the Edge has plenty of smartwatch capabilities. Control your music, check the weather, even read and respond (depending on the phone you have) to messages. But the standard inundation of notifications is replaced by a clean interface that clearly does not like being disturbed. This is the casual fitness tracker for those who value a distraction-free workout.

First things first. I’ve been wearing mine 24/7 for the past couple of weeks, and it’s nothing if not supremely comfortable. Bands are simpler to attach and detach than any other watch I’ve tried, and the new magnet bands are easy to make snug.

From the get-go, the band selection has been excellent. My personal favorite is the magnetic silicone band in Mahogany. It’s got a look that comes off as more upscale than the materials described typically do. Paired with the slim bezel and overall slight shape, it’s a handsome wearable that draws a lot of compliments. I won’t repeat what one friend of mine said, but I’m pretty sure it means she liked it.

The completely revamped Fitbit interface is intuitive and has everything you need just a swipe or tap away by default. You can tinker with the home screen, but having heart rate and total steps, alongside the time and a quick workout start button, displayed by default feels instructional. Everything is readable and I genuinely feel like my mother-in-law could understand how to use it. Like I said, it’s not a Pixel Watch, but it’s certainly taking usability and design cues from Google’s other line of wearables.

As a Fitbit, nearly everything about the Edge is an evolution. The only problem is I’m also comparing it to all the smartwatches out on the market too. I can use literally any other smartwatch in my rotation to tap into my office building with a digital badge, and pay for lunch with Apple Pay or whatever equivalent. With the Edge, no luck on any of these NFC-powered interactions. And because I’m using it with my iPhone, I can read my incoming messages but can’t respond to anything.

On paper, these are flaws, but in reality they allow me to interact with my fitness tracker without getting too distracted. The lack of customizability compared to an Apple or Pixel Watch simply equals less time sitting around and setting up your watch, and hopefully more time going outside and living your life. Which isn’t to say I wasn’t bugged by some of the limitations. The viewable data is not quite as in-depth as some others, and looking at your phone to check your reps sorta ruins the whole distraction-free thing.

In that way, it’s more like a fitness band than a smartwatch. It can track a lot of data on its own, but ultimately the only way to see all of that is to eventually open your phone. For me, that trade-off is worth it to not be getting constant buzzes on my wrist every time I go for a run.

When it comes to fitness tracking, the hardcore still have Garmin. For something more casual, the Fitbit Edge has a great look, and as an Apple Watch user, certain aspects of the simplicity are genuinely refreshing.

#6807. Mckenna Grace Is a Bigger ‘Hunger Games’ Fan Than You

The actor has a way of approaching everything dialed up to 100: her work, her relationships, her fangirl enthusiasm. With Sunrise on the Reaping, it really paid off.

Mckenna Grace is operating on two hours of sleep when she opens her Zoom window. Fresh off a night shoot, she is losing her voice and has the beginnings of a black eye from taking an accidental knee to the face. She uses the camera as a mirror to check for damage, joking, “I’m so thankful that this is what I get to do and have my butt kicked on.”

She goes on to enthusiastically detail how her days on set have been filled with snake wranglers, poison ivy, and feral kittens found in the woods. It’s all very Hunger Games–coded and very fitting, of course, considering Mckenna stars in the upcoming Sunrise on the Reaping as Maysilee Donner, a snarky tribute from the fictional world of Panem’s District 12 (Mckenna also plays Maysilee’s twin sister, Merrilee, in the movie).

It’s an adventure and not one without risk, but she is very much here for it, having spent most of her life throwing herself—literally—into the universes she loves. From Scream to Ghostbusters to The Hunger Games, Mckenna has been working on her favorite franchises since she was 5 years old (“I grew up on sets, out of a suitcase,” she shares). Her IMDb page is already longer than a CVS receipt, with eight credits in 2025 alone, several in 2026, and the soon-to-premiere Netflix series Scooby-Doo: Origins, in which she plays Daphne. (If you’re curious about just how big a fan of that project Mckenna is, she named her dog, who she’s posing with on her Cosmopolitan cover, Scooby Doo and her cat Scrappy Mew.)

The enthusiasm bleeds into her relationships, too, and comes through in how she speaks about her boyfriend, her Regretting You costar Mason Thames (“my best friend”), and her Sunrise on the Reaping costar Joseph Zada, with whom she spent many nights playing chess while shooting in a remote village in Spain (“I beat him constantly. Put it in print”). Because one thing about the 20-year-old is crystal clear: Whatever she decides to tackle, she’ll be going all in.

The one thing it would require is Mckenna Grace. No, but I’m just out here clawing my way through, trying to get jobs and do things I’m proud of. It’s scary because unlike in the ’90s or early 2000s—where your favorite actors did the same thing in a bunch of movies—now with social media, people get really sick of seeing people really fast. It’s like, “This is the hot new commodity, the new face we’ve been wanting.” Three weeks later, everybody is hating on them.

The internet is a big part of the industry but very fickle. There was a time where people wouldn’t give you an interview because you had less than 3 million followers.1 Yet it’s a catch-22 because if you’re too present…but, hey, I’m just thankful to be here. And lately, I’ve been blessed to be able to do these franchises that I’m a huge fan of. I am the biggest Hunger Games fan.

1. Mckenna has a total of 13+ million social media followers.

I was very invested in all of it—the headcanons and the fan base. I had this huge Hunger Games poster. I got a bow and arrows so that I could be like Katniss. I told [director] Francis Lawrence when I got to set: “Dude, I’ve watched these movies and read these books a million times. I’ve edited these cornucopias. To be running off my own podium toward the cornucopia, this is not real to me.”

Why did it have to get back to Josh [Hutcherson] is my thing. I played it so cool for a year and a half of knowing him, and he never brought it up. But everyone keeps reminding him. Just let it die; let a girl have some dignity. I do regret it in a way, but I am also just like, “I am a real fan, a fangirl. I’m a CapCut warrior.”

I keep a journal for my characters with pages dedicated to fan things. For Maysilee, I’m like, Okay, they want to see the braid, so I’d pull Francis aside, like, “Look, man, she needs this braid in her hair; she needs this pin.” He’s like, “Sure, Mckenna.”

She does get a bad rap, and she has that snark to her, but she has a kind heart. She cares about the people she loves.

You think I’m going to slap Glenn Close? Hell no. I am terrified of her in the best way. I love her to death.

At this point, I definitely don’t do nudity or very hypersexual things. I respect anybody who can, but it’s terrifying to me. I don’t know if that’ll ever change. It’s not like I only do wholesome things—my character literally gets gutted by Ghostface in Scream—but my dream is to try and be a Disney princess someday.

As a kid on set, you’re expected to act like an adult until you’re on camera. Then you’re a kid until everybody is mad at you because you’re acting like a kid. Now it’s cool to be an adult and be able to give my opinion and have a bit more ownership over characters. I’ve really enjoyed sitting down with producers and pitching all my ideas.

I always wanted to go to a school dance. When prom season came around, I told all my friends who were single, “I don’t care where you are, I will come to your prom.” I ended up going to three proms. I didn’t know the people there. I just showed up, had a good time, and then dipped.

Your girl is happy. I’m feeling very lovey-dovey. I have somebody I can be a complete nerd with. I got my best friend, and so I don’t see the point in not loving loudly.2

2. Mckenna posted a birthday tribute in July to her boyfriend, Mason Thames, singing “honeybee” by Olivia Rodrigo. One commenter wrote, “This couple is the Gen Alpha Tom Holland and Zendaya.”

There are moments that are just for you and your person. But I don’t see the point in not celebrating who you’re in love with. A lot of people’s hesitation around this stems from the idea that if you post about someone a bunch and then you break up, that’s embarrassing. But why would I even think about that? I’m just going to focus on the present.

It’s a terrifying thing in a relationship to surrender yourself to that thought of, I’m just going to be at my most vulnerable and trust you, and this part of my life is fully in your hands. But I don’t see the point in building a relationship based on fear. I am the biggest fan of the person I’m with, so why wouldn’t I be like, “This is my person. I am so stoked I have this”? We’re always on each other’s sets anyway. He’s like an honorary member of District 12 at this point.

I hope to still be as excited waking up for work every day, even though it’s tiring and I get bruised and half the time people may hate me for things I can’t control. I’m thankful to still be feeling that way 15 years in, so I hope that 25 years in, I feel the exact same way.

3. For her birthday, Mckenna was supposed to go to the aquarium with her parents and Mason. Her shooting schedule ran too late, so her mom and Mason waited up to surprise her in shark onesies instead.

If I’m 80 and people are like, “Oh, you’re the girl from The Hunger Games,” I’ll be like, “Yes, I am. I did that. That’s so cool.”

#6806. Patrick Stewart Remembered as a Colossus of Stage and Screen

“He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love,” Ian McKellen shared following the actor’s death.

Actor, writer, and activist Sir Patrick Stewart died on Wednesday. He was 86. In a statement issued via his social media on October 29, his family wrote that the Star Trek star and renowned Shakespearean thespian left us following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. “He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion, and humanity he brought to every role—in his art and life,” the statement read.

Since the news surfaced, an outpouring of grief rippled from his closest colleagues and collaborators. Notable among them, Sir Ian McKellen, a true friend and screen partner of Stewart’s for over 50 years across stage and film, wrote an emotional tribute to Stewart over social media.

“Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end,” McKellen wrote. “He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.”

In 1987, Stewart was already a renowned stage actor in the UK with a handful of credits in movies like Excalibur and David Lynch’s Dune when he landed his star-making role: Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation. The series ran until 1994 and made Stewart a household name. Then, he starred in the summer blockbuster X-Men (2000), playing mentor Charles Xavier with McKellen opposite him as Xavier’s once-close friend turned philosophical antagonist, Magneto.

Fellow actors who worked with Stewart across Star Trek, Marvel, and beyond also penned tributes and personal anecdotes in memory of Stewart. The Next Generation co-star LeVar Burton wrote in a public statement: “He was family. There is no other context in which to hold him that makes sense. I am lucky to have known and loved so many of the facets of a soul so rich in talent and generous of heart. Of all the dames and knights I’ve known, he was deep down the silliest.”

Hugh Jackman, who starred in several X-Men installments with Stewart—including their acclaimed 2017 hit Logan—wrote on Instagram: “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”

Television creator Seth MacFarlane, a noted Trekkie who cast Stewart in a handful of bit parts across Family Guy, American Dad, and his 2012 R-rated comedy Ted, said Stewart was “that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful.”

Wrote MacFarlane: “I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day 1 of a new film. He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, ‘Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed.’ We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend.”

Dafne Keen, who worked with Stewart extensively in Logan as a child actress, remembered the late performer on her Instagram: “He was such a kind, genuine, funny, unique, caring and charming man. I remember his endless jokes, nurturing nature and colourful reading glasses. Every single day spent working by his side was an honour and a privilege I can’t quite believe I had. He was a walking master of his craft, and of life. One of the greatest of our time, on stage and on screen.”

She continued, “I will forever hold those months we spent together close to my heart, and will always think of him as a pivotal part of how I view the world around me.”

Shortly after the news of Stewart’s passing broke, players on Star Trek Online gathered in the game’s social areas to hold a virtual vigil in Stewart’s honor.

Below, you can read more social media remembrances from Stewart’s many colleagues and creative partners, as well as theaters that were lucky enough to have Stewart grace their stages. As Jean-Luc Picard once said, “Make now always the most precious time. Now will never come again.”

#6805. 8 Fresh Ways to Wear Corduroy Pants—To Work, on the Weekend, and Beyond

Like clockwork, corduroy pants make their initial cameo in the early fall. This year, however, they’re also having a moment on the runway—and in the latest street style. A mainstay at The Row—available in a variety of pant shapes—this season featured a handful looks built around the pant, starting off with a bright white pair and a little black jacket, following a light brown pant with sharp tailoring. At Tory Burch, a low-slung trouser with wide whale in a mustard hue stole the show, teamed up with light blue shirting and a wool sweater. At Isabel Marant, corduroys got a striking update in cobalt blue.

Throughout fashion month, we saw various sightings of corduroy—at times as a pant alone, other times as a full set. What makes the textured pant so compelling is its ability to straddle various sensibilities: classic yet of the moment; polished yet unpretentious, textural yet easy to style. As far as choosing your own pair goes, you can lean into fall’s playful mood by experimenting with bold hues or stay seasonally on theme with an earthy shade. We’ll show you it works with both, below.

Inspired by The Row’s runway, pair white corduroy pants with a cropped black jacket. Ground the look with white booties, and keep jewelry to a minimum.

The second look of Tory Burch’s fall collection featured corduroys, inspired by those her father wore. Follow the runway’s styling and pair it with a colored button-up, woven belt, and chunky wool knit. Bonus points for a playful tote.

Go all in on color, taking cues from the Celine runway, by pairing a red sweater with burgundy corduroys for a bold color story. Finish with a tan bag and a pair of black leather wedge boots.

Put all your essentials to work in one streamlined look; the addition of black corduroy pants gives it welcome contrast.

Add a bit of western flair to your fall corduroys by pairing them with a plaid shirt, a vintage-inspired belt, and some cowboy boots.

Dress up dark cords with a blazer and brooch for a Thursday dinner—your choice of loafers or boots to complete the look.

For a weekend spent wandering museums, the corduroy trouser can take you from 9 to 9. Style yours with a grey sweater, then add fresh accessories like a silver pendant and a little white shoe.

Why not make blue corduroy pants your denim alternative? Toughen them up as you would any pair of jeans with a leather jacket, snakeskin boots, and shield sunglasses.

#6804. How to Master Layering Clothes This Fall

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Some might call layering clothes an art. But whether you have a natural talent for it or not, one thing is certain: The best layered fall outfits always start with a good foundation of basics.

“I love layering because it allows us to dive into our closet favorites and think of new ways to play with beloved pieces, creating personality and depth to our looks,” stylist Sarah Slutsky Tooley tells Bazaar. “It makes outfits more versatile, allows us to extend the lifeline of our clothes, and helps us master the tricky 40-degree chilly morning and still be comfortable as the day hits its sunny high.”

Slutsky Tooley has a few personal tips to get the most out of those favorites. “Don’t be afraid to layer category sisters,” she says. “I love a denim jacket layered with a leather jacket, showing a range of textures and scale. The trick is making sure the proportions are complementary.” She also recommends layering a black or white T-shirt under an oversize sweater so that you have options to peel away. “It has an effortless cool about it—very the Row.”

As we combed through the most recent street-style looks from Fashion Month, a myriad of outfit formulas went straight to our Saved folder for inspiration. Use our guide below as your personal master class on layering, featuring ten outfit ideas that demonstrate how to layer clothes like a pro this fall.

Band jackets were everywhere during Fashion Month. Layer yours the modern boho way, styling an army green version over a cream ruffled blouse with relaxed blue jeans—a little Sergeant Pepper, a little Penny Lane, and all the right attitude. Pointy black boots and tinted aviator sunglasses complete the look with a little rock ‘n’ roll edge.

Minimalists can wear color, too—and this showgoer proves that a pop of red goes a long way. Layer a bright short-sleeved knit over a crisp white button-down, then pair with a midi pencil skirt for a polished work outfit. Pointed-toe pumps and Prada’s Carry mini bag lend a refined finish, while keeping the look on-trend with some of fall 2026’s best accessories.

Playing with varying necklines is one stylish technique Slutsky Tooley champions, as this look shows how chic it can be. By adding a gray crewneck T-shirt underneath a navy V-neck sweater with relaxed jeans, you get a little extra texture and contrast. Square-toed shoes and a brown shoulder bag add off-duty finishing touches.

Don’t be afraid to lean into maximalist prints when layering. Contrasting prints come together beautifully when you stick to a tonal color palette. A paisley velvet jacket layered over a silky leopard-print blouse strikes the right balance of rich textures and bold pattern, while straight-leg jeans, a simple black shoulder bag, and peep-toe mules keep the look grounded.

The street-style set knows that a little extra texture and color can go a long way, especially with a knit casually thrown around the neckline—a trick we see season after season. Bring life to an oversized brown blazer, flared jeans, and black accessories with a chunky red cable-knit cardigan artfully tied over the shoulders for an effortlessly layered look.

For a bold, unconventional take on layering, try a blue poplin shirt layered under a sleeveless leather tunic top. We’ve already highlighted how contrasting textures reap stylish results, so this is one way to take the idea one step further. Double down on the textural contrast with leather straight-leg pants, then keep accessories subdued with classic loafers and a brown suede top-handle handbag.

Collarless jackets were the sleeper hit of Fashion Month (especially peplum ones). This fall, try styling a white crewneck T-shirt underneath that peeks out ever so slightly along the collar. Classic accessories like a structured top-handle bag and high-vamp pumps keep the look polished and pulled together.

Layering is all about the element of surprise. Start with the basics—a white tank top under a striped button-down, topped with an oversized blazer and relaxed straight-leg jeans. It all seems straightforward until you wrap a contrasting, bright striped top around the neck for an unexpected jolt of color and pattern.

For a more directional take, trade your classic moto jacket for a brown leather gilet to make more of a statement. Layer it over a washed black T-shirt and menswear-inspired trousers in a similar tone, then add a studded belt around the waist. Take the look a step further with a matching faded long-sleeved top tied below the belt for a multi-tiered layered effect.

Break up neutrals with a vibrant color. One way to do this is to layer a fitted red turtleneck under a cobalt crewneck. It works especially well within an all-black, gray, or navy outfit. The layered pieces instantly give any look, like this tailored jacket and indigo jeans outfit, a little extra punch.

#6803. For His 40th Birthday, Drake Flexed a Custom Rolex and a $250,000 Watch in the Space of 24 Hours

The rapper marked his milestone birthday with two extravagant timepieces, including a one-of-a-kind Daytona worth millions.

Turning 40 is a milestone worth celebrating in style. And to nobody's surprise, Drake did just that.

As you'd expect, the Canadian rapper's birthday outfit was not exactly understated. In fact, his watch rotation featured not one, but two rather extraordinary Rolexes. Why settle for one when you can have two?

The first was a custom, sapphire-covered Daytona, while the second was a colorful Day-Date 36 with a reported six-figure price tag. There are certainly worse ways to welcome a new decade.

First up was the Rolex Cosmograph Daytona, a watch that makes even the most extravagant diamond-set timepieces look positively modest. The one-of-a-kind creation features a diamond-pavé dial, brilliant blue sapphire hour markers, and a bezel set with baguette-cut blue sapphires. But the real showstopper is the bracelet, which is covered in a gradient of blue sapphires that gradually fade into diamonds.

And if all those precious stones weren't enough to make your eyes water, the estimated price tag certainly might. The one-of-a-kind creation has reportedly been valued at anywhere between $2 million and $5 million. Although, given that Rolex made just one, it's difficult to put an exact figure on it.

While you might assume the rapper had commissioned the watch especially for his big birthday, he actually debuted it back in August. Still, when you've got something quite this spectacular sitting in your watch collection, it would be a shame not to give it another outing.

The second Rolex was a rather different kind of extravagance. Drake also showed off a rose-gold Day-Date 36 featuring the brand's famously playful puzzle dial. Instead of traditional hour markers, baguette-cut sapphires surround a dial made up of brightly colored jigsaw pieces. And rather than displaying the usual day and date, the apertures reveal inspirational words and emojis, including a little red heart. It's about as far from your grandfather's Rolex as you can get.

The watch has been valued at around $250,000 which, rather remarkably, makes it the considerably cheaper of Drake's two birthday watches.

Of course, Drake has never been one for doing things by halves, particularly when it comes to watches. And while most people would be more than happy to receive a single Rolex for their 40th, it seems the rapper couldn't quite settle on one.

#6802. Maya Hawke’s Guide to Joining a Global Fandom (Again)

The Stranger Things and Inside Out 2 alum thought she knew what it was like to be a part of a major franchise. Then came Sunrise on the Reaping.

It’s Maya Hawke’s day off. But you wouldn’t know it based on what she’s done so far: a few hours of making flash cards for an upcoming project followed by a full slate of meetings, one per hour. Now we’re at dinner in New York City, talking about her role as the brilliant, unconventional victor Wiress in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

Stepping into a beloved pop culture franchise is nothing new for the 28-year-old multi-hyphenate (she played both the smart, sarcastic Robin Buckley in Stranger Things and the voice of the perpetually frazzled Anxiety in Inside Out 2). Neither is existing in a curious state of constant motion. In the past year alone, Maya has released a folk-pop album, Maitreya Corso; filmed and appeared in multiple TV and film projects; served as a Prada brand ambassador; and gotten married to singer-songwriter Christian Lee Hutson.

Yet beneath the impressive velocity, Maya is interested in all the quiet she can get. “I’m working on being a little less busy,” she says. “Doing half as much twice as well is my current goal.” For now, she’s still able to wander museums and walk through New York without the celebrity disguise of sunglasses and a baseball hat. She’s soaking it in because she knows that come this winter, she’ll be under an arena-size spotlight thanks to Sunrise on the Reaping—and that for her, everything might be about to change.

I am the great joiner! On Stranger Things, I was joining a cast that had done the first two seasons. That held a different kind of weight. With this film, everyone had this newness to them. We are all in it together and will sink or swim as a team. There’s something relaxing about that.

Elle’s Effie is amazing. People are going to lose their minds. I was like, Whoa, that’s how you step on set! I had a different amount to work with. Amanda has three minutes total screen time as Wiress, and what we’ve seen of her character is someone who has been transformed by the events that unfold in Sunrise. We don’t know what she was like before that trauma happened.

I read the book a bunch of times. I rewatched the movies. I was deep in the script. Wiress was not a bright-eyed Capitol kid. She’s a tribute fresh off her win, which she accomplished in a really unusual way. She didn’t hurt anybody. Someone who wins the Games without betraying their moral compass is an extremely special person.

How much power corrupts. It’s not the person in power; it’s what power does to the person. That’s a very clear thesis that runs through the whole story. To make something that is both popular and anti-fascist is pretty crazy. What the books and films are doing is like protest art in a pretty explicit way.

I can get really nervous when I realize how much attention is on something like this. If I start looking at whether people are happy about the casting and the discourse that follows, it’s like the Eye of Sauron. I’m working on caring less about that.

1. Maya’s cowriting contributions are also featured on Phoebe Bridgers’s latest album, Lost Weekend.

The scene when she comes out of her coma—the whole crew got quiet; you could hear a pin drop. When nobody breathes, everyone knows that magic is happening. It grounded me to earth like a big tree. It woke me up. Like a little arrow saying, “Go that way.” And I’ve been following it ever since.

In the beginning of my career, when I was balancing fashion and acting, I had a boyfriend once call me an “AMW”—an actress, model, whatever. The “whatever” was so charged. I had some embarrassment around it. And I wanted to be like, “I’m not a model.” But I didn’t like “actress.”

When I go to Milan to work with Mrs. Prada and Raf Simons, I consistently feel good about myself. Even my husband pointed it out. I was recently auditioning for a project where the character needed to be really confident and he was like, “Be who you are when we go to Milan.”

I filmed Hunger Games and One Night Only back-to-back. They each have these two sorts of apocalyptic fascist governments. My joke on the set of Hunger Games was like, “Beetee,2 we have to have sex right now. We’ve got two hours—let’s go!” Government control in your bed? Horrible. The idea of taking it to that degree is just repellent. I want to be able to explore love on my terms. Bedtime TV, sex, kissing, and love. I mean, who would I be without these things? It would be punishment and torture.

2. Beetee Latier, played by Kelvin Harrison Jr., is an inventor and fellow former victor from District 3 who returns to the arena with Wiress for the Third Quarter Quell. Jeffrey Wright originally portrayed the character.

I consider myself a hopeless romantic. The closest we get to magic is what can happen between two people. Until I actually fell in love with my husband, I was falling in love all the time. I fall in love with my friends every day. I love them very romantically, like how can we spend Christmas together romantically and familially? My biggest heartbreaks of my life have been friendships ending.

It hits different because when you fall in love in a romantic way with someone, some part of you understands that there is a chance that it might expire. There are a lot of things that have to go right for it to work. But with a friendship, you don’t go in with that armor up. You go in so vulnerable, and when it doesn’t work, it’s the biggest tears I’ve ever shed. I hesitate to say this because it’s embarrassing, but I talk about my biggest friendship heartbreak from high school at least monthly, probably weekly. It was really formative.

I’m not going to lie and be like, “I never for one second considered it.” I genuinely thought about it. But the only thing I’ve known that I wanted to do on my wedding day since I was a kid was walk with the whole wedding party.

And they were, to their credit, extremely noninvasive. No one saw them. No one was upset by it. No one got hurt. I was kind of happy that those photographs ran in People because I had thought about doing a story about the dress. I worked with Prada, so it felt like a way to honor them without having to go out in public and say, “Look at me.”

I am not egomaniacal enough to think I will ever not be in my post–Stranger Things era. It will always be a beautiful shadow of my life. I will still consider myself to be in the aftermath of these experiences.

Exactly. I will sign posters until the day I die. Happily so.

#6801. Zara’s New Arrivals Have Fall and Winter Dressing Covered

If you’ve been waiting for an excuse to refresh your winter wardrobe before the holiday season kicks into high gear, Zara’s latest arrivals offer plenty of them. The Spanish retailer has been particularly busy lately, rolling out everything from party-ready pieces and fashion-forward workwear to cozy staples and new designer collaborations.

One of the key moments this week is the latest iteration of Zara’s partnership with Caramel London, the British label known for its playful prints and slightly nostalgic aesthetic. The new collection is filled with versatile separates, printed dresses, and charming accessories.

There are also still standout pieces available from last week’s fall/winter 2026 Studio release, Zara’s limited-edition line of premium-feeling fabrics and intricate details. This time around, the assortment feels especially suited to the holidays, with lace, jacquard-like textures, and embroidery appearing alongside a rich palette of tobacco, oxblood, and chocolate brown.

That translated into velvet dresses ready for party season, sequin wrap skirts that can make even office dressing feel festive, and textured coats that do the heavy lifting over otherwise simple winter outfits. Beyond Studio, Zara’s main collection is making a strong case for refreshing your 9-to-5 wardrobe with tie-detail blouses and collarless blazers, while trendy outerwear (think: funnel-neck jackets), corduroy pants, and other cold-weather essentials cover the winter staples category.

And then there are pieces designed for after you clock out. Weekend-ready separates abound, alongside statement skirts finished with sequins, lace trim, and prints. Festive accessories provide the finishing touch, from metallic shoes to satin clutches and drawstring pouches that can transform your most reliable little black dress into a spotlight-worthy look.

Whether you’re shopping for the office, a holiday party, or a Saturday afternoon, Zara’s new arrivals make a case for embracing more texture, color, and sparkle this season. Our favorite picks from the drop, ahead.

#6799. Is Walton Goggins Leaving Fallout?

"Just took it off for the last time" the actor wrote in a cryptic social media post.

Walton Goggins may have just said goodbye to Fallout. Though Prime Video hasn’t made any announcements yet about wrapping production on the upcoming third season, Goggins posted a video to social media on Thursday, October 29, that alludes to the end of his time on the video game adaptation. At least, that’s what we think it means...

“Just took it off for the last time.. Season 3… Gatdamn this felt good,” Goggins captioned a video of himself driving through the California desert, lip-syncing to “Ramble On” by Led Zeppelin. “I wish this road or this song would never end,” he continued. “Gonna miss you California… til the next time. #Fallout.”

While it’s clear that Goggins is finished with season 3, his phrasing implies that he’s wrapped on Fallout entirely. “Just took it off for the last time” sounds like a permanent goodbye for The Ghoul—his gun-slinging character from the Fallout series who is transformed into a post-apocalyptic mutant. His caption could also imply that Fallout season 3 marks the end of the series, though that would be a bit of a stretch considering the show’s sustained popularity and acclaim. Prime Video has yet to comment.

Whatever Goggins means by “the last time,” at least we know now that Fallout season 3 is closer than ever. It’s been a long year since season 2 premiered on Prime Video, with the finale releasing in January earlier this year.

Fans are dying to see what will become of Lucy (Ella Purnell), Maximus (Aaron Moten), and everyone’s favorite noseless bounty hunter. In the season 2 finale, Lucy’s father, Hank (Kyle MacLachlan), triggered a switch that made him lose all memory of himself and his time at Vault-Tec. That couldn’t have come at a worse time, as Caesar’s imposing Legion approaches the ruins of New Vegas. As for Goggins’ Cooper Howard, he’s on his way to Colorado, chasing the slim chance his family may still be alive.

In January, Goggins told Esquire that Cooper is in the pursuit of hope, odds be damned. “What happens [to the Ghoul] is what happens to all of us, which is we hope," he said. "Even before we had language, [we had hope] of finding warmth or shelter or what's on the other side of that rock. That's just who we are as people.”

Let’s hope that Goggins’ time on Fallout isn’t the end. But if it is, he better get the greatest send-off we’ve ever seen on television.

#6798. Beauty Marks: The Best Beauty Looks of the Week

Welcome back to Beauty Marks: Vogue’s weekly edition of the best moments in celebrity beauty, from Vogue editors’ IG feeds, and all the glam of the fashion and pop culture landscapes. Each week, we curate the nail art to pin for your next nail appointment, new recruits to ‘Team Bob’, and major red carpet moments from the week’s most glamorous affairs. As always, it’s as much about celebrity beauty as it is about the makeup artists, hairstylists, and nail artists, as well as the creators crafting the trends you’re about to see everywhere.

This week, beauty was all about making an impression. From Chappell Roan’s fiery Titian-red waves and Lily Allen’s lash-grazing bangs to Amandla Stenberg’s sculptural kiss curl, hair took on a particularly theatrical turn. Elsewhere, Doechii made a case for head-to-toe glitter, Charli XCX doubled down on smoky, indie-sleaze eyes, and Nara Smith brought frosted lids back into focus. Whether borrowing from the beauty archives or pushing things somewhere more experimental, there was plenty to look at.

Scroll through the week’s best of celebrity beauty and pop culture’s glam below, and head to the app to vote for your favorite.

For the second night of her Super Graphic Spectacular benefit shows in Los Angeles, Chappell Roan leaned into a more romantic, Pre-Raphaelite kind of beauty, all while keeping that theatrical glam. Hairstylist Virginie Pineda created a custom-colored wig in a fiery, coppery Titian red, styled in cascading, tousled waves with a wispy, curled fringe framing her face.

Makeup artist Dee Carrion complemented the look with a dreamy wash of iridescent lilac and mint across the lids, exaggerated black feline flicks, fluttering lashes, and a delicate flash of white liner. A softly sculpted, peachy complexion, and warm terracotta lips brought some warmth.

Nara Smith makes the case for the return of frosted lids. Makeup artist Lake Sanu created a dreamy, luminous look that was all about light-catching textures: shimmering champagne-pink eyeshadow, glossy, high-shine cheekbones, softly flushed coral cheeks, and a diffused, cocoa-toned nude lip. The secret to that almost wet-look glow? Dior Beauty’s Forever Glow Luminizer in the limited-edition Sun-Kissed 003 shade, swept across the high points of the face.

Hairstylist Kendra Alia crafted a softly swept-up style and delicate, face-framing bangs.

McKenna Grace indulged in some method glam this week. On the New York press trail for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the actor, who plays a young Maysilee Donner, paid homage to the franchise’s original heroine, Katniss Everdeen, with a braided crown hairstyle that recalled one of Jennifer Lawrence’s most memorable looks. Hairstylist Glenn Coco wove a delicate blonde braid across the crown of her sleek, center-parted lengths, while makeup artist Tuddy Nanna added sharp black winged liner, rosy flushed cheeks, and a soft pink lip.

Old Hollywood glamour is a go for AnnaSophia Robb. For the Los Angeles premiere of I Play Rocky, the actor leaned into a classic screen-siren beauty look, courtesy of hairstylist Clara Leonard, who styled her buttery blonde lengths into glossy, sculpted S-waves with a deep, sweeping side part and plenty of volume. Makeup artist Melissa Hernandez painted a softly smoky, bronze-rimmed eyes, fluttering lashes, rosy cheeks, and a delicate pink-nude lip.

Doechii is bringing body glitter back, back, back. The rapper wore a head-to-toe dusting of shimmer courtesy of makeup artist Chelsea Uchenna and Worship Mina. Her eyelids were coated in frosted silver shadow, offset by dramatically winged liner and thick, fluttering lashes. A metallic, chocolate-brown lip added some ’90s edge. Hairstylist Matthew swept her dark hair into a silver-studded headband with flicked out ends.

Makeup artist Yasmin Istanbouli blended charcoal-gray and soft black shadow across her lids and out toward the temples, creating a hazy effect. Her signature full brows were brushed upwards, while a glossy, rose-brown nude lip and softly luminous skin brought a little polish to the grungy eye makeup. Hairstylist Corey Lee Morrell kept her raven-black lengths loose and voluminous.

For the Wildwood premiere, hairstylists Loftjet and Marcia Hamilton swept the actor’s hair into an ultra-sleek, pulled-back style, with a single, perfectly circular kiss curl positioned high on the forehead. The rest of the beauty look focused on glass-like skin, a wash of rosy blush extending towards the temples, subtly defined eyes, and glossed rose-brown lips.

Hairstylist Byron Morgan styled her chocolate-brown lengths poker-straight and glossy, with a precise side part. Makeup artist Tobi Henney paired elongated, inky black winged liner with feathery lashes, softly shaded taupe lids, honeyed skin, and a muted pinky-brown lip.

Lily Allen went jet-black and full-fringed for her second Melbourne show, with hairstylist Chad Maxwell creating poker-straight, waist-skimming lengths and thick, lash-grazing blunt bangs. Makeup artist Lilly Keys leaned into the mood with kohl-rimmed eyes, spiky lashes, and a glossy nude lip.

Model Zaina Sarah sports some sculptural hair courtesy of George Curran, who fashioned her lengths into a looped, bow-like updo with a trailing ponytail and sharply shaped micro-bangs. Makeup artist Amir paired the futuristic style with exaggerated berry-pink blush swept towards the temples and graphic winged liner.

#6797. Whitney Peak Is Not Online But About to Be Everywhere

She doesn’t read the comments, doesn’t think of herself as a public figure, but still gets followed through airports by screaming teens. Now, as Lenore Dove Baird in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, she’s bracing for a fandom she can’t fully evade.

Whitney Peak was walking home late at night, headphones on, when she saw the fight. A group of people were arguing loudly across the street, and things were getting physical. She ducked in and out of a bodega and was steps from her front door when somebody grabbed her arm. It was one of the women who’d been shouting down the block, now yelling in Whitney’s face.

“You’re that girl from that movie! Can I get a photo?” Everyone crowded into a group selfie, recounts Whitney now, smiling into a cup of coffee. “And then they all went back across the street and continued the fight,” she says.

Whitney, now 23, first broke out in HBO Max’s 2021 Gossip Girl reboot with a lead role as scholarship student Zoya Lott. She went on to play the teenage Becca in Hocus Pocus 2 and has since starred alongside Sabrina Carpenter in the singer’s “Nonsense” video and started a partnership with Chanel. It’s a résumé that means sometimes people pause fistfights to speak to her, and sometimes packs of adolescents charge after her through airports.

“There was a group of 13-year-old girls, and they were adorable,” she says of another recent encounter. “I was walking ahead of them with my headphones on and they ran up behind me, so all I could feel was the stomping.”

In hindsight, it’s all been a preview of the fandom Whitney is about to meet with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. In the film, she plays Lenore Dove Baird, a fierce, musical girl whose great love is Haymitch Abernathy. (Fans know Haymitch as Katniss Everdeen’s weary mentor, but in this story, he’s a teenager who is separated from Lenore Dove when he’s forced into being a tribute for the 50th Hunger Games.) But despite all the excitement around the movie—and Whitney’s nearly half a million Instagram followers—she says she’s not super online, and she insists, “I don’t carry myself as a public figure. I never think about my career as a whole—I feel like I just got here.”

Even so, the fuss over this latest role will undoubtedly still shape her life in some way. Maybe that’s the strange bargain of playing characters people love: You can choose not to live online, but the work follows you into the world.
