#6795. Toxic Friendship: How to Spot One—and What to Do About It

When Alexa met Amelia at an event, she felt an instant kinship. They had so much in common—they were both in their mid-30s, both working at wellness startups, and both reeling from recent breakups. They exchanged numbers and started texting immediately. Their first “date” was at a neighborhood wine bar where they sipped vermouth and commiserated about the terrible thrill of being single again. Soon after, they were hanging out all the time—pilates on Tuesday mornings, dinner on Friday nights, takeout in Alexa’s living room on hungover Sunday afternoons. “We were so alike and in such similar life stages; our friendship felt almost cosmically aligned,” Alexa says.

That is, until about a year in, when Alexa started to sense that something about their dynamic wasn’t quite right. For one, Amelia’s problems had started to dominate their conversations—how much she hated her new boss, how she thought her new apartment was a dump, how frustrated she was that yet another guy she liked hadn’t texted her back. It seemed like her grievances were all they ever talked about now.

“It was all legitimate and I wanted to be supportive, but I started to feel drained whenever we hung out,” Alexa explains. “She rarely asked how I was, and if she did, somehow the topic always shifted back to herself. I started to feel like a therapist, not a best friend.”

Still, Alexa stuck it out. She figured everyone has bad months, and, anyway, they used to have so much fun. Maybe things would turn around. Then, Alexa landed a new job: a top position at her dream company. Naturally, Amelia was the first person she called. “I expected her to be excited for me, but all she said was, ‘Well, I’m not surprised. I’ve heard they hire anyone.’”

Alexa was stunned. After all, Amelia knew how much time she had spent preparing for each interview; how badly she’d wanted this job. “When I told her my feelings were hurt, she got kind of mad. She said that I was being too sensitive.”

The exchange was a wake-up call. Alexa began reconsidering other moments she’d previously brushed off—how Amelia would sometimes cancel plans last-minute or make little jabs. Had their friendship always been this way? Or had something fundamental changed? And what, exactly, should she do about it?

It’s a familiar dilemma for anyone who’s watched a once-close friendship turn unexpectedly fraught. After all, even the healthiest relationships have their ups and downs. So how do you distinguish a run-of-the-mill rough patch from a truly toxic dynamic? Here, psychologists and relationship experts provide insight on how to navigate the rocky terrain of a toxic friendship.

Even our truest ride-or-dies can occasionally get on our nerves, disappoint us, or say something mean. That doesn’t necessarily mean the relationship is unhealthy. In fact, licensed mental health counselor Carla Haughton says it’s important to remember that “toxic” is a word that gets thrown around a lot: “‘Toxic friendship’ is an everyday description, not a clinical diagnosis,” she notes. “It describes a friendship where harmful behaviors become a recurring pattern: belittling, manipulation, disregard for boundaries, or pressure to put one person’s needs above the other’s.”

Another key distinction, experts say, is how two people handle conflict. In healthy friendships, disagreements can be talked about openly, both people are willing to take responsibility for their actions, and neither one feels like they have to sacrifice who they are in order to maintain the relationship. There’s mutual respect, along with room for personal growth and the occasional bad day or slip-up. “You should be able to say, ‘That hurt me,’ without being humiliated for bringing it up,” Haughton says.

In other words, a toxic friendship is one in which the emotional math isn’t mathing: You give a lot, get little in return, and somehow feel worse about yourself along the way. When that dynamic becomes the rule rather than the exception, it’s worth paying attention.

The tricky thing about toxic friendships is that the red flags aren’t always crystal clear. Sometimes they arrive in the form of a weird compliment, a joke at your expense, or jealousy about spending time with other people. When those things happen once in a while, they can seem pretty innocuous. But when they happen again and again, they can take a toll.

“We picture toxic friendships as loud and volatile, with fight after fight, but it’s much quieter than that,” explains Dr. Paulette Didia, a licensed clinical psychologist. “It is as if there are two people in the room but only enough oxygen for one.”

One especially tell-tale sign is when you begin changing your behavior to accommodate the other person. Maybe you hesitate to share good news because you know they’ll find a way to rain on your parade. Or you find yourself laughing along with jokes that sting or carefully rehearsing what you’ll say because you anticipate criticism or competition. Haughton calls this “editing your happiness.”

Sometimes, however, the most revealing clue is really just the way you feel after you’ve spent time with this friend. Do you go home feeling cherished, supported, inspired, and energized, or do you leave feeling anxious, exhausted, pathetic, and sad? “The sign isn’t necessarily that your friend does something obviously wrong. Sometimes the sign is that you may be hiding or changing parts of yourself in order to maintain the friendship,” Didia explains.

Obviously, spending time with someone who regularly criticizes, dismisses, or undermines you can make you feel pretty crappy—and sometimes, that can lead to a sense of self-doubt that seeps into other areas of your life. You might begin second-guessing even the most mundane decisions—like the wording of a text—or feeling stressed about interactions that once seemed effortless. “When you spend enough time in a relationship where your feelings are minimized, you may eventually begin minimizing them yourself,” explains Dr. Dani Renée Moye, a licensed marriage and family therapist.

The effects can be especially insidious because they often develop gradually. A person who once felt confident may begin scrutinizing the way they show up in all their relationships. They might apologize unnecessarily, struggle to assert their needs, or become increasingly dependent on gaining approval. “The damage can show up in the questions you start asking yourself,” Haughton says. “‘Was that hurtful?’ becomes ‘Am I too difficult to be friends with?’”

If a friendship consistently makes you blue, it seems wise to simply end it. But, as anyone who’s ever struggled with a complicated relationship knows, it’s rarely that simple. For starters, even a toxic friendship can have good times—there might still be fun nights out, heart-to-heart talks, and moments of true connection.

The result can become a case of cognitive dissonance in its purest form—you might constantly be trying to reconcile this seemingly great person with behavior that feels no bueno: Well, she did buy concert tickets for my birthday and make a big deal about getting the cake she knows I love; she can’t be that terrible of a friend.

Then, there’s the emotional pull of shared history. Unlike a relatively new acquaintance, a longtime friend may have witnessed some of the most significant moments of your life—breakups, divorces, childbirth, health scares, everything. They know your sister, remember your old boyfriends, and have every hilariously embarrassing story memorized from decades ago. Walking away from them can feel like walking away from an earlier version of yourself.

But sometimes the reasons we don’t want to leave a friendship can go even deeper. According to relational expert Jola Jovani, embodying certain roles within a friendship can make an unhealthy dynamic feel strangely rewarding. “You might have taken on a role like ‘the mom’ or ‘the saviour’ in the friendship and this can make you feel special or needed even if you do not receive the same consideration or support,” she explains.

In other words, being the person someone always turns to for advice or reassurance can provide a sense of purpose—even when the relationship is decidedly one-sided. These tendencies can have deep roots. According to psychologist and marriage and family therapist Stacey Simmons, people who learned early in life to earn affection through caregiving, people-pleasing, or self-sacrifice may find themselves repeating that dynamic in adult friendships. “When patterns feel familiar we think they’re normal,” she explains.

Then there’s the prospect of actually ending the friendship. Unlike romantic breakups, a friendship breakups rarely come with an established script. There is no acceptable “It’s not you, it’s me” for besties. Worse, a friendship rift can have consequences for an entire social circle, especially if the two of you have a ton of mutual friends. “Leaving a toxic friendship can be very lonely,” Simmons says. “The security of having a friend is gone, and the only one who understood the dynamic is you.”

Thankfully, a friendship that’s gone rogue isn’t always beyond repair. But as with any relationship, salvaging it requires both people to acknowledge what’s happening and be willing to change.

Moye encourages first distinguishing between a temporary rupture and a destructive pattern. The former might involve an insensitive comment, a misunderstanding, or a disagreement that can be resolved through honest communication. The latter occurs when the same hurtful behavior continues despite repeated attempts to address it. It’s a cycle, not a one-off.

Of course, both situations might require having a potentially uncomfortable conversation. But rather than making sweeping accusations about your friend’s character—you’re always such a Debbie Downer!—experts recommend identifying specific behaviors and explaining how they affect you. For example, you might say, “I care about you, but when you make jokes at my expense, it hurts my feelings, and I need that to stop,” suggests licensed marriage and family therapist Kati Morton.

Establishing boundaries is also helpful. That can look like refusing to engage in conversations that become disrespectful, limiting how much support you’re able to provide, or making it clear that certain topics are off-limits. Crucially, a boundary should also establish what you will do if the behavior continues. For instance, you might explain that you’ll end a conversation if your friend continues making snide comments about your weight, hair, boyfriend, green juice habit, or whatever it is that’s been bumming you out.

Your friend might not love this. They might even get a little defensive. But what matters most is what happens next: Do they reflect on what you’ve said, take accountability, and make an effort to change? Or do they dismiss your concerns and go about their day? “An apology is a beginning; repair is what happens in the interactions afterward,” Haughton says.

Sometimes, despite your best efforts, a friendship simply can’t be repaired. But before making the decision to part ways, Moye suggests asking yourself a few questions: “Have I communicated my concerns clearly? Has this person demonstrated a willingness to understand my experience? Am I remaining in this friendship because of who we are today, or because of who we used to be?”

As for the actual breakup, there’s no one-size-fits-all approach. Depending on the situation, you might gradually fade out, create distance, redefine the friendship, or have a direct conversation explaining your decision to move on.

For those who prefer a straightforward approach, Morton suggests something along the lines of, “This friendship hasn’t felt healthy for me for a while, and I think I need some space.” You don’t need to convince your friend that they’re responsible for the relationship’s demise—in fact, it might be better to simply communicate your decision clearly and compassionately without rehashing every past disagreement or assigning blame.

If you find yourself missing your friend afterward, that’s understandable. Much like a romantic breakup, ending a friendship can involve a lot of grief—not only for the relationship itself, but also for the memories, rituals, and future experiences you’d imagined. It can also bring up a complicated swirl of emotions, including sadness, anger, guilt, regret, and even relief. But as Moye puts it, “You can honor what a friendship once meant to you without continuing to participate in what it has become.”

Which brings us to one final point worth considering: Sometimes you’re the one contributing to an unhealthy dynamic. It’s an idea no one likes to consider, but experts say it deserves some honest reflection. After all, nobody navigates every relationship perfectly. We can all be jealous, self-absorbed, defensive, or inconsiderate at times without realizing how our behavior impacts others. “Having unhealthy behaviors doesn’t necessarily make you a ‘toxic person,’” Didia assures. “We all mess up sometimes, especially with our friends who (hopefully) get to see all sides of us.”

Being willing to recognize our not-so-cute behaviors and take responsibility for changing them can make all the difference. Maybe consider how you respond when a friend shares good news. Are you actually happy for them, or do you secretly compare their success with your own? When someone tells you that you’ve hurt their feelings, do you listen and try to understand, or immediately become defensive? And when it comes to emotional support, are you giving as good as you get?

Ultimately, true friendship requires self-awareness, humility, and a willingness to grow on both sides. It’s always easier to point out the ways in which other people mess up instead of holding a mirror up to ourselves.

Alexa eventually came to a similar realization herself. Her friendship with Amelia eventually fizzled out—but not before she had to face a few uncomfortable truths about herself. “I spent so much time ruminating about all the ways she was being a bad friend that I never really considered my own role in the situation,” she says. “I wasn’t really communicating what I needed. I was just kind of expecting her to know. But being a friend sometimes means saying things you’d rather avoid.”

#6793. The Best Rhode Skincare Products, According to Experts

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

I’ve tried every single one of Hailey Bieber’s Rhode products, and these are my all-time favorites

The Hailey Bieber effect is real—from inspiring others to wear pimple patches on their feet to creating a chrome nail craze. If you are staying up to date with her, then you likely already know that Hailey Bieber sold her brand, Rhode, to e.l.f. Beauty for a whopping $1 billion, just a short three years after she launched the brand. Since the sale, the brand has only accelerated, creating viral product after viral product.

While a billion dollars is a lot, the sale doesn’t come as much of a surprise when you consider the popularity of the products. The formulas are fan favorites among those on TikTok, as well as among the Bazaar team. In a sea of celebrity brands, Rhode stands out, partly because Bieber enlisted the help of skincare professionals like cosmetic chemist Ron Robinson, who created his own line, BeautyStat, and New York dermatologist Dhaval Bhanusali to help formulate the products.

“My ethos behind the brand is that we want to make one of everything,” Bieber told Bazaar when the brand launched in 2022. “One really good moisturizer, one really good hydration serum, one really good lip product. I believe in curating your essentials in your closet the same way I believe in curating your essentials in your skincare.”

Rhode now has seven skincare formulas (including the latest Glazing Mist launch) and has even expanded into making creamy blushes, plush lip tints, and shaping lip liners. But the skincare offerings are still at the core of Bieber’s brand. Ahead, our favorite Rhode skin products that are worth the hype and deliver on the promise of Hailey Bieber-worthy glazed doughnut skin.

Rhode’s Glazing Milk is the product that converted me to a Rhode stan. While the milky essence category continues to grow, Rhode was one of the first Stateside brands to jump on the bandwagon.

The Glazing Milk has a lightweight yet creamy consistency. The ingredient list is like a vitamin shot for your skin, featuring a trio of ceramides, beta-glucan to calm the skin, and a blend of magnesium, zinc, and copper that protects your barrier. It’s the perfect hydration base layer for your skincare routine or can be mixed with a foundation to create a DIY skin tint.

It sounds gimmicky that this mask can depuff and sculpt the face, but the caffeine- and peptide-powered formula truly leaves skin firmer, tighter, and brighter in under 10 minutes.

The Peptide Glazing Fluid was one of Rhode’s first products, offering a glimpse into Hailey Bieber’s plumping skincare routine. While hydrating serums sometimes conjure thick, gloopy textures, this formula is more like a light gel that instantly sinks into the skin. It gently hydrates skin, leaving a subtle glow. My skin drinks up this serum, and it’s the perfect layer under makeup or as an extra layer of hydration and plumping before bed.

There’s a reason this cleanser won a Harper’s Bazaar Skincare Award, and why it’s become my go-to cleanser. With most face washes, I still feel dirt, makeup, and grime left on my face even after a thorough scrub, but the lather on this balm-to-foam cleanser is unmatched—it takes the day off in one fell swoop. Pineapple is the star of the show in this cleanser—specifically pineapple enzyme, which sloughs off dead skin—while polyglutamic acid and green tea extract hydrate.

The Peptide Lip Boost, a nourishing lip mask from Rhode, may be our favorite lip formula from the brand. It’s thicker than the Peptide Lip Treatment and feels more like a hefty balm, providing extra hydration and cushion. Plus, it leaves behind a very slight tingle, which feels more refreshing than painful and plumps the lips and softens fine lines.

Ever since Rhode launched its cooling and depuffing eye patches, they have been staples in Bazaar editors’ routines. The patches instantly smooth and depuff the under-eye area, and they don’t budge, so they are perfect for multitasking.

The brand’s latest skincare launch is like an SOS button for parched, irritated skin. A thicker, more hydrating iteration of the brand’s Barrier Restore Cream, the Barrier Butter harnesses the power of hyaluronic acid (utilizing five different molecular weights of the ingredient) and ceramides, along with nourishing, rich murumuru butter, to lock in moisture.

I love using the rich, buttery cream as the last layer of my nighttime routine, but also on any dry patches from head to toe. Hailey Bieber told us she uses the Barrier Butter everywhere—from her neck and chest to her hands and even her arms.

The lip balm that started it all, Rhode’s Peptide Lip Treatment went viral when the brand first launched, and for good reason. While the texture of this skincare-infused treatment feels more like a gloss than a traditional treatment balm, it leaves lips with a high-shine finish that also plumps courtesy of peptides. The treatment has now expanded into tinted versions and has even inspired other peptide-forward lip products, such as the Peptide Lip Shape liner.

The brand’s newest launch is a hydrating face mist designed to refresh the skin and add a glow with a single spritz. While I haven’t gotten my hands on the Glazing Mist yet, it has all the hallmarks of a great mist, including a superfine mister. The formula boasts a ceramide trio to improve the skin barrier, ectoin to keep skin hydrated throughout the day, and panthenol to soothe skin.

Many moisturizers on the market contain actives such as acids or retinol, but Rhode’s face moisturizer has zero actives—just ingredients that focus on calming, softening, and hydrating the skin. When my perioral dermatitis flares up, I reach for this lightweight yet moisturizing formula, which is filled with squalane, peptides, niacinamide, shea butter, and açaí.

While Rhode wasn’t the first to jazz up pimple patches, these 100 percent hydrocolloid patches stay in place while healing and protecting breakouts. You can also use them on blisters, as demonstrated by Bieber.

#6792. This Revamped Field Watch Is More Fall-Coded Than Pumpkin Spice

Watch collaborations can sometimes feel they have been randomly cobbled together, two disparate brands fusing to make something wholly uninteresting. This isn’t the case for Huckberry or the Canadian military watchmaker Marathon, which supplied timekeeping equipment to Allied forces in 1941. The natural alignment between brands gave Huckberry the perfect excuse to rummage through the archives and collaborate on the all-new, 41mm CeraShell Navigator, a pilot’s watch whose design traces back to the Steel Navigator developed with Kelly Air Force Base in 1986.

Military and heritage references are already a big part of Huckberry’s in-house brands, particularly Flint and Tinder. For its take on the Navigator, Huckberry focused on the dial, color, and tweaked a few distinct details rather than changing the watch too dramatically.

That starts with Marathon’s matte-black CeraShell case, here paired with an Arctic white dial for the first time on a CeraShell Navigator. The familiar 12- and 24-hour scales remain, while Huckberry swaps the usual red seconds hand for its hunter orange. Branding has also been kept to a minimum, with Huckberry’s tree logo placed on the crown instead of the already slightly crowded dial.

Together, the black case, white dial, and orange second hand simplify the Navigator’s appearance, but doesn’t drown out its classic military timepiece pedigree. The case is made from Marathon’s CeraShell, a proprietary combination of bio-sourced plastic and ceramic powder that helps keep the watch lightweight. It measures 11.5mm thick and is fitted with a sapphire crystal, while tritium tubes provide constant illumination for the hour and minute hands, hour markers, and bezel pip.

Inside the 41mm case is an ETA F06.115 HeavyDrive quartz movement, with water resistance rated to 60 meters. The watch comes with two straps, an olive-green DEFSTAN nylon strap and a coyote-brown HANK strap made using neoprene and Kevlar, extending the military influence beyond the case and dial.

The watch sits in the duality of being both rugged and completely refined, which is, in some ways, a perfect distillation of both brands. The Navigator is available now exclusively through Huckberry’s site.

Surprise! Dancing With the Stars is taking a break from its normal schedule and airing tonight (Monday, November 2) on ABC and Disney+. The show moved up a day for ABC’s election coverage on Tuesday, November 3, and if you’re wondering what time to tune in tonight...same as always!

Dancing With the Stars airs tonight at 8 p.m. ET on both Disney+ and ABC. Which, yes, means the cast had one less day than usual to prep their dances for the upcoming theme: Disney Night! More specifically, a Broadway-themed Disney Night, guest judged by none other than Cynthia Erivo.

Here’s a reminder of the songs and performance styles from our eight remaining couples tonight:

Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov: Dancing a quickstep to “A Star Is Born” from Hercules

Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold: Dancing a waltz to “I See the Light” from Tangled

Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach: Dancing a samba to “Under the Sea” from The Little Mermaid

Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson: Dancing jazzto “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious” from Mary Poppins

Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy: Dancing a quickstep to “Be Our Guest” from Beauty and the Beast

Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa: Dancing paso doble to “Satisfied” from Hamilton

Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas: Dancing a jive to “You Can Fly! You Can Fly! You Can Fly!” from Peter Pan

Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik: Dancing contemporary to “Easy as Life” from Aida

There will also be two team dances set to “Zoo” from Zootopia 2 and “We’re All in This Together” from High School Musical. Connor Wood and Tatyana Ali are the team captains—with Tatyana’s team consisting of Alfonso Ribeiro, Jan, Maura, Mark, Amber, Pasha, Julia, and Ezra, while Connor’s team has Julianne, Rylee, Ezra, Dani, Jenna, Val, Harry, and Jenna.

See you tonight at 8:00 pm ET on both Disney+ and ABC.

#6786. The Best Restaurants in Paris Now, From Classic Bistros to Cutting-Edge Tasting Menus

Choosing the best Paris restaurants is a fool’s errand. It depends on your mood, what you’re craving, and how a particular spot on a particular night lines up. Even for a Paris-based food journalist who lives and breathes the restaurant scene, keeping up with new openings while making time to revisit the institutions feels like a marathon with no finish line. Paris is insatiable.

That’s part of what makes Paris the dynamic city it is today, bursting at the périph with creative energy. Classics continue to reinvent themselves. Neo-bistros sprout like springtime wisteria on both banks, no longer clustered in the 11th. Chefs pop up and collaborate. They champion one another. They cook with joy and often seem as excited about the scene as the diners who sustain it. The city’s non-classic French cuisines, having arrived through colonization, immigration, or a mix of both, form the fabric of Paris and have only grown more versatile.

Some of the most delightful experiences are found in the surprising and the unexpected: the restaurant on an unremarkable street in the 20th arrondissement with wood-paneled walls and cooking that rivals the technique and care of heavy-tablecloth spots in the Golden Triangle; the intimate, Scandinavian-sleek counter in the 4th arrondissement, where the fresh-faced chef decorates your plate with a thumb-sized, barely dressed bundle of herbs picked earlier that day from the restaurant’s garden in Montreuil. They’re also found in the soul-warming comfort of consistency: the reliably tingly green curry at Belleville’s favorite Thai-Laotian restaurant; the peppery bite of the silky sauce on the petit filet mignon at the cult-worthy bistro that is worth the hype.

There are countless great restaurants in Paris worth trying. But when it comes to the best, these are the ones that make you want to return.

Opened in 2025 in the Parmentier neighborhood of the 11th, Lissit is a restaurant for gourmands. Behind the petite spot that quickly became a Paris scene is Claire Grumellon, previously of Vaillant, who forms part of the rising tide of young chefs reviving the art of charcuterie, alongside Alexis Lissitzky, formerly of Soces, who oversees the dining room and the carefully sourced wine list, which spans from classic and biodynamic to natural and funky—from a Domaine Pierre Prieur Sancerre to Domaine Grain par Grain by winemaker Caroline Ledédenté.

There are plenty of dishes for the faint of heart, like the excellent oeufs mayo with a sliver of pickled herring, and line-caught Vendée mackerel with pepper sauce. But the true joy of Lissit is for the bold eaters, unafraid to dig into quail’s neck sausage (excellent, surprisingly un-gamey) and their famed tarte Tatin boudin poire—a mashup of the classic dessert, swapping apples for pears, and layered with blood sausage. Per Alexis, even the PFW set can’t resist this dish that hits all the sweet and savory and buttery notes.

Le Bistrot Paul Bert has become a modern-day institution, alongside spots like Le Baratin and Septime. (Gift Shop, unsurprisingly, teamed up with them to offer a signature line of swag.) Opened in 1997 by Bertrand Auboyneau and partner Gwénaëlle Cadoret, it’s the always bustling 11th arrondissement destination for well-executed classics like steak au poivre, a blushing filet mignon with glossy pepper sauce, a nest of crispy fries on the side, and Dover sole meunière with buttery new potatoes. Desserts can be as simple and satisfying as field-grown strawberries with a tuft of raw cream. Reservations are recommended, though sometimes tricky to come by. Next door, La Cave Paul Bert, which features a rotating cast of pop-up chefs, is a solid walk-in only alternative, with an excellent wine selection.

Ask a native Parisian about the must-try dishes in their city, and, if they know their stuff, you can bet they’ll name-check the saucisse purée at Les Arlots in the 10th arrondissement. The signature dish, which Chef Thomas Brachet tweaks every year or so, is a beautifully browned, crispy-skinned sausage, packed with herbs like sage and rosemary, topped with chopped chives and served on a pillowy bed of whipped, mashed potatoes made with AOP Pamplie butter, pooling with deeply savory homemade jus. Aside from the famed sausage, Chef Brachet’s menu changes regularly, and the dishes are always a bit lusty: tender scallop tartare topped with toasted hazelnuts and dainty wildflowers; a well-confit’d duck leg served with potatoes sautéed with wild garlic. For dessert, don’t skip the chocolate mousse, a blend of three fine chocolates enriched by farm-fresh eggs, no cream.

As reservations can be tricky, their next-door sister cave à manger, Billili, is a solid alternative for an apéro—wine (mostly natural) and thinly sliced saucisson or generously mayo’d oeufs mayo—or a succession of small, shareable plates like a crisp green bean salad and Réunionese steamed dumplings stuffed with umami-rich pork. Walk-ins are welcomed by the smiley servers, but arrive early (before 7 p.m.) to score a seat.

On a narrow street off the rue de Belleville hill, Le Baratin is the OG bistro that influenced a generation of chefs, including Iñaki Aizpitarte (of the mythic Chateaubriand). Opened in 1987, Argentine chef Raquel Carena has led the kitchen since day one, preparing honest, hearty bistro cuisine.

The two snug dining rooms feel homey, decorated with books (like La Vie de Léon Tolstoï) and a portrait of Samuel Beckett. The daily menu, written in cursive on a blackboard, makes the rounds of the dining rooms, with starters like head cheese and pig’s foot terrine; mains like oxtail parmentier, sweetbreads with new potatoes and Swiss chard, and cuttlefish ragout in tomato sauce. Wines are scrawled on a separate board next to the bar, with a selection that leans French, starting at €7 a glass, while most bottles are priced in the mid-€40s.

The hill that slopes from lower to upper Belleville is lined with laidback bars and restaurants. But only one has a line winding out the door and up the hill most evenings—Lao Siam. The family-owned, second-generation Thai-Laotian restaurant, opened by the Souksavanhs in 1985, is a favorite among locals and Paris chefs—always a sign worth following. It’s a relatively sprawling (and kid-friendly) space, where the service is speedy, and the cooking always hits.

The secret ingredient here is consistency. For over four decades, the menu has remained unchanged—nicely spiced papaya salad, crispy fried chicken with chili sauce and pickles, green curry with shrimp, pineapple stuffed with shrimp, sausage and dried pork, and much more. It’s a comfort food spot that works equally well for a celebratory meal or a quiet Sunday night dinner.

In 2002, Stéphane Jégo took over a humble Basque tavern in the 7th arrondissement and breathed new life into it, turning L’Ami Jean into one of Paris’s iconic bistronomy spots. The idea here is to keep the focus on the cuisine, not the space, which nonetheless charms with its red leather banquettes and tiled floors. The chef’s style is rustic and French at heart, with winks at the location’s Basque roots—dishes like roasted octopus with smoked paprika, tomato salad with Bayonne chili and burrata, the chef’s dad’s country terrine, roasted pigeon with thyme, and butter-roasted sweetbreads. Carnivores have plenty of dishes to taste and the true challenge is finishing them—portions are generous. The wine list traipses around l’hexagon, with carefully selected French bottles and glasses, from Burgundy and Loire whites to characterful reds from Saint-Émilion, Savigny-lès-Beaune, and beyond. Rice pudding might be giving nana’s favorite dessert, but this one, with roasted nuts and homemade caramel sauce, receives rave reviews from serious eaters across the board.

There are many pizza places in Paris, and there are many pizza places that claim to be the best in Paris—and there are some pizza places that inexplicably have hour-long waits for mediocre pies. Oobatz, opened in 2024 by the team behind Le Rigmarole, isn’t particularly loud on the media side. And they don’t have to be. With chef and co-owner Dan Pearson in the kitchen, they quietly churn out some of the tastiest pizzas, on sourdough crusts, in the French capital. I don’t know anyone who’s ever had a subpar meal at Oobatz.

It starts with the crust—thin but sturdy enough to support toppings, a subtle but noticeable hint of salt. And those toppings—always changing, always seasonal in that particular French way (asparagus and new potatoes with lemon confit in the spring, beautiful, barely sweet garden-fresh squash in the summer), leave you wanting to return to try more. The drink menu, with well-chosen IPAs, lagers, and lambics, and natural wines by the glass or pichet, feels on brand for this straightforward, delicious pizzeria.

As a New York native who's lived a few years in Spain, my heart yearns for a well-stirred dirty martini and a proper Spanish tortilla—both surprisingly hard to track down in Paris. Winona, a new cocktail bar and restaurant in the 11th, helps right these wrongs. Open since July, it’s already a scene. The space is a sexy take on the Parisian bistro, with a horseshoe-shaped bar topped with Bordeaux-hued marble, a lacquered ceiling, and finished concrete walls, white with dabs in a deep red hue that calls to mind pata negra.

A recent dinner began with the Winona dirty martini—petite and properly briny. My dinner mate ordered the Piparita Margarita, and while Yves Carlier's cocktail menu is thoughtful and precise, they weren't sticklers, happy to sub in mezcal as requested. The tortilla rivaled some of the best I've tasted in Bilbao's Casco Viejo: firm outside, barely set inside, begging you to mojar el pan—soak it up with a hunk of sourdough. Smaller dishes like warm, pickled figs with funky Roquefort are easy crowd-pleasers. Mains like the impressive red tuna belly felt like a refined version of a menú del día in Madrid—a hefty, bone-in fillet served with thin-sliced fried potatoes splashed in vinegar and crisp garlic. Chef Cecilia Munguira, the Madrid-born, Gijón-raised young chef, makes a strong case for showing more love to France's neighbor to the south.

Chef Pierre Touitou made a name for himself at the vibey 10th arrondissement spots Vivant and Déviant, which drew chic crowds for their great cooking, excellent wine, and hip-hop playlists. 19 Saint Roch is Touitou’s latest project and feels like a coming of age of sorts. In the 1st arrondissement, it’s just a few skips from the Tuileries Gardens. It may be a bit more buttoned-up, but the fresh, seasonal, technically on-point cooking remains. It’s also a welcome addition to a central Paris neighborhood that’s a bit short on great restaurants you’d want to become a regular.

The succinct menu features amuse-bouches like Touitou’s take on the Cantonese lo bak go, or turnip cake; sophisticated entrées like poached veal brain with tomato confit and a Basque pilpil sauce; and mains like a delicate steamed skate wing with Sichuan spices, rounded off with a few well-chosen cheeses and seasonal sweet creations. At a recent lunch, I was taken with the presentation, served at an unhurried pace on vintage-looking porcelain with floral edges. When Paris visitors ask me where to book, 19 Saint Roch has become one of the spots I always recommend.

Arriving an hour before your reservation is usually a faux pas, especially when you’re dining solo, but the first time I ate at Bittikesu, Jules St. Cyr’s new restaurant in a quiet pocket of the 4th arrondissement, it turned out to be a happy accident. My embarrassment vanished like the pét-nat in my glass as I chatted with the Montreal-born chef about his time cooking in Copenhagen (at Noma, among other restaurants) and his travels throughout China. The earthy, Nordic influence appears throughout the space, mixed with Chinese touches: a smooth Burgundy oak counter that seats 14 diners, stone worktops in the kitchen, restored wooden ceiling beams fitted with paper lantern-esque light fixtures, and a single bouquet of bay leaves hanging above a sleek wooden bench near the entrance.

The tasting menu progressed through a succession of small bites on handmade ceramic plates, from a bundle of herbs from Bittikesu’s garden in Montreuil—essentially the Brooklyn of Paris—to “tear” peas with silken tofu and a perfect fillet of mackerel topped with chrysanthemum. The entire experience feels intimate, like a dinner party at a design-savvy friend’s place. You might walk in as a solo diner and find yourself chatting all night with newfound friends.

If one spot can be considered the rage in Paris right now, it’s Paulownia. Co-owners Tess Duteil and Geoffrey Belin, sommelier and chef, respectively, met during their time at L’Arpège. At Paulownia, which opened in 2023, they bring the precision and thoughtfulness of a Michelin-starred temple to a sleepy street in the 20th arrondissement, formerly home to a lovely paulownia, or foxglove, tree—hence the restaurant’s name.

At Paulownia, the daily lunch and dinner menus depend on the day’s deliveries from regional producers. They source meat mostly from Normandy and work with a trusted fishmonger in Le Guilvinec, Brittany, for impeccably fresh seafood. Seated at the counter before the open kitchen, watching the team work quietly like a four-person ballet, we feasted on lightly grilled turbot with a Savagnin-kissed beurre blanc and roasted Burgaud duck with tender, stewed prunes. The mille-feuille dessert, layered with creamy almond-hazelnut cream, was ethereally light—as it should be. Tess, a former caviste, regularly visits their winegrowers and brings the same thoughtfulness to Paulownia’s wine list.

At Waly Fay, a West African bistro in the 11th arrondissement dating back to the early aughts, I had one of the most delightful lunches in recent memory. An open kitchen is the heart of the spacious dining room, with exposed brick walls, vintage Gispen chairs, and industrial tables set with wax paper.

It’s tricky to choose what to order from the expansive menu, a collaboration between Cameroonian chef Jeannie Tientcheu and Senegalese chef Dalla Sankare. Starters include golden cod fritters and Ivorian alloco, or fried plantains, an excellent sucre-salé way to start a meal. For mains, you’ll find Nigerian jumbo shrimp in a Creole sauce scented with fresh ginger and Senegalese chicken yassa—fall-apart-tender chicken stewed with caramelized onions, lime, and green olives, all served with sticky broken rice. If you’re not sufficiently stuffed, there are several sides to add on, including attiéké, a cassava-based couscous, and chikwangue, cassava cakes wrapped and steamed in banana leaves.

The dishes are unfussy and comforting but nail all the details: my maffé had just the right touch of spice and the texture of organic peanut butter; ribbons of steamed carrot and a sprinkling of freshly chopped parsley brought it to the next level.

A meal at a “Palace” hotel—the highest luxury designation doled out by the French government—rarely disappoints. But my meals at Cheval Blanc Paris have consistently been exceptional. Hakuba, the brainchild of chefs Takuya Watanabe and Arnaud Donckele (the sauce master behind Plénitude as well), along with pastry chef Maxime Frédéric, is a standout in Paris’s growing Japanese culinary scene.

On the hotel’s ground floor, the restaurant is designed to feel organic and soothing—a tsukubai stone and bamboo fountain trickles near the entrance, while black walnut walls evoke the forest. With glassware from Kyoto and ceramics from southern Japan, the Omakase menu combines the finest French and Atlantic coast ingredients. It’s a decadent experience—the “Yume” menu will set you back €420, and if you’re feeling particularly indulgent, there’s an optional sea urchin temaki for €30 and fresh truffle for €95.

Maison Sota is one of those restaurants that Paris chefs consistently name as one of their favorites. The space alone is unlike most anything you’ll find in Paris—down a narrow 11th arrondissement alley, an airy maison with exposed wooden beams, peach-toned terracotta floor and wall tiles, and an open kitchen with the wood-fired oven on display. A 26-foot-long wooden table sits at the heart of the restaurant, though counter seats offer a front-row view of Chef Sota Atsumi’s cooking. The menu (five courses for lunch, seven for dinner) showcases the chef’s honed French techniques with Japanese touches—dishes like wood-fire grilled peas with brown shrimp, a pea jus, kombu butter, and rich egg yolk; sweets like their golden “blown sugar dessert” with lychee foam, green kiwi, pomelo, candied kumquat, and bergamot oil.

#6785. Why Is It So Hard to Call Someone Out on the Group Chat?

Read the rest of GQ’s special report on Cornell here and here.

The screenshot, circulated in reporting on the allegation of sexual assault by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell in 2024, is painful to look at, and painfully familiar: a more extreme example of an episode that plays out on our own phones. Someone in the group chat says something fucked-up. You cringe as laughing emojis roll in. You think about saying something. You probably don’t. And you feel worse for it. Northwestern sociologist Aaron Shaw, who has studied how groups talk to each other online, explains why it happens.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

This kind of interaction is seen linked to the general disinhibition effects documented in digital communications: If your face isn’t there, and if you’re not confronted with the presence of other people, it’s a lot easier to behave in ways that may break with normal social conventions. There’s a long legacy of misogynistic groups existing and thriving. Some people might want to say, “Oh, this is a problem because of Snapchat,” but what research in the last 30 years suggests is that people will find ways to connect no matter what digital communication platform they are using. Research about online communities dates back to the 1980s and ’90s, and some of the high-drama incidents occurring in that time were around rape culture.

Gaming is an incredibly heterogeneous space of human activity, but there are some communities where violations of social norms are not just okay, but important: “If you want to play the game, you’ve got to get over it.”

They might be communicating at multiple levels in ways that are hard to see from the outside. By drawing on particular words they’ve used in the past, they might be signaling things to each other, like their membership in the group, their commitment to each other. Their desire to stay connected with each other may be more powerful than the desire to speak in an empathetic way about, in this case, the experience of a young woman.

Some research on bystander effects suggests that the larger the group size, the less likely any one individual in that group is to speak out against it. Individuals may feel like they don’t have control or that they can’t be responsible for the behavior of everybody in the chat. If their sense is that others in the group think this is okay—or would be willing to ostracize them if they were to speak out—they’re less likely to be willing or able to speak out.

There’s also a performative element. They are putting on a show; they are onstage for each other. Group chats really do serve that purpose. It’s hard to know what elements of that performance are, in a sense, fiction and what elements are a factual representation of the events that night in the frat house. The tropes these young guys may be using may be profoundly objectionable, may be hyper-misogynistic, may undermine the humanity and rights and autonomy of women, but it doesn’t necessarily equate to evidence of rape. In some ways it’s like cultural expression.

It might feel comforting to say, “Well, we can’t fix culture easily, but what we can do is kick people out of group chats or ban fraternities from campus.” But there’s lots of reasons to believe that that’s not going to actually address the root causes. There’s evidence that a lot of young men feel left behind or excluded by prevailing cultural and political and economic forces. I’m not saying that’s factually true, but the feeling seems to have made some young men hateful towards those they perceive to be not like them, who they perceive to be threats to their authority. It’s heartbreaking, not just for the alleged victim of sexual assault, but also for the people who engage in the chat. I don’t think that’s going to give them the sense of security and self that might allow them to behave more generously and respectfully towards others, either. ◼︎

Fraternities control access to coveted resources. They use humiliating rituals to bond with each other, enforce hierarchy, and belittle outsiders. Sound familiar?

#6784. The 50+ Best Deals from Amazon’s Pre-Black Friday Sale

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Markdowns on Apple, designer watches, and the Samsung Frame are worth buying early.

In the good old days, Black Friday was one simple (albeit chaotic) day a year; now it’s a whole month of debating whether or not we should take the plunge on a deal or wait for it to get better. Who has the time? We do, because it’s our day job. We spent hours browsing Amazon’s pre-Black Friday deals so you don’t have to.

Here’s the deal: For now, select Apple tech, the best art TVs (including the Samsung Frame), several respectable designer watches, and our all-time favorite T-shirt are already on decent sale, so you don’t have to wait on those. But sit tight on things like Kindles, Ray-Ban Meta glasses, and big-ticket furniture—for now.

Expect Amazon to ramp up Apple deals throughout the month (we’re holding out hope for the already-cheap MacBook Neo to go on sale for the first time and are almost positive the AirPods 5 will drop below $100), but for now, these are the only Apple deals remotely deserving of your attention. FYI: Apple AirTags are currently the cheapest they’ve ever been.

Art TVs are reigning supreme when it comes to Amazon tech deals right now—perfect for watching Thanksgiving football or displaying a fireplace screensaver over the holidays. Several of our favorite art TVs are already marked down, including Hisense, Samsung Frame, and TCL. (Though the Frame deal stands to steepen.) Kindles haven't been discounted yet, but we expect them to be on Black Friday.

Esquire editor staples like Lacoste polos and Levi’s jeans are already heavily discounted on Amazon. Shop early to secure a Thanksgiving outfit that’ll impress those random family members you rarely see. You’ll have better luck shopping for running shoes and workout gear if you wait.

Amazon sales are our secret source for great watches. Right now, you can save up to 40 percent on timepieces from Citizen, Bulova, Casio, Tissot, Timex and other respectable makers. Additional models will be discounted around Cyber Monday, so don’t give up hope if the one you’re eyeing is still full price.

LEGO sets make for crowd-pleasing gifts for that niece or nephew of yours (or, you know, older brother), but we’re just as likely to keep these discounted sets for ourselves. (Hey, anything to take a screen break.) We’ve seen LEGO deals sell out fast in years past, so shop early while stock is plentiful.

Amazon’s pre-Black Friday sale can also help you prepare your home for holiday hosting duties. You can bet on finding cleaning gadgets, cookware sets, leaf blowers, mattresses, coffee makers—you name it—for less than full price in November. Deals on large furniture items like sofas and dressers are so-so as of now, but that should change in the coming weeks.

Airline travel is expensive enough, so don’t waste money on full-priced luggage. Samsonite, Troubadour, and other popular brands are already offering discounts on checked suitcases, carry-ons, duffels, and backpacks—but Away and Monos are still full price, so stand by if you have your heart set on those.

Skip a trip to the store (and save a few bucks in the process) by picking up personal care products during your next Amazon haul. Now is a great time to invest in a new electric razor or restock your cologne, but we’d wait to buy beauty gifts for the women in your life until closer to Black Friday.

FYI, Madden NFL 27 and NBA 2K27 games for the latest Xbox and PlayStation models are currently discounted on Amazon (though sadly, the gaming systems themselves are not—yet). Supportive swivel chairs, curved computer monitors, over-ear headphones, and other gaming essentials are also on sale. Upgrade your setup now so you can enjoy it over the holiday break.

In this economy, who can afford to spend full price on holiday gifts? Shop wisely before Amazon’s Black Friday-Cyber Monday sale, and you can check loved ones off your list early for up to 40 percent less. If the gifts you’ve already been eyeing yourself are still full price, hold off; there’s a strong chance they’ll be marked down in the coming weeks.

#6781. Young Men of Cornell Want to Talk. Why Are Older Men So Quiet?

Read the rest of GQ’s special report on Cornell here and here.

One night in early October, activists broke a glass door at the entrance of Cornell University’s Day Hall, an administrative building that houses the office of president Michael Kotlikoff. They also vandalized its façade with the messages “Smash the patriarchy” and “At Cornell rapists are protected, protesters are expelled.” The next day, thousands of students and faculty gathered in Cornell’s Ho Plaza. When I stood in front of Day Hall, 36 hours later, much of the evidence had been erased. College life seemed to carry on as normal. Midterms, or “prelims,” were underway; students zoomed stoically past on electric scooters. The shattered panels had been replaced with planks and a sign directing visitors to an alternate entrance, and the graffiti had been power-washed to dark-gray smudges.

Cornell is situated among the gorges of Ithaca, New York, and I drove up from New York City to understand how men were making sense of a civil suit brought in September by an anonymous accuser, called Jane Doe in legal documents and media reports, alleging that she was plied with ketamine and sexually assaulted by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. All the men have denied wrongdoing. Jane Doe’s suit also alleges that Cornell failed to appropriately safeguard her from sexual assault. University administrators acknowledged that they had “fallen short and [are] taking meaningful action.”

According to punishment summaries obtained by The New York Times, Cornell had conducted a Title IX investigation, which resulted in the expulsion of two fraternity brothers and suspension of two others. The Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office declined to pursue criminal charges. (New York governor Kathy Hochul criticized the Cornell police and the Tompkins County DA for their handling of the allegations and appointed attorney general Letitia James as a special prosecutor to investigate.) Among the materials included in Jane Doe’s suit was a photograph of a phone displaying a Chi Phi group chat, with reportedly more than 50 people, in which one of the men advertised Jane Doe’s “free pussy.” Some cheered. One asked if “the shop” was still open. In the screenshot, not a single voice raised an objection.

Men’s perspectives have been underreported during past sexual assault crises, perhaps out of the well-intentioned belief that we should prioritize listening to women. But when such moments to object to a woman’s dehumanization arrive, I wanted to know, why do men so often stay quiet?

Several people told me that my trip coincided with Ithaca’s most beautiful season, and, in person, the landscape did indeed look quintessentially autumnal. (My visit also coincided with the time of year in 2024 that Jane Doe alleges her assault in the Chi Phi house took place.) In the Arts Quad, Oscar, 21, was on his way to class, although he didn’t seem to have anything with him besides his phone. He was dressed in sweats and a boxy yellow tee, and he told me that he had joined a fraternity because he wanted to make friends. He had just left a Sexual Assault Prevention and Safety Club meeting for members of sororities and fraternities, where he and other students had discussed how the Greek system can develop stronger guardrails. One promising approach, he told me, was to delegate prominent members of frats to speak up about sexual assault. “It’s a scary and really hard conversation to have with your friend, especially somebody you think wouldn’t do something like that,” he said. “That’s what our meeting is about: How can we try to make these conversations more normal, more open?” Oscar was generous with his thoughts but grew reserved on the topic of fraternity culture.

Over by the Library or “Libe” Slope, an idyllic stretch of lawn on a rolling hillside, two guys tossed a Frisbee. I sat on the bench next to theirs while they hydrated. “A lot of people are saying, ‘If you were in that group chat, you should have said something,’ which I agree with,” said Hudson Tumey, who graduated last year. “You absolutely should have.” Tumey is a member of Cru, a Christian ministry on campus, and was visiting with William Canlis, a sophomore, who is also involved in Cru. “If I was in that group chat, I would’ve hoped with all my might that I would’ve said something,” Tumey said. “But I think I’d be lying to say that I would’ve for sure said something.” Tumey and Canlis explained that their faith offers them a man to emulate in Jesus Christ. “If a man doesn’t have that standard to look up to, that’s where bad things happen,” Canlis said. “If you don’t have Him, then what role model is left? The world? Look how broken the world is.”

I started looking around for other male role models. Near Sage Chapel, a non-sectarian church on campus, two clergymen visiting the campus said they hadn’t known about the Chi Phi case until that morning. One of them told me he preferred to stay out of it. Just outside Schoellkopf Field, an associate basketball coach asked me to email him. At the ROTC offices in Barton Hall, an Army poster read “Sexual assault. Sexual harassment. Not in our army.” A master sergeant paused his lunch to talk with me. He sat for a moment, then left to call his superior. After five minutes he returned and, with a half-apologetic inhale, said that he couldn’t speak with me until it’s brought up the chain of command and that I should email him. A roving police officer said that the only person on the force approved to speak with the press was Eric Stickel, Cornell University Police Department’s recently appointed chief of police, and I should email him. Ultimately, I approached almost two dozen non-student men associated with the town or the school and only one talked to me on the record.

At the Morrison Dining Hall, a seven-hour sit-in was underway, roughly matching the length of time Jane Doe spent in the Chi Phi house until she lost consciousness, according to the lawsuit. One of the sit-in’s appointed press contacts was John Hartnett, a 19-year-old sophomore representing Students for a Democratic Cornell, a group that had also helped organize the protest earlier in the week. He was proud of that turnout, as it was one of the largest protests at Cornell since the Vietnam War, but incensed by the irony of the school’s history of suspending students involved in other protests. He was also taking inventory of how he and his peers influence each other.

“It’s a difficult thing because you have to realize that some of your past actions—not sexual assault—perpetuated these things,” he said. “It’s something that men have to ask themselves: What am I not doing in terms of not holding the people around me accountable?” My phone rang. Someone from Cornell’s media-relations team informed me that the school was aware of my presence on campus and that none of the administrators were available for comment.

Reporters from Telemundo, The Ithaca Voice, and Reuters descended on Hartnett, and the sheer number of us bombarding him cast the reticence I encountered from his elders in a new light. While an inevitable chorus rose up to defend fraternities or disparage Jane Doe, some young men on campus seemed to be earnestly reckoning with the case or struggling to find their voice. But their community leaders appeared, at most, disconcerted. Perhaps those older men were grappling internally or opting for silent solidarity; whatever their reasons, I was struck by the persistence of their absence.

Later in the evening, I attended a Common Council meeting downtown at Ithaca City Hall. More than 50 people squeezed into a room set up for half that number. Ithaca mayor Robert G. Cantelmo oversaw the proceedings. A dozen or so students found spots on the floor; the local television station was filming. There were complaints regarding the closure of a parking garage, concerns about winter snow plowing, and, eventually, a proposed moratorium on some of Cornell’s event and noise permits, which was put forth as an effort to limit Greek-life activities. The floor was then opened for public comment, but only to those who had filed a slip.

“I think sacrificing some of the fun is more than justified by protecting people from these heinous crimes until the university gets off its rear,” John King, an Ithaca resident, said in support of the moratorium. “I applaud the city government for being willing to do so instead.” Sam Poole was a freshman when Jane Doe first reported her assault to the Cornell police. “I live in a Cornell co-op,” he said. “Co-ops host parties just like fraternities do, plenty of student organizations do, but we decided we’re not going to host parties until the moratorium is over.” Almost a week after the meeting, Cornell banned frat parties for the current academic year.

A few rows behind me, a man in a C-SPAN hoodie and tech pants was growing agitated that he had not been called on. “Michael Tracey,” he called out repeatedly. Mayor Cantelmo explained that Tracey’s name was not among the comment slips given to him by the clerk. “Motion to reconsider,” Tracey yelled out. “You’re definitely not eligible to make motions, because you’re not a member of this body,” Cantelmo replied. Tracey alleged his slip was thrown in the trash. “You should be ashamed for using the power of your office to conclusorily [sic] declare that any American citizen has committed crimes as heinous as gang rape before any semblance of adjudicative process,” he said as he walked out. I passed him my number.

Tracey asked to meet in the lobby of the Canopy Hotel. On my way there I learned that he is a contrarian Substack journalist, known for social media provocation; recently he argued that aspects of the Jeffrey Epstein case were overblown. He’s made multiple trips to Ithaca, where he’s filmed himself cross-examining students and faculty and showing up to public gatherings. He told me that he had driven from Jersey City to Ithaca to report on the Cornell case, motivated by his belief that Jane Doe’s identity should be made public. The previous week, he tweeted out her name before deleting the post. Internet sleuths published her address online. Then, according to Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, on the night before the meeting at City Hall, Jane Doe was swatted—that is, someone made a call to the police reporting invented violence at her home, prompting a large-scale police response. Giuffra told CNN that his client has been “terrified.”

Plaintiff anonymity is “used to manipulate the court system and thereby the public as a PR tactic to create pressure,” Tracey told me. “I have nothing against Jane Doe. She seems kind of cool, actually.” He showed me a text he sent to a number he claims belongs to her: “Given that settlement funds are being sought, especially considering that criminal investigations have been triggered, I consider it in the public interest to report on your identity.” When I pointed out that anonymity enables sexual assault victims to come forward with less fear of vitriol and death threats, he described the death threats he has received. This is what one of the loudest male voices I encountered in Ithaca sounds like.

I walked down Ithaca Commons to peer into Moonies, the bar Jane Doe visited before the alleged assault, but it was closed for the night. On Instagram, it appeared to be business as usual, with promotions for “Flash Friday” and “Saturday Surge” parties. In the suit, Jane Doe says she left a sorority event at this bar, went to another bar, and then “stumbled alone” to a party at the Chi Phi house. (Moonies is named in Jane Doe’s suit and its owners have denied that it illegally served alcohol to the underage Jane Doe.) I got into my car and headed to the frat. Even from the cozy confines of my rented Toyota Corolla, that path seemed uninviting. There’s a brick-and-stone charm to downtown Ithaca that dissolves once you cross over the gorges and onto frat row. Flashy trucks and clusters of mega-mansions run by very young adults bordered the drive. I spotted a handful of bongs resting on windowsills. For a minute, I couldn’t find the actual Chi Phi house and when I finally spotted it—massive, menacing—I was nearly relieved.

The next morning, campus cleared out for fall break. Visiting faculty member Mark Brown Jr. sat on the steps of Goldwin Smith Hall and finished a game of virtual chess before speaking with me. “I think frat culture is incredibly toxic,” he said. Some undergraduates in his art classes preferred to discuss the subject in a “roundabout” way. The potential of repercussions, he said, may be deterring open discussion.

I approached two students sitting under a statue of Andrew Dickson White, Cornell’s first president. “All men are honestly guilty for this,” said Daniel Suh, a junior studying public policy. “You ask any man if rape is okay and they’re going to tell you no. But men expect a perfect victim.” His friend, Anand Patel, also a junior, sat next to him. With their baggy pants and gleaming sneakers, Patel and Suh seemed so sweetly boyish, young, and on the brink of adulthood. But also fed up. While Suh felt regulating frat parties wouldn’t directly address the issue of college sexual assault, Patel was much more critical of frat culture. “Where the true issue lies is what happens when you have a friend who does it, or someone you know. Are you going to act like nothing happened? Are you going to support him, or are you going to cut him off? Because that’s ultimately what happens in these frats,” Patel said. “These men don’t draw a line in the sand saying, ‘Okay, you’re out now.’ ”

These students offered a stark contrast with the many older men I had tried to speak to, on and off campus, who couldn’t or wouldn’t add their voices to the conversation. For Patel and the other students I spoke to on campus, things seemed so clear: We should all call out bad behavior when we see it, because we know what bad behavior looks like. When did that get so complicated? ◼︎

Fraternities control access to coveted resources. They use humiliating rituals to bond with each other, enforce hierarchy, and belittle outsiders. Sound familiar?

A sociologist who studies online groups explains how social dynamics play out on our screens.

#6780. Gigi Hadid Cut the Ribbon on Her Fourth Guest in Residence Store with Cashmere, Caviar, and Caricatures

The best house party in New York City on Thursday evening wasn’t at a home at all, but inside a Madison Avenue boutique where Guest in Residence has officially taken up, well, residence. The hostess? Model and founder Gigi Hadid, clad in a shrunken top and tartan skirt, who was celebrating the debut of her label’s fourth U.S. store—and its very first uptown address. Friends, family, and VICs came out for the occasion, filling the two-story space with all manner of colorful knits.

The first surprise was a trio of pretzels twisted into the letters G, I, and R at the entrance. Inside, florists busied themselves preparing custom arrangements, a three-piece band played beneath a sloped skylight, and a caricature artist stationed near the bar had guests voguing for their portraits and later comparing their likenesses.

Martini glasses were filled with one of two things: martinis, of course, but also cigarettes. Meanwhile, caviar in every conceivable configuration made the rounds: atop passed blinis, with potato chips and crème fraîche at a help-yourself station, and even crowning freshly baked potatoes.

As with pulling off any great party, this one took a village. The flowers were courtesy of Kelsie Hayes of Pop Up Florist, a personal friend whom Hadid has called on for birthdays and gifts over the years. The Nines supplied the aforementioned boujee spuds—a signature of the NoHo haunt’s menu. “We started downtown—Bond Street is the heart of our company,” Hadid told Vogue. “So this night was about bringing downtown uptown.” Even the Guest in Residence team had been assembled through a web of friendships and former colleagues, some dating back to Hadid’s earliest days in the industry. “It’s like parts of my life and people and friendships that I’ve accumulated over time have all come together,” she said. “When I look around, I see that journey.”

A similar sentimentality extends to the interiors. Each Guest in Residence outpost borrows something from places Hadid holds dear, from the street-level stonework of SoHo to the brickwork of Los Angeles. For Madison Avenue, the idea was to recreate something supremely homey. “We wanted this store to feel like our little residence in New York.” Manhattan by way of the Alps, that is: pale wood paneling lends the space the feel of a chic chalet, prompting one guest to tell Hadid she detected a certain French sensibility in the interiors. “Merci beaucoup,” a delighted Hadid replied.

On the second floor—where a living room, bedroom, and dining area offer space for private styling appointments and future workshops—guests enjoyed the books and board games on display and made themselves at home. The only thing missing was the crackle of a fireplace, though with so many people gathered in their cashmere, additional heat hardly seemed necessary. “I always want the stores to feel like somewhere that people can walk in and sit on a couch and have a yap,” Hadid said.

And yap they did. A fashion publicist spoke of bringing Hadid his famous cheesecake to try, while a model excitedly pointed out their shared trainer. Jordan Barrett, who had just stepped off a plane, swung by to show off his vivid polo. “The first word that comes to mind when I think of this brand is ‘cozy,’” the model said. “Gigi has brought together such a nice, beautiful crowd. I’ve seen a lot of familiar faces and really, really kind people. She always surrounds herself with really good people.”

Beyond old friends, there were also a handful of top customers in attendance, including one woman proudly showing off her just-launched Guest in Residence denim. “Oh my God. I love seeing people in the jeans,” Hadid exclaimed. “It’s so crazy and fulfilling. People have so many different personalities and styles, and pull off the pieces so differently. It’s the biggest honor to see it.”

Eventually, out came four cakes: one for each Guest in Residence store now under Hadid’s belt. It wasn’t long before the festivities and conversations spilled out onto the sidewalk—as Hadid made her way to a waiting black car with friends, smiling and thanking guests one last time. As far as hosts go, she took the cake. Literally, as she carried one off into the night.
