#6762. Wales Bonner and Adidas Are Still Cooking With Gas

Just over a year ago, Grace Wales Bonner was announced as the next creative director of men’s ready-to-wear at Hermès. The move made history, making the superstar British designer the first Black woman to lead a European luxury house; her hotly anticipated first collection is set to debut in Paris in January. It was quickly confirmed that even as Wales Bonner stepped into her role at Hermès, she’d continue to work on her beloved namesake label. What was slightly less clear is if her new position would have any effect on Wales Bonner’s ongoing collaboration with Adidas, one of the most fruitful partnerships in sneakers. But in the months since the Hermès announcement, the partnership has hardly slowed down. If anything, it’s only continued to cement itself as the gold standard for linkups between fashion houses and athletic brands. And this week, the duo drops its latest collection, another killer mix of new silhouettes and luxed-up favorites.

For fall-winter 2026, Wales Bonner and the Three Stripes are bringing the BW Army and Gazelle into the fold. Neither model has received the Wales Bonner treatment just yet, though the timing is just right for the former. The BW Army has been a sleeper hit in 2026 and designers like Wales Bonner riffing on it will only serve to further elevate its profile. Her take on the OG military runner swaps trades its typical smooth leather for paneled pony hair and croc-printed leather. It comes in two colorways—a simple black and a burnt gold with rich maroon interior lining.

The rest of the collection features some more familiar faces, including the Gazelle, Adizero Adios, and Wales Bonner’s signature Karintha silhouette. The latter comes in croc-stamped leather with gold-brushed eyelets, which calls to mind the designer’s beautiful navy blue Sambas from a couple years back. On the techy Adizero Adios, Wales Bonner paired an off-white suede construction with exaggerated stitching and a royal blue interior. Rounding out the group is the Gazelle in a similar colorway to the Karintha: croc-printed leather with an off-white tongue and heel tab, plus a gum sole and a royal blue lining.

Alongside the shoes, Wales Bonner cooked up some of the sleekest Adidas apparel we’ve seen this year. There’s a blue jumper inspired by football kits, long a staple of the collaboration, plus a boldly striped sweater in tones of auburn, brown, and red. The designer’s takes on Adidas tracksuits remain as flawless as ever, with this collection adding a navy blue pinstriped short version to the canon. The true highlight of the clothes offering, however, is a leather zip-up blouson in a rich dark brown with Adidas stripes down the arms.

The fashion world is waiting with bated breath to see what Wales Bonner delivers at Hermès, with all the resources of a historic maison at her disposal. For now, though, we’re just stoked that the new gig doesn’t seem to have abated her deep love for true-blue sportswear one bit.

The Wales Bonner x Adidas Originals fall-winter 2026 collection is available now via CONFIRMED and select retailers.

#6761. Newly Minted Mr. Darcy, Jack Lowden, Responds to James Bond Short-List Rumors

Nothing more iconic than going from Mr. Darcy to 007.

We’re this close to finding out who the next James Bond is, and the short list? Callum Turner and Jack Lowden—the latter of whom is in the middle of a truly iconic run in Slow Horses, not to mention about to play Mr. Darcy in Netflix’s upcoming Pride & Prejudice adaptation.

According to The Hollywood Reporter, “several sources” confirmed that final screen tests for the Denis Villeneuve-directed film were taking place in London last week, which…presumably means Bond has been chosen. Cut to Jack, who was asked about the rumors in a recent GQ interview.

“On this… It’s all very flattering,” he said. “It’s nice to be mentioned—for any role—and I’m just not really going to add to the noise.”

Speaking specifically of his Slow Horses costar Gary Oldman saying he hoped Jack would get the part, he said, “It’s very nice, and Gary’s a sweetheart—it’s particularly lovely, coming from someone like him. But I don’t really listen to it. As a young male actor, generally, the minute you’re not playing a zany artist type, the minute you’re in a suit, people fling it at you.”

Not exactly a denial! Meanwhile, Callum told THR over the summer, “I know as much as you do—really, I know as much as you do. I’ll tell you what’s so funny about the Bond thing: Even your best friends ask you, people text you that you haven’t spoken to for 10 years—and you know nothing! It’s such a weird thing of something happening and nothing happening at all. I genuinely know nothing. I just find it quite amusing.”

Honestly, I’d take either of them as Bond. Or both! Just happy to be here.

#6760. Inside the Underground Harry Styles Hospitality Network

It remains one of Gillian Harmon’s great pop culture regrets that she never got to see One Direction live. The 26-year-old is from Irvington, a small town in Mobile, Alabama, where major artists rarely make so much as a pit stop. “I think the closest they came was either Atlanta or New Orleans,” she says, though at the time Harmon was too young to make the trip across state lines on her own.

A year ago, she moved to New York City, which is more frequently graced with the presence of pop stars. Especially these days, as Harry Styles performs a 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden, with fans coming from all corners of the world to attend. But Harmon, who lives on the Upper West Side, had something many of them don't: an apartment with a spare bedroom. So, in the spirit of fandom and hospitality, she figured she could give someone else the experience she wished she had and started inviting out-of-state Styles fans to crash—for free.

Harmon isn't the only one. Around the city, a small hospitality network has emerged among Styles devotees, with fans opening their apartments to strangers traveling to New York to see the residency. They offer up their couches, guest rooms, and even subway directions, acting as something closer to a tour guide than a host. For fans coming from places where seeing Styles requires a flight, hotel, and a considerable financial commitment, their generosity can make a huge difference. To these fans, seeing Harry Styles in concert is not a luxury. It's an inalienable right.

When tickets for the MSG residency went live this past January, not all New York-based Harry fans were feeling so magnanimous. Some fans who couldn’t get tickets complained of tourists swooping in and snatching them up. Harmon, however, saw an opportunity. If fans were coming all the way to New York City to see Styles command the stage in a rotation of business casual get-ups while singing the hits from his four solo albums, she could help ease the financial burden. When she posted a TikTok offering her spare bedroom to roving fans, the response was immediate. More than halfway through the residency, she has already hosted four people, with more scheduled to arrive for Styles’ final run of shows. Her roommates, who aren’t particularly devoted Harries themselves, were game. After all, they are used to Harmon's adventures in popstar-chasing, and they liked the idea of meeting new people.

Harmon gave priority to people who told her it was their first chance to see Styles, particularly those coming from places where the cost of both travel and accommodations would have been difficult to absorb. When too many fans wanted room and board for the same dates, she would simply spin a wheel.

The arrangement has made Harmon’s five-bedroom apartment a kind of accidental commune. She has personally shepherded some of her guests to the Garden by subway, shown first-time visitors how to navigate the city, and met up with them post-concert to debrief. They’ve gone to pop-ups, ridden boats in Central Park, and explored Roosevelt Island. “It was really wholesome,” Harmon says.

She has experienced the financial and logistical hell of trying to attend a Harry Styles concert firsthand. Harmon has traveled to Nashville for Styles shows herself, sometimes with friends from college, and has been scammed trying to get tickets. She remembers the humbling experience, later, of unknowingly buying bad seats. But she was grateful just to be in the building. The MSG residency marked her fifth time seeing him live. And she recently watched her best friend, who flew from Alabama for his first-ever Styles concert, have the time of his life in the pit.

It’s fitting that friendship has become part of the Harry Styles fan experience. During the 32-year-old’s Wembley show in June, he announced that “being somebody’s friend is the most incredible, beautiful thing you could possibly be to someone.” Throughout his solo career, Styles has returned to the intimacy of friendship as both a thematic linchpin and guiding philosophy: the people you find, the people who stay, the people who make an otherwise lonely life a little less so. Fans have especially latched onto the motto "Treat People with Kindness,” from the Fine Line track of the same title. “They’re happy,” Harmon says. “They’re positive, uplifting, encouraging.”

Across town, 32-year-old Carolina Sanchez saw Harmon’s video and got inspired. Originally from Mexico, Sanchez has been a Styles fan since he was first discovered on X Factor in 2010 and later moved to New York. When she saw a slew of comments from eager fans needing a place to stay under Harmon’s videos, she offered up her own two-bedroom in Staten Island.. Soon, messages came pouring in.

“I just want to be part of something special,” Sanchez told me. Her first guests arrived in early October. At first, Sanchez admits, the idea of allowing strangers into her home made her nervous. But she started vetting prospective guests on Instagram and getting a sense of their connection to Styles and his music. Eventually, she created a Google form asking for basic information and identification to make sure the person she had been speaking with was the person who arrived her the door.

Her husband was initially surprised by the arrangement but understood the compulsion. He had seen firsthand how expensive Sanchez’s own ticket to the concert was. If hosting another fan meant someone could put that money towards a ticket of their own, Sanchez wanted to help. Now, her husband is cleaning their guest room and putting together goodie bags for the people staying there.

Sanchez hopes the connections will last beyond the residency. She imagines visiting some of the women she meets on future trips, including one who is coming from Florida. The idea, she says, is to make friends and treat other people well. In the process, she is also making New York feel a little less like a city of strangers. “When I've told people what I was doing, they're like, Are you insane? Are you crazy?," recounts Zaia Rodriguez, one of Sanchez’s lucky guests. “I think part of it is stan culture; we make these connections on the internet with absolute strangers, and we talk to these people so often, we bond over the things that we love, and we become friends.”

For other fans, the journey is a little more complicated. Maria Miglio, a 29-year-old surgery resident from just outside Detroit, flew to NYC with a coworker and stayed a 15-minute walk from MSG. The hotel was $500-a-night, and tickets to the concert set her back another $200. Residents in Miglio’s program get only four days off each month. She flew out Friday after work and was back in Detroit by Sunday.

“Concerts are just such a community-based thing, especially for me,” says Erowyn Walsten, a 20-year-old student at the Fashion Institute of Technology. For her, the neighborly instincts demonstrated by Styles devotees are innate to One Direction fandom. She attended her first 1D show when she was nine, and even had a Harry Styles doll; he was always her favorite. She saw him again at 16, and is now preparing to go to MSG alone, where she expects to make friends, like she has at other concerts.

“I really think that honestly, as long as I've even been a Directioner, it truly felt like a family,” she says. The fandom’s largely female community, she believes, has made it easier to form lasting connections with people who are, ultimately, total strangers. Some of her closest friendships have grown out of mutual acquaintances met through Styles. “I think it's one of the most beautiful things,” she says.

The residency has also given the Garden a particular significance, the same way it’s Mecca for fans of the New York Knicks. Styles has called the venue “Harry’s House,” a phrase that has stuck with devotees. Cara McDonald is planning to fly from Ireland for the historic residency, the longest single-engagement run in the venue’s history, even with the steep price of hotels and flights. But she’s been saving up. Like Walsten, Mcdonald’s first concert was One Direction, giving the trip a certain emotional resonance. Even the cost of attending has become part of the story: McDonald’s resale pit ticket for the residency cost more than the ticket she bought for his previous tour in Los Angeles. But that's her primary indulgence, she says. “Concerts and rent, that’s it.”

There’s also a sense that this moment might be more fleeting than it seems. In a September 9th email to fans, Styles wrote that he “doesn't know what comes next,” a line that sent fans online into a frenzy of speculation. For those old enough to remember the collective emotional whiplash of One Direction’s indefinite hiatus announcement, there’s a particular appeal in making the trip now, while there's still a chance.

#6758. Just One Thing: Polo Ralph Lauren’s Polo Blaze Bag

Who says you need to know how to ride a horse to dress like an equestrian? Certainly not Polo Ralph Lauren, whose new Polo Blaze collection brings the elegance of the stables to city streets. (In equestrian parlance, a blaze is the distinctive white marking that runs down a horse’s face.) With its sweeping curves, rich leather, and saddle-inspired stitching, the collection has all the hallmarks of traditional saddlery, interpreted through a decidedly modern lens.

Of course, horses have long been part of Ralph Lauren’s design vocabulary (see: the iconic Polo Pony, the saddle-inspired Polo ID bag, and the Ricky, which takes some of its cues from a 19th-century saddle carrier). The Polo Blaze continues this tradition, but with a softer, more sculptural approach to the familiar codes of the stable. The collection includes shoulder bags in two sizes as well as a top-handle style, but we’re particularly taken with the larger shoulder bag.

There’s hardly a right angle in sight. From the gently curved double flaps to the sweeping, wing-like sides, every element of the bag seems to follow its own graceful arc. Even the two slender shoulder straps emerge from pointed leather tabs that recall the workmanship of a saddle. Open it up, and there’s a suede-lined interior, complete with a zippered pocket. And dangling from one side is a detachable door-knocker charm featuring the Polo Pony, a playful reference to hardware found on a Polo bag from the 1990s. Available in Black, Currant, Ash, and Chestnut, the Polo Blaze looks particularly appealing in the latter two earthy shades.

As for how to wear it? We’d pair its saddle-inspired curves with something a little less buttoned-up: a worn-in leather jacket, an oversized knit, or a favorite pair of jeans. No matter which side of the English-versus-Western debate you fall on, with the Polo Blaze, there’s no need to play favorites.

#6757. The Best Men's Crewneck Sweatshirt in 2026, According to GQ

There’s no such thing as ‘the best men’s crewneck sweatshirt,’ at least not in the objective sense. As tactile and quantifiable garments can be, the truth is it’s all open to interpretation, and comes down to personal taste (even if your personal taste sucks). That said… I do have some strong opinions on what makes a good sweatshirt and have tested too many to name. I grew up wearing cheap, serviceable sweats from places like Walmart. I’ve also invested in unreasonably heavy 24-ounce sweatshirts and became obsessed with the unyielding craftsmanship of Japanese reproductions that required rare loopwheel machines.

Through decades of experience, I’ve honed in on what makes a sweatshirt special. A good crewneck sweatshirt should be comfortable, and that all comes down to fabric and fit. The fabric, usually made of either a French terry or a brushed fleece, should be both dense and soft. The silhouette shouldn’t squeeze, but should be relaxed enough to layer over a T-shirt or even a button-up. I’ve also dialed-in on the things you should avoid, like when sweatshirts are too tight in the neck, especially as a guy with a thicker gullet for my frame. And I really hate when sweatshirts are too long. As a long-torso individual, you’d think this wouldn’t be a problem, but it’s something that feels endemic to the genre.

Now that I’ve given you a brief tour of the weeds, let’s get into what you came here for. Through rigorous research and far too much time on our hands, here’s what’s what in the world of crewneck sweatshirts.

Reigning Champ has been in the sweats game for generations, producing some of the absolute finest hoodies, sweatpants, and crewnecks around. When I was first introduced to the brand an unspeakable number of years ago, it left an impression on me. The idea that something so basic could be so good revealed to me that my base line for quality was much lower than I’d realized.

Though we here at GQ have adored their slim-fit crewnecks for years, Reigning Champ's more classic-fitting sweatshirt is one that will stay steady through the fickle fashion trend cycle. It's made with custom-knit midweight French Terry fabric, cut with a relaxed but clean fit, and sewn with super smooth flatlock seams to cut down on bulk. While most sweatshirts will opt for either raglan sleeves or set-in sleeves, Reigning Champ’s crewneck stands out for its unique construction that uses both techniques. The result is a more tailored set-in sleeve look at the front with raglan details at the back to give the wearer a freer range of motion.

The brand’s name alone sets high expectations, and in every aspect, Reigning Champ’s crewneck sweatshirt meets and exceeds them. While $125 isn’t by any means cheap, the stunning quality from the fabric to the fit and finish all equate to a sweatshirt that punches well above its weight class. If I really had to nit-pick, though, I'd like to see the color palette expand a little more, especially for such an essential piece of kit.

If your sweatshirt budget is decidedly smaller, your first stop should be Russell Athletic, the Alabama sportswear stalwarts who literally invented the crewneck sweatshirt way back in 1926. Almost a century later, they're still turning out the best bang-for-your-buck fleece crew on the market. It's got all the classic details that made Russell a household name: ribbing at the cuffs and hem, a V-insert collar, and a classic cut (size down if relaxed ain't exactly your thing).

The midweight 9 oz. fleece is pleasantly soft and warm, and it's moisture-wicking and breathable so if you run a little hot, it won't emphasize the sweat in ‘sweatshirt’. The thing I like most about Russell’s crewnecks is that they still fit like the vintage joints—but you don’t have to work yourself to death bobbing between vintage stores trying to hunt one down.

No list of the best crewneck sweatshirts would be complete without Champion's reverse weave joint in the mix. Todd Snyder’s legendary collab (see below) has got style and function down pat for the new-school, but the OG heavyweight pullover deserves a crown of its own. The sturdy cotton-poly blend is soft but will hold its shape after countless wash cycles (loungewear and pizza go hand in hand—residual stains do not). Fabric aside, the fit is just right: not too slim, not too baggy, and with slightly dropped shoulders to make your neckline really pop. We pick quality over quantity any day, but with this classic sweatshirt you get the go-to year-round layering piece for the fewest amount of dollar bills.

If you’re expecting a soft, motherly embrace, I hate to tell you this, but Champion’s iconic Reverse Weave sweats aren’t the softest. In fact, they’ve got a pretty rough hand. But don’t worry about that too much because that’s just straight out of the box. What you get in return is an unquestionably beastly durability. And the longevity you get out of them means they’ll only get softer and luscious with age.

You can’t ignore the impact that vintage clothing has on the modern fashion landscape, not just for the endless references and inspiration it gives designers, but also for the sheer explosion of secondhand style. Vintage-obsessed dudes like myself will search high and low for forgotten garments with esoteric details, from jeans left in abandoned barns to rare leather jackets tucked away in grandpa’s attic. And if you’re thrifting skills aren’t up to snuff or if coughing up the dough to a dealer is too big of a hit, the best thing to do is to look to Japan where they’re even more obsessed with reviving the grails of bygone eras.

While many repro brands deserve their flowers, I’m particularly keen on Buzz Rickson’s' interpretation of the perfect vintage sweatshirt. The fabric is made using ultra rare loopwheel knitting machines that knit the terry material methodically and slowly, using the natural tension of gravity to achieve a product that’s shockingly soft for its density. It also results in a fabric that’s totally seamless around the torso, an old-school detail that’s hard to come by but oh-so-satisfying once you do. The crewneck sweatshirt also features low-profile flatlock seams, tall ribbing at the cuffs and hems, and the throwback V-neck insert for easy donning.

HAVEN's Excel crewneck employs the label's telltale details like custom ribbing and underarm gussets for increased range of motion. But the star of the show has to be the fabric which comes from rare 1980s Azume knitting machines, lauded for producing low-tension French terry with unrivaled softness and character.

Lady White Co.'s methodical approach to jersey knits has brought them to the top of the heap not just for tees and sweatshirts, but for the entire wardrobe. It's mini crewneck uses custom-milled terry fabric that's cut to a flattering cropped silhouette and garment-dyed for depth.

Look, I'm just as surprised as you are that Gap's heavyweight sweatshirt is not only $70, but actually that good. It's legit heavy and will handily knock out other sweats in beefier weight classes, especially since you can often find it on a mega discount.

The kings and queens of American-made cotton fleece at Camber make their crewneck from a beefy 12-ounce cotton fleece with just enough elastic in the body panels to make it feel like a big hug. Plus you can get it in 11 colors.

Dyed one at a time by hand, each sweatshirt from the New York-based indie label Buckets is completely unique and certainly distinct from the droves of potassium-dyed, sun-faded, vintage-inspired sweats that have flooded the market in recent years.

NYC-based 3sixteen has built out a line of carefully dialed-in menswear, like this hardy crewneck made with a fleece that's, quote, "some of the heaviest available on the market." And yet it's the pockets, surreptitiously slipped into the side seams, that have us nodding in appreciation.

Known for its chef-approved T-shirts, Whitseville's reproduction sweats deserve equal praise for its heavy all-cotton fleece, tubular construction, and double-V gussets that reference rare vintage crewnecks.

Quince's 70-30 cotton-poly blend recalls vintage sweats of yesteryear, the kind that were as soft as they were durable and didn't break the bank. Its Everyday fleece crew ticks all the boxes.

There are levels to sweatshirts, as humble as they are. What we look for in high-quality sweatshirts comes down to fabric, construction, and fit. Sweatshirt fabrics should be soft, certainly, but many high-quality options are quite burly and stiffer than you'd think. Most of the time, that means the more material goes into the sweatshirt the longer it'll last. And if you're willing to commit to them, they'll get softer and more comfortable the more you wear and launder them.

Most garments are made by overlapping fabrics and sewing them together. That may be fine for a dress shirt, but sweatshirts are made of a thicker, knit fabric which can bulky and irritating when it's sewn like this. We like sweatshirts that are made with flatlock seams which are made by butting two fabrics next to each other rather than overlapping; the result is a smoother, flatter seam. On rarer occasions, some sweatshirts are made the old-school way on either tubular knitting machines or very rare loopwheel knitting machines which produces a sweatshirt without any side seams on the body. Garment nerds go gaga over this kind of detail, but it's by no means a requirement for a good sweatshirt.

Sweatshirt fabrics are typically made from terry cloth, French terry, or brushed terry. (If that sounds familiar, it's because terry cloth is the same stuff that's used to make bath towels.) Terry cloth features loops of yarns which are absorbent and insulating. But the main difference between your bath towel and your sweatshirt is that sweatshirts only have the loops on the inside of the garment. Often, those loops are either brushed or shorn to give the material a luxuriously fluffy hand.

Fit is always subjective, but classic-fitting sweatshirts will fit somewhat relaxed all-around and fall at the hips. Slimmer sweatshirts will fit better if you want to layer them under a jacket and look cleaner with slim-fitting pants. For a fit that's more of-the-moment, opt for a sweatshirt that's boxier and cropped to go with some high-waisted, baggy trousers.

The humble crewneck helped Steve McQueen evade capture in The Great Escape, cemented John Travolta’s heartthrob status in Grease, and made Eddie Murphy a badass in Beverly Hills Cop. Paul Newman, the patron saint of laid-back menswear, wore one religiously. And today, a roster of famous—and famously stylish—dudes still put their trust in it. The only difference now is that it comes in a rainbow of different colors and silhouettes, not to mention fabrics far beyond the staid French terry.

Like many menswear staples, crewneck sweatshirts were born from athletics and have transcended into everyday leisure. You could style a crewneck with baggy jeans and sick sneakers for a streetwear-leaning aesthetic, dive headfirst into a preppy look with a pair of chinos and loafers, or turn up the lounge-factor and double it up with some sweatpants and classic sneakers.

Like The Bachelor, we had a flock of hopefuls vying for our love. But instead of hot singles, we had to dole out roses to a gaggle of cozy sweatshirts. One by one, we got to know each sweatshirt, taking them out on dates (literally), and looking intently for rock-solid characteristics, flaws, and dealbreakers. We wore every sweatshirt like any other piece of clothing in our closets, styled them with our favorite pants, scrutinized their fits, put them through harsh laundry cycles, and repeated the whole process over again. What we ended up with is this A-team of great crewnecks, from budget options to luxurious upgrades, and everything between.

#6755. My Two Wedding Dresses Were a Love Letter to My Haitian Roots and New Ghanaian Family

I was looking for just one perfect gown, but what I got was a beautiful story of bridging heritage, family, and belonging. (And of course, two absolutely stunning custom pieces.)

I thought I would cry. There I was perched prettily on a podium in a gorgeous champagne wedding dress and mantilla veil. My mom and three sisters beamed up at me in between their sips of bubbly, awaiting my enthusiastic proclamation that this dress was, much like my fiancé, The One.

A soft violin rendition of an inspirational song slowly crescendoed through the speakers, and it all felt like signs that this was the gown I’d say “I do” in. I stared at myself in the mirror almost blankly, tilted my head, and asked my family, “Really? This is beautiful but is it me?” I tried to find the words to explain to my heart-eyed audience that there were no butterflies, no fireworks, no cinematic overture, no little voice spelling out yes.

I waited, hoping the rush that was supposed to sweep me away was a little off schedule. But...nothing. Isn't this the part where I’m supposed to burst into tears? I couldn’t rationalize how all of the frenzy and booked appointments came down to this level of underwhelm. I left without a dress that day, and even though my wedding was in a mere two months (yes, really), I wasn't panicked—yet.

I know what you’re thinking: “Isn’t it a little late to be wedding dress shopping?” And normally, you’d be right. But after getting engaged in November 2025, my fiancé and I decided to skip the long engagement. There was just one tiny detail: We had two months to plan the entire wedding, which meant finding the dress of my dreams was officially a race against the clock.

Unfortunately, this dress scenario played out several more times. By the time I got to Kleinfeld Bridal, the iconic New York City shop featured on TLC’s Say Yes to the Dress, I was positive I would find the perfect wedding dress there. I felt confident, primed to cancel future dress appointments, telling myself this day would end with the happy tears and excitement that I dreamt of as a little girl playing dress up. My mom and sisters were aligned, and kept their eyes open for any “wow” moments. Then my stylist brought out an every-bride-would-love-this custom Pnina Tornai gown that had a compelling backstory. A sucker for some good lore, but not an emotional buyer, I was okay with not having it. Once again, I left another bridal salon dress-less.

All of this had me perplexed: I loved how I looked in every gown, but it felt like it was something bigger missing and made me consider meeting with a therapist to figure it out. Was it wedding jitters? I dissected myself after every boutique visit, and often wondered, “What’s wrong with me?” Conscious of the clock, part of me wanted to just pick one and keep the peace. Appointment after appointment, maybe I was too difficult to please? But I refused to talk myself into a dress—I am allergic to settling, after all.

I grew up Haitian-American, and in my family, there was a real appreciation for presentation and what you wore. You dressed up for church, celebrations, and even going to the grocery store. Don’t get me started on school picture day. Even in college, while my classmates wore sweats to class, I’d be pumping through campus in heels. My family instilled in me that you showed up looking good because looking good was part of showing up. It was more than superficial; looking good was a way of showing respect, taking pride in yourself, and representing your family with honor. So I wasn't just trying to find a beautiful gown. Before I took on a new last name, filled with new traditions, I needed to recognize myself—where I come from—in it.

Everything shifted on a solo trip to San Francisco. I was luxuriating in bed at the Palace Hotel when a thought landed on me like fresh dew in the morning: I, a Haitian-American fashion girlie, was marrying a Ghanaian artist—I was entering a marriage that brought two cultures, two families, and two creative identities together. What if I wear a Haitian designer for the ceremony, and then honor his culture with a Ghanaian traditional gown during the reception? I thought. Finally, the feeling I had been searching for started coursing through my body.

For my Haitian piece, I began researching and it ended almost instantaneously when I stumbled upon Jean-Ralph Thurin, a Haitian designer I was already following on Instagram. We met years ago during NYFW when I was getting my start in the industry. I reached out and scheduled an appointment for as soon as I landed back on the East coast.

Jean-Ralph’s atelier was elevated, with cream, ivory, and white gowns displayed throughout the luscious showroom; each one reminded me of some special element of Haiti. The loveseats created an intimate, almost familial feeling, like you’d come over to someone’s beautiful living room and settled in to watch a show.

The family vibes only intensified as the appointment went on. Jean-Ralph’s wife, a fellow designer, helped me in and out of dresses, and his daughter was his attendant. It felt like being at my aunt’s house, and suddenly it made sense why none of the other shops worked for me—I was meant to be here.

As my sisters oohed and ahhed at me in a dress that I couldn’t stop smiling in, Jean-Ralph sketched an entirely new option for me in his notepad. It was a rendition of what I had on (which was sadly too big and couldn’t be altered due to the elaborate detailing) and totally me. “I’m inspired,” He told me. “I’m going to design this for you.” I was honored. It’s like he saw past the weeks of hidden disappointment I’d been hiding behind my smile, and he knew there was a story begging to be told through my dress.

With just five weeks until the wedding, I held my breath through every fitting, clinging to hope. The gown, which was for the ceremony, had a pearl-beaded lace bodice in a warmer ivory champagne. The moment I put it on, everyone—my mom, my sisters, and yes, myself—said it: “This is the one.” I never felt so sure, so complete. I felt like me: the once-shy Haitian-American girl who grew up to be a woman of the world.

And yet, we were only halfway there. For my second look, my fiancé’s entire family helped bring it to life: His brother, a menswear designer in Ghana, connected me to a talented seamstress; his sister bought the material; and his mom searched for the accessories and we discovered renowned Ampy Bridal fans. One WhatsApp call after the other, an ocean away, my gown came together: a vibrant purple and fuchsia ombré, complemented by rich kente detailing, glistening stones, and flowery embellishments.

When it finally arrived, I knew this wasn’t something even a fairy godmother could have conjured. As the first child and eldest daughter of immigrant parents, I was used to forging the path and getting things done. This time, it was a family affair, and I was catching a glimpse of who I was becoming. What started as a dress became something much bigger: a beautiful merging of my Haitian heritage and his Ghanaian roots, stitched together by the family I was becoming part of. And somehow, before we even said “I do,” I already felt like I belonged.

And then, after a dizzying two months, there I was: walking down the aisle feeling like royalty in my custom Haitian designer gown. Every emotion came flooding to the surface. The butterflies I’d been waiting for were swirling in my stomach. At the reception, I changed into my one-of-a-kind traditional Ghanaian dress, dancing towards my husband as every piece of me was on full, beautiful display: a Haitian-American, a new wife, a woman who loves a Ghanaian man and his culture. My Haitian gown let me honor where I came from; my Ghanaian gown let me honor the culture I was marrying into. And together, they felt like coming home.

#6754. Ask Earl With Laurel Pantin: How to Style Leopard as a Neutral

We all have that one friend we turn to for fashion advice. On the internet, that second set of eyes is Laurel Pantin—a writer, editor, mom, and entrepreneur-about-town—whose never overdressed or underdressed. Ask Earl is a direct line to Pantin’s brain, where once a month, she’ll help you solve the age-old question of what to wear—and how to wear it, well—for any possible scenario. Trying to figure out how to style work pants without looking corporate? Or how to pack for a long-haul flight with toddlers? Maybe it’s summer outfit ideas that don’t involve dresses... Whatever your question, Ask Earl is where you’ll find the answer—and Earl URL is where you can shop it, too.

I *love* animal print. I say “animal” as a catchall because I wear leopard, cheetah, jaguar, ocelot, lynx, etc. patterns all pretty interchangeably. My favorite animal prints come from the big cats—tiger, too—but I think for a lot of people it can be intimidating. Remember the Mob Wife trend from a few years ago? Yeah, that’s not what we’re going for, but I know when a lot of people see animal prints, that’s the direction their minds immediately go when it comes to styling.

The whole “leopard is a neutral” thing is a cliché because I think it’s true. The colors are neutral! And the print is so familiar and so wearable that it goes with basically everything. But for the purposes of this article we’re going to assume the reader is brand new to styling spots, stripes, and scales, and I’m going to break down some of my top tips for making animal print wearable.

How gorgeous are these calf hair trousers from Arma? The fit is divine, the feel is super soft, and I love that the zebra stripe is dark brown against beige rather than black and white. Black and white is so graphic and loud, this quiets it down. Then, a brown satin shirt (this one is Comme Si) is nicely tonal with the pants. But… if I had stopped there it would risk looking like theme dressing. A little too literal and on the nose, like “fashion person on safari.” The blue Homme Girls button-down layered in breaks it up, brings in a sense of humor and casualness, and keeps the outfit from feeling one-note. The shoes, which are perfect, are Herbert Levine.

This is an EXTRA statement skirt, being both leopard and fully sequin. (It’s Ashish, and it was custom made for the store, and we have just one!) I wore it in Paris with a khaki button-down and a bright red sweater around my shoulders (concept 1!) and it was perfect. I also love it with a sweatshirt like this. Sweatshirts are a must-have for me to make an outfit less precious, and this one is Suzie Kondi. I love it because it’s a classic color and shape, but terry so it has an interesting texture, and the sporty casualness of it helps the skirt sing without dressing it up even more.

I don’t typically do snakeskin, but I like this snakeskin dress from Chan Luu a lot. Snake to me feels very capital-S sexy, so instead of bringing sexy back, I’d like to put sexy back. A cotton knit from Kallmeyer and an oversized Rùadh jacket help make the print feel more approachable.

This shearling spotted coat from Arma is heaven! The brand’s shearling and leather are all by-product material from the meat industry, and they make some of the most beautiful leather, suede, and shearling pieces I’ve ever seen. To keep it from going Mob Wife, I went with the most relied-upon styling trick of all time: denim. These jeans are Rùadh and I love the narrow fit and dark-ish wash. The jeans make it feel day-to-day and super wearable. I also love bright red with animal print, and this merino sweater from &Daughter makes it feel special without being too attention-grabby.

This Róhe coat is so beautiful, so elegant, so obviously tasteful. I love the little look I had on under it too! The leopard coat on its own with the look underneath could come off as being a little too traditional, vintage-inspired, or staid. To make it more interesting, I put on this Zankov sequin embellished scarf. Making it slightly less traditionally “elegant” makes it feel more personal and less like a costume to me.

Want more? Shop September’s Ask Earl, below.

I’ve always loved shopping, but lately I’m feeling exhausted by it. There are too many links, too many newsletters in my inbox, too many discount codes on Instagram, etc. I’m trying to shop less but also find my way back to loving clothes. Do you have any advice for how to make my old clothes feel new again and style them with more recent purchases?

I hear you. I never thought I’d grow tired of shopping, window shopping, casually browsing, or just checking things out, and yet—here I am. I write a fashion and styling newsletter (called Earl Earl), and I own a small shop in Beverly Hills (of the same name), but so often when I’m online or on Instagram, my mind plays this funny trick where almost any picture of clothing I look at morphs into an AI slop pile of rags and fabric… just more and more and more stuff, multiplying before my eyes, crashing into me like a tidal wave of fast-fashion synthetic blends that will never, never, biodegrade!!!

I do love new things. I love to collect. But every so often, it’s nice to just say enough and dedicate yourself to wearing what you already own. There are pieces in my closet I’ve worn since high school (I’m 40) and others that I brought home last week, and I delight in wearing them all together. Here are a few ways I make that work:

Contrasting something well-worn (old band tees, your favorite jeans from 10 years ago,the perfect blazer you bought with your first paycheck, etc.) with an item that’s a bit morepolished keeps your outfit feeling harmonious and intentional, rather than simply old.

Instead of wearing my hoodie from sophomore year of boarding school with my Gap chinos from 2006, for example, I’d wear it with a tidier pair of blue jeans that aren’t super worn-in or distressed. And I’d wear the old Gap chinos with a crisp, newish button-down.

Special-occasion dresses are hard to re-wear casually. A special top (maybe a beaded cardigan or a chiffon blouse) is much easier to repurpose. I like to wear these items with pleat-front trousers and flat sandals to make it feel a little more masculine and laid-back. The same goes for the opposite configuration. A jazzy skirt looks great with a sweatshirt or men’s button-down, or something casual and low-key.

If I splurge on a trendy piece, I have a hard time letting it go. (Looking at you, The Row jellies.) It may have felt right in the moment, but now it’s a bit too reminiscent of that time. So I let the item “rest” in my closet. Usually, it needs to be on ice for at least three years before I bring it back out.Sometimes longer. Once it’s no longer in our consciousness— i.e., once all the fast-fashion brands are finished making dupes—then I consider bringing it back out. This is my favorite way to wear my past purchases; it’s such a thrill to rediscover a “vintage” gem in your own closet. Knowing exactly when to bring a look back is intuitive. Keep in mind, though, that if something lights you up inside and makes you feel like you’re covered in glitter—even when you aren’t covered in glitter—then youmust really love it. No amount of time or advice in Vogue can take that away from you. So do you, and it will be great.

Want more? Shop August’s Ask Earl, below.

For someone who grew up in Texas in extreme heat and now lives in Los Angeles, I am especially intolerant of the heat. I hate it. I don’t like feeling my skin roasting through the windows of my car, I don’t like burning my feet on the pavement around my house, and I especially don’t like getting dressed when it’s over ninety degrees outside. I know what to wear and what to do (wear as little as possible and stay indoors) but that kind of one-and-done dressing, or going purely for the practical runs against my grain. I like to put outfits together, I like when there’s a little bit of an artful mismatch. I really like layering.

But it’s impossible when I’m this hot, and as much as I feel bummed out throwing on a dress and heading out the door, most days it’s necessary. Most days, not every day. I had a lot of fun playing around with the items we have in my store, Earl IRL, playing dress up and imagining ways I could feel layered without feeling hotter. I pulled from a mix of our summer items and a few new fall deliveries and devised a few strategies.

This is a good one, because no matter what you put it with you’ll feel a little more styled and considered. Basically, a long necklace (one that hits just about below your breastbone) will help break out your outfit and add another layer of interest. No matter how light and cooling the rest of your look is, whether it’s a tunic from Comme Si and Birrot pants like this, or a gauzy sundress, an interesting long necklace will help it feel more pulled together. This one is from Presley Oldham.

I also love to add in a sheer element. This plaid Tibi top lets me wear a very skimpy little camisole without it actually looking like I’m wearing a skimpy little camisole. The sheer layer allows for a breeze that helps keep me cool while also introducing a nice textural element.

One of my absolute favorite summer outfits is a sarong with a button-down worn on top. It feels so sexy but also grown-up—I just love it. In the city, however, the sarong shows a little too much leg. I like to adapt the look by wearing my sarong over a fuller circle skirt with something fitted like this Birrot tank on top. Suzie Kondi’s gingham skirt has volume and keeps my legs super cool, and the Chan Luu sarong doesn’t add any weight to the outfit. I like this noisy clash of colors and prints, but of course, you could always go with solids.

A wide variety of textures will also help your outfit feel more layered and intentional. This wrap skirt from Chan Luu has a fabulous crochet pom pom detail around the hem, and the wrap feature gives it even more of a layered feel without being any warmer. I love it with this ultra-light cashmere tee from Lisa Yang because the fuzziness of the cashmere with the linen skirt plus pom poms creates so much interest and variety, it feels like a much more complicated and “styled” outfit, despite it being just two pieces. This tee looks like it would be quite hot, but it has a super open knit weave and feels like almost nothing on your body.

I bet you saw this one coming! Is it the most creative outfit ever? No. But it does the trick. Adding a big, gorgeous belt amps up your summer dress and makes it feel more interesting. This belt in particular is a winner because it’s a wide, stretchy swath of a material called Lay. It’s by Birrot, and I love the way it wraps around and can tie in the front. Some belts slide around all day and you find yourself constantly fussing with it to get the buckle to stay in the right place, but this one just stays put. No fussing necessary.

I often see people suggest wearing a button-down completely unbuttoned all the way down the front and open. I don’t love that look—I think it looks unfinished and just not that great. My workaround when I do want an actual layer over my tank is to button just the bottom few buttons instead. I like the shape that it creates with the shirt and it still lets lots of airflow in around my arms. It can also help something like drawstring “soft pants” (like these from Suzie Kondi) look a little more pulled together and a little less like pajamas.

Not because I don’t like my legs, not because I don’t like them generally, there is really no easy reason why I don’t like wearing, and have a hard time styling shorts. After my mid-30s, I started to feel they were a bit infantilizing. I felt silly wearing them, like I was dressing up as a little kid. It took me a while to figure out what kinds worked for me, and which I could wrap my head around (the flat-front chino J.Crew shorts of the early 00’s are a no-go, so are pleat-front khakis—too old on me), but it all took a lot of trial and error.

Living in Los Angeles where it’s warm year-round and can be absolutely boiling in the summer, I had to figure it out—as tricky as I find shorts, miniskirts are worse!—but now I think I have a good handle on the situation as a woman in her 40s. I tried on some of my favorite ones I have in my store, Earl IRL, to show how I’d wear them with some of our other new deliveries.

I actually really like my legs. I do a lot of heavy resistance training and they’re strong and I like them. However, my style typically doesn’t show much skin. I like to wear things oversized and relatively covered, so to balance these Made Some board shorts out, I went with an oversized Comme Si button-down in Grecian Blue. A logo-heavy tee would feel a bit too Gen Z for me, I’m really not trying to look like I’m in my twenties over here. These little classic blue sneakers also help. Whenever I wear little shorts like this I like to keep my foot covered so that I don’t feel like it’s just flesh out all the way down.

I don’t like to say anything has been “trending” but, boxer shorts have been trending for a few years. I love them in concept—they’re boyish, comfortable, cool, and generally pretty affordable. The trick here is to make them look like shorts, not underwear. A special knit on top works (if it’s too hot for a knit, try a little sleeveless linen blouse). This one is from Zankov and very lightweight. I also like to wear sandals that look very polished and special, like these from Herbert Levine. They’re burgundy suede and gorgeous. The boxers are Comme Si and come in a zillion colors, but I like the dark navy in the shorts. I also think this isn’t the typical way to wear them (I usually see them paired with a coordinating button down or a white tee) which makes them feel a little more grown-up and serious.

These Rachel Comey shorts are so cute, they have a lot of volume, are a great color, and an interesting shape. They’re very sporty, but clearly not true athletic shorts. I love them with another bright sporty piece, like this Rachel Comey sweatshirt, but like the boxer shorts, I prefer to wear them with slightly more polished shoes to keep them from looking too literal. These embellished suede flip-flops are also Herbert Levine and they are so, so comfortable. A tidy little leather pouch instead of a canvas tote also helps this feel like real clothes.

The only way I’m wearing denim shorts is long. Short jean shorts are too reminiscent of my childhood in Texas, so I prefer something slouchier and more skater now. This is the kind of look I typically go for: baggy, oversized and raw edge jean shorts worn low on the hips like a boy, but I love them dressed up. It’s unexpected and interesting, but totally works. In this case, the Kallmeyer Ellis shorts go beautifully with this Kallmeyer sculptural poplin top. The bell shape of the top offers a nice contrast to how straight the shorts are; it’s a great tension between masculine and feminine and feels very adult.

These jean shorts from Róhe are technically part of the long denim shorts, but they’re loooong. I love these. If they were a different material or had a pleat-front they’d be a totally different vibe and a little harder to style. I think those (on women over 40) can look a bit too granny-ish. These, however, are graphic and clean, and so boyish they can really support this embellished Zankov knit vest. Sparkle with denim, boyish and girlish, special and mundane—this whole look is just….perfect. You can do any shoe here: a heel would dress it up, a ballet flat would, too, but I like the idea of your most basic rubber flip-flops. A nice mix of all the things I love.

#6751. The Best Men's Jean Jacket 2026: 12 Fall Layering Essentials

Adding the best men's jean jacket to your closet is like drafting Lebron to your rec league team: you’ll end up with a ‘ship no matter how bad the rest of the squad is. Whatever you want to call ’em—jean jackets, denim jackets, trucker jackets—the all-American stalwarts are the layering MVPs of every outfit on the brink of an L. Makes sense considering blue jeans, the jacket’s southern equivalent, can do the exact same thing for your wardrobe. Workwear roots bestow the humble piece of outerwear with utilitarian features, durability, and classic proportions—a surefire formula that churns out menswear icons like double-knee pants and chore coats.

What started out as a work jacket to accompany the blue jeans made from the same burly denim material, jean jackets have grown out of their pragmatic uniform and are more of a fashion statement these days. Be it a luxurious runway riff, an upgraded take, or a down-home workhorse, every flavor of denim jacket has the potential to make every outfit pop. Of course, the trucker jacket is what comes to mind first. But denim jackets come in many forms and aren’t limited to the Levi’s version you likely have in your mind’s eye. Denim’s enduring appeal and boundless applications have seen it merge with chore coats, trenches, Harringtons and more, expanding the scope of jean jackets. That’s great news for anyone looking to find one that truly speaks to themselves, but terrible news for anyone attempting to wade through all the options.

So we did the denim digging for you. We went out and scraped the market for the absolute best men’s jean jacket, from the tried-and-true to the new-age startups and everything in-between.

This shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone. And if it is, as this company’s self-proclaimed Denim Guy, it’s definitely my fault for not teaching you. Levi's is the grand daddy of all jeans which puts them on a rarified level few others could ever hope to approach. The brand’s iconic 501 jean gets most of the (deserved) praise, but the Levi's trucker jacket also warrants recognition.

The very first iteration of the Levi's trucker jacket debuted in 1905 and has since gotten several updates, but the one most ubiquitous today is known as the Type III. It's the picture you have in your head when you think of a trucker jacket and it's great for so many reasons. The midweight denim is ideal for year-round wear, the trim and cropped silhouette has transcended trends for decades and, like the five-pocket blue jean, pairs with just about everything (and looks better the more you wear it). If you only have a hundred bucks to spare and enough room for just one denim jacket in your rotation, it had better be this one.

A chore coat isn’t what most people think of as a ‘jean jacket’. But I’m proposing this as a more practical, no-less stylish alternative to the usual trucker jackets you’re used to seeing. And if you’re taking the term ‘denim jacket’ liberally, any outerwear made of denim would count. Anyway. Chore coats are more commonly made of a sturdy canvas or heavy moleskin cotton fabric, but denim's resilience make it another reliable option for the workwear genre. It doesn't get much better than this one from Alex Mill.

The brand's range of modern menswear staples is no slouch when it comes to fabric and construction and its line of chore coats is among the best out there, even compared to the multi-generational stalwarts like Carhartt and Dickies. This one’s made with sturdy, yet broken-in 100% cotton Japanese denim and comes with dual chest pockets and hand pockets, not to mention a stealthy phone pocket. The relaxed fit borders on boxy and is roomy enough to layer over a sweater or thick hoody once the temps drop. But if you're not the denim type (why are you even here?) Alex Mill makes its work jacket in a range of different fabrics, too.

To me, Alex Mill’s chore coats are nearly perfect. They fit like a dream and come with just the right vintage details that make guys like me swoon. I’ve compared it with my vintage French chore coat and not only are the details almost identical, the craftsmanship is virtually the same. So you could search for hours for a vintage one, or you could save the time and money and just get Alex Mill’s.

Levi’s may be the dominant denim trucker jacket, but they aren’t the only ones with a classic trucker jacket etched into the annals of menswear history. Lee’s left an indelible mark on the American denim landscape and is rightfully considered one of the so-called Big Three along with Levi’s and Wrangler. Lee’s famed Rider jacket was first introduced in 1948 and is considered one of the best denim jackets of all time.

Today’s modern reproduction is made by the brand’s retro sub-label, Lee 101, and features the same left-hand twill denim the brand is famous for, this time woven by a storied Japanese denim mill. The signature zig-zag stitching details at the collar and front placket still remain, as do the cateye buttons at the waist, and the slim, hip-length silhouette. If you’re hardcore, I’d recommend you go with the raw denim version and earn those fades yourself. But if you can’t be bothered to put in the work for five years straight, then stick with the light wash version.

Fans of the Japanese brand Kapital are quick to point out the brand's head-spinning takes on denim. From painstaking boro patchwork stitched by hand to far-out interpretations of blue jeans, the cult-loved label is a true innovator in the denim space. Its catalog is chock full of certified grails, but if you’re focusing in on jackets, it doesn’t get any crazier than its boro jacket. From the outset, it looks more like an antique pile of fabric than a jacket—and that’s kind of the point. The jacket is made of dozens and dozens of fabric scraps, each one meticulously distressed—and then repaired— to look like worn-out vintage textiles before sewn back together as a single garment.

As you can imagine, the process is extraordinarily time-consuming. That immense dedication results in a jacket that’s truly not for the faint of heart or those with shallow pockets. This particular jacket takes inspiration from Type I denim jackets and features a single flap pocket, rear cinch, and a boxy cropped fit. It may look shredded, but putting it on feels like absolute butter thanks to the custom, boro-printed satin interior.

Kaptain Sunshine has long been known for its loving recreations of heritage American workwear, but the artful way it approaches its designs has earned it a ton of crossover appeal with the fashion crowd. Case in point: This one-pocket denim jacket, which is constructed according to classic selvedge standards, but has enough interesting details (including a buckle back) to inspire the envy of any runway show attendee. Wear it carefully—you never know which menswear nerd could be nearby and hoping to swipe it from your chair.

The circle of iconic denim jackets is small. Even so, there’s one that doesn’t get as much attention it ought, and that’s the Type II trucker jacket. Levi’s introduced the Type II in 1953, the long-awaited follow up to the Type I. The features were much the same, but the main difference was the addition of a symmetry-imposing second pocket and adjustable waist tabs instead of a cinch back. The result is one of the most geometrically pleasing jackets ever. The boxy fit and spare details are very much in line with workwear designs, but there’s something also very minimalist about it, too. No wonder it still gets referenced and duped by modern designers.

Levi’s will always be the OG when it comes to the Type II, but if you really want to get one, The Real McCoy’s is the one to get. The Japanese brand is known for going insane lengths to reproduce the most coveted and iconic pieces of vintage menswear and their rendition of the Type II is a prime example. The denim was designed from the ground up, using a specifically sourced vintage loom that was able to deliver the kind of slubby character of ‘50s denim at a consistent clip. The result is one of the most accurate reproductions you can get. That is, if you can even find it. Thanks to the limited fabric production and high demand, the jacket is so sought after that it’s been sold out for ages.

Don’t let Gap’s iconic khakis ads make you forget that the iconic brand got its start in denim. That DNA is still prevalent today as Gap’s stable of denim offerings is as strong as ever. Case in point, this faithful take on the famous Type II trucker jacket featuring knife pleats, dual chest flap pockets, and a boxy cropped fit—all done in a hearty all-cotton denim.

If we didn’t tell you, you might not realize this was denim too. But even though it's finished in soft corduroy, there's a full denim jacket inside, taking trompe l’oeil to a new level. While most attempts would easily fall flat in the uncanny valley, Jeanerica's result offers the best of both worlds (and textures).

Before Ralph launched his western-inflected RRL line, Polo was still making workwear hits. And denimheads could easily miss this pitch-perfect take on the Type II trucker jacket with its impeccable cut and spot-on vintage wash.

J.Crew and Lee's collaborative iteration on the denim jacket is a true sleeper hit, featuring a mix of details from a corduroy collar, trendy (and practical) plaid lining, and those beautiful, unmistakable Lee trucker pockets. This is the denim jacket to take with you into fall.

Ralph's premium ranch-hand line has been quietly making the best faded denim in America for decades: The 'Leeland' wash has genuine depth to it, and even better—the buttons are embossed with “Cowboy.”

Material and construction: With denim jackets and jean jackets, the most important factor will be the denim itself. Make sure that the denim feels substantial and weighty. Good quality denim shouldn’t be too thin or loosely woven. Though I personally prefer denim without any sort of elastane, you may want to consider opting for a jacket with some stretch built into it for ease of movement. Even then, I’d advise you to limit the percentage of stretch to no more than 2%. Selvedge denim and Japanese denim are often a good sign of a high-quality fabric, but non-selvedge and non-Japanese denim can be well-made too, so don’t put all your trust in provenance.

Fit: Fit is subjective, but most trucker jackets follow a tried-and-true formula with a hem that hits right at the hips. They may have a leaner silhouette or a boxier cut, but a hallmark of trucker jackets is truly the cropped length which helps emphasize your natural proportions and lengthens your legs (without having to spend tens of thousands of dollars and months of agony). Denim jackets with hand pockets are often a little longer than those without, so if you may want to factor that into your decision.

Silhouette: Sizing is key, as well. Most denim jackets are cut on the more tailored end and around hip length. Make sure that the shoulder seams line up with your shoulder bones if not a little past. Keep in mind that you may want to layer underneath, since that will affect how snug the jacket will feel. With time, the sleeves of a trucker jacket will tend to get shorter as the elbow creases set in so if the sleeves are a tad long, you’re probably in a good place.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6747. Brancusi’s Appeal Is Eternal: Read Vogue’s 1995 Appreciation of the Sculptor

“Spare Essentials,” by Michael Brenson, was originally published in the October 1995 issue of Vogue.

For more of the best from Vogue’s archive, sign up for our Nostalgia newsletter here.

Constantin Brancusi and Pablo Picasso both settled in Paris in 1904, became integral parts of the city’s artistic avant-garde, and both, of course, became world-renowned artists. But in virtually every other respect they were opposites. Picasso had a remarkable, if not unprecedented, ability to transform aggression and violence into sources of unrestrainable creative energy; Brancusi made sculpture that is restrained even when it takes flight. Picasso changed styles all the time; Brancusi’s sculpture of 1940 looks much the same as it did in 1910. Picasso’s paintings are intensely autobiographical, but it is difficult to find evidence of Brancusi’s life in his work. While Picasso (born in 1881) made art that welcomed, indeed almost gauged, the convulsiveness of twentieth-century life, Brancusi (born in 1876) wanted his sculpture to offer a reality beyond the self, beyond the artist, beyond the nightmares and corruptions of politics and history.

In a society that tends to measure success in terms of products becoming bigger and better each year, Picasso’s series of distinct and sometimes startlingly different styles remains the model of appropriate artistic development. Brancusi’s career, in contrast, cannot be easily approached in terms of a word like development. The distinctions among most of the sixteen versions of Bird in Space that he modeled, carved, and polished over 20-some years are so subtle that it is difficult to tell even the order in which they were made. They suggest not a succession of moments but rather a single recurring moment, defined once and for all in its first formulation. Picasso’s flashy, unpredictable, copiously productive oeuvre energized the art market. Brancusi, though successful with American collectors, never had a dealer or gallery in Paris, where he lived for the last 53 years of his life.

Brancusi and Picasso also embody two fundamentally different experiences of time. Picasso’s style is so changeable, his imagery and compositions often so disjunctive, that his work implicitly argues that time stops for no one and threatens to destabilize everything as it marches relentlessly ahead. For Picasso, the new was power; its will to render obsolete what came before was as irresistible as a force of nature. Brancusi believed in timelessness, as Margit Rowell, one of the two curators (with Ann Temkin) of the landmark Brancusi retrospective that opens at the Philadelphia Museum of Art this month, points out. For him, newness, suggested by his spankingly clean surfaces and his recurring images of eggs, embryos, and swollen bellies, was itself timeless, a truth that connected him and everyone else to other cultures and ages. Time for Brancusi is a seamless, accepting, ever more expansive moment in which new and old, past, present, and future, forever coexist.

If Picasso was a poet of shock, Brancusi was a poet of fusion. He studied Plato, as well as Buddhism and other Eastern religions, and was familiar with theosophy, that influential late-nineteenth-century attempt to synthesize the religions of the world. He simplified not only to refine and purify but also to concentrate and embrace. In his variations on the motif of the kiss, he sealed together man and woman, and made the acts of looking, touching, and trusting equally indispensable. Brancusi’s refinement grew out of knowledge of the inspired economy of non-Western and preindustrial artistic traditions. It also reflected the widespread avant-garde belief that it was possible, through distillation and simplification, to strip away European values and conventions that many early modernists blamed for the Great War. In his 1937–38 memorial to the thousands of civilians who held off the German army in 1916 in Tirgu-Jiu, Romania, not far from his place of birth, Brancusi achieved a monument to fusion, a synthesis of monumentality and intimacy, movement and prayer, grandeur and simplicity, sculpture and site, that has haunted sculptors ever since.

Brancusi was both an outsider and an insider. He knew everyone. He was admired by Picasso and Henri Matisse. He worked briefly for Rodin and taught Amedeo Modigliani how to carve. Isamu Noguchi worked as his assistant. He was friends with Ezra Pound, James Joyce, and Erik Satie. Marcel Duchamp was essential to his success in America. But Brancusi always remained very much on his own. He never married. In 1934 he had a son by the English musician Vera Moore, but he and his son never met. Throughout his life, he enjoyed the company of young women, but those relationships remained private. Brancusi could be talkative, even garrulous, but about his personal life he was unfailingly discreet. He shared with many avant-garde artists an admiration for non-Western cultures and a belief that by exploring the mystery of form it was possible to arrive at basic truths. But he was never part of any movement. While it is difficult now to imagine the modernist mainstream without him, he was never really a mainstream figure.

While Picasso changed addresses many times, Brancusi basically lived in one place. He moved to 8 Impasse Ronsin in Montparnasse in 1916 and, twelve years later, to number 11. As he grew old and fragile, he became anxious about keeping his work together. He put more and more energy into making his studio a sacred and self-contained world, a temple in which he, in his increasingly famous white beard and white work clothes, would act as prophet and priest. The studio included furniture he made, as well as wood and stone sculptures, and ghostly works in plaster, among them giant versions of Endless Column and The Cock. “By the end of his life,” Pontus Hulten, the former director of the Pompidou Center, wrote in the book Brancusi, “every single object was assigned a specific location on the floor or on the tables, to within a centimeter. Whenever Brancusi sold a sculpture which would leave the studio for good, he would make a bronze or plaster cast of the work, preparing in advance for the spatial and spiritual void the sale would create.”

What the roughly 90 sculptures, 30 drawings, and 50 photographs in this retrospective—the first in the United States in 25 years—make clear is why Brancusi is one of the few modern sculptors it is impossible to go beyond. His sculptures are aristocratic yet humble. His shapes are so finished, so resolved, so self-contained, and yet so subtle in their inflections and modulations that they always seem open to discovery and change. Marble and onyx are hard stones, but Brancusi’s endless rubbing, guided by his sensitivity to the individuality of each stone, makes them seem like translucent bodies whose interiors can be sensed, if not seen. Almost all the metal and stone sculptures appear not only to hold light but also to attract it, so that they are always both self-sufficient and eager for contact with the space around them. The sculptures are born of enormous effort, but they never seem labored. Each line, edge, and surface has a rightness that is the result of a concentration and will so powerfully present that they feel almost as sculptural as the material. Brancusi’s sculpture is intensely physical, in love with this world, yet it is always in the service of something beyond the material. It is as much mind as body, spirit as matter.

The retrospective, which comes to Philadelphia after a remarkable success at the Pompidou Center in Paris this summer, also makes it possible to consider Brancusi’s extraordinary influence. The tilted heads and lean figures carved by Wilhelm Lehmbruck on the eve of World War I suggest the expressive economy of Brancusi’s 1906 and 1907 works. The history of organic abstraction that runs through Jean Arp and Henry Moore is unimaginable without the inner vitality of Brancusi’s rounded shapes. Carl Andre, Dan Flavin, and the minimalists learned from Brancusi’s serial imagery and the anonymity of his luminous, streamlined forms. Ellsworth Kelly has written, “For me, his art was an affirmation; it strengthened my intention to make an art that is spiritual in content.” Brancusi was an inspiration to Scott Burton, whose stone tables and stools reinforced Brancusi’s challenge to a clear-cut hierarchical distinction between objects of spirituality and objects of utility. And Brancusi also left a mark on Martin Puryear, one of the few contemporary sculptors able to make distilled economical shapes metaphorically and sculpturally convincing.

But there are problems raised by Brancusi’s career. At a certain point—during World War II, when he remained in occupied Paris—Brancusi seems to have essentially stopped growing. In his last years, he produced little, choosing to concentrate on his studio. After the war, making sculpture seemed to be inspired not by participation in the spirit and magic of the world around him but rather by a need to take refuge from it.

In the same period, an aesthetic of inelegance and unfinish took hold. Many artists and critics felt that in the wake of the Holocaust it was irresponsible to lose oneself in the contemplative object. Brancusi’s faith in form and timelessness began to be identified with good taste, self-protection, and escape. In short, his approach is seen by postmodernists as a denial of the crisis of faith and experience of trauma that Picasso considered permanent elements, not just surmountable phases, of the human condition. Brancusi’s sculptures are now dismissed by many young artists as merely commodities for the rich.

The big question raised by this retrospective is what use artists will make of Brancusi’s achievement. It will always be possible for artists to make beautiful objects influenced by his example. But can his way of working still provoke a new way of seeing? Can his optimism and sweetness and yearning for synthesis and fusion still generate surprise and wonder? Can Brancusi’s ecstatic and inexhaustible simplicity inspire sculptors to reinvent their medium again? Don’t bet against it.
