#6746. 33 Gifts for Wives Who Hope You've Been Listening

One of the great pleasures of being married is bearing witness to your life partner's tastes and obsessions. And you'd think all that inside knowledge would make buying her a gift a cinch, and yet here you are, looking up the best gifts for wives. No judgment—we've been there. Whether it's an anniversary, a birthday, or just an occasion to remind her how much you appreciate her, we've rounded up a few things that have been on our radar all year. And yes, you should probably make that dinner reservation, too.

Still got names on your list? We've got ideas. Peruse the rest of our gift guides, and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for a regular dispatch of things we think are worth your money.

It's easy to get distracted by all the excellent cashmere at Banana, but the brand knows its way around silk, too. This shirt is cut roomy and relaxed, with the sort of effortless drape that makes getting dressed easy.

Coach's Empire Carryall comes in a whole family of sizes, all cut from the brand's soft glovetanned leather. It's a beautiful bag on its own, but I'd suggest picking out a few charms to dangle from the handles to make it hers.

Phoebe Philo's Peak sunglasses are aptly named: the shape is, quite simply, peak. An absolute stunner of a pair, and just imagine her walking into brunch wearing them.

Depending on whom you ask, the Moon Shoe might just be Nike's defining sneaker of the moment. Credit Jacquemus, whose collaboration turned a relic of the brand's running history into one of fashion's most coveted shoes.

J.Crew has barn jackets on the brain this year, and its considerable efforts might just have you lusting after one yourself. I'm partial to the studded version, but there's plenty to choose from, including corduroy and faux shearling renditions.

A silk scarf is an endlessly good gift, if only because there are endless ways to wear one. Around her neck, in her hair, knotted onto a handbag, however she pleases, really.

Brooches are all over the runways right now, and might just be the easiest way to lend an outfit a little extra panache. This dangly little number from Lie Studio features carnelian stone, with a rich, brownish-red hue that feels of the moment.

A coworker Chris first put me onto Simuero, but it wasn't until a trip to Barcelona earlier this year that I got to see the Spanish jewelry label's work in person, at Bassal Store. Beautiful stuff, with an organic, slightly imperfect quality that's even better up close.

This is about as chic as it gets, as far as under-eye patches go. The silky patches promise a little firming power, and the set also includes the Le Lift hand cream as an extra treat.

Makeup, of course, is a tricky thing to gift, but a colleague of mine showed up to the office wearing this purple blush from Violette_FR, and I was immediately sold on the shade. I've had it on my running list of recommendations ever since.

Soft Services has shrunk its beloved exfoliating Buffing Bar down to miniature proportions, with four little bars in a very giftable set. A posh way to keep skin in check, and low-key great for travel.

There was plenty of oohing and aahing when a small sample of Maison Francis Kurkdjian's Oud Velvet Mood landed on my desk this year. A gorgeous oud with notes of peach, suede, and leather.

Dr. Sturm has built quite a following for her science-minded approach to skincare. This travel-friendly set brings together some of her signature formulas, all tucked into a fuzzy fleece bag.

Sidia's Braless Duo pairs a subtly scented mist and serum, a welcome salve for winter-weary skin.

Rocco's game-changing beverage fridge now has a more affordable sibling. The Essential holds more than 100 cans and costs considerably less than the flagship Super Smart Fridge, while retaining the same compressor.

One floral and bittersweet, the other peachy and citrus-forward, these botanical aperitivi are deliciously complex without trying to taste like booze. Serve over ice or topped with soda.

Caraway isn't the first to make a coffee maker with an all-glass-and-steel brewing system, keeping hot coffee away from plastic. But it might just be the best-looking of the bunch, which counts when it's one of the first things they see in the morning.

What, your dinner parties don't involve serving salad with horn-handled, mother-of-pearl spoons? Gohar's nautilus shell-inspired salad servers are spectacularly unnecessary, which is why they make such a great gift.

Hario might be best known for its coffee gear, but the Japanese brand knows its way around matcha, too. This gift set includes a double-walled glass bowl and everything she needs to prepare a prower bowl of matcha.

Just the thing to christen that new matcha set. Kettl sources its teas directly from growers, and I'm currently taken with its Okuju matcha. Developed with a longtime partner in Uji, Japan's storied tea-growing region just outside Kyoto, it's a particularly fine powder with a delicate nuttiness and a wonderfully smooth finish.

Edie Parker's gemstoned lighter case has long been a go-to gift around these parts, but this year we've got our eye on the matching ashtray. No smoking equired—it makes a pretty fab catchall for jewelry, keys, and other little things.

I love the freaky pop-art vibes of this collaboration between Dusen Dusen and Venetian glassmaker Laguna~B. The pitcher is great on its own, but you can also spring for the set with two matching glasses.

Apple's new AirPods 5 come in two tiers, and the more giftable of the two is the version with the wireless charging case. You get longer battery life and swipe-to-adjust volume controls right on the stems.

For the record collector, U-Turn's Orbit Plus is one of the finest midrange turntables around. This version has a built-in phono preamp, so she can get straight to spinning records with a pair of powered speakers.

Taking its cues from Kodak's '70s-era 110 camera, Camp Snap offers a screen-free digital experience with an 8MP sensor, which is modest by today's standards, but entirely the point.

Nothing says great gift quite like an overengineered personal fan she'd never buy herself. Dyson's bladeless design is the clever bit, delivering a steady stream of air that's whisper-quiet.

If she's going to track her health, she might as well do it with the latest Oura Ring. The fifth-gen model is 40% smaller, with more proactive insights and personalized guidance to help her make sense of all that data.

Electric toothbrushes aren't exactly paragons of sustainable design, but Suri is doing its damnedest to change that. Its Pro 2.0 has recyclable plant-based brush heads, a repairable body, and a rechargeable battery designed to keep the whole thing out of a landfill for longer.

How could Theragun possibly improve on its already excellent mini massage gun, you ask? By adding heat, of course. The Mini Plus combines percussive massage with warming therapy to help loosen up sore muscles.

If cupping is good enough for the sporting elite, it's certainly worth a spot in her recovery routine. Wthn's kit includes eight silicone cups for a gentler take on the practice that can still help relieve muscle tension.

Wonder Valley's hinoki-scented bath products have won over a few of GQ's more relaxation-minded staffers. This set pairs a handsome bar of soap with a sachet of bath tea, which can be steeped a few times before it's finally spent.

Red-light technology is coming for sex toys, and Lelo's Mona Spectra is among the first to get in on the action. Expect to see plenty more of it in the years ahead, but there's nothing wrong with being an early adopter in this particular department.

#6742. How Heidi Klum Transformed Into a Giant Hand For Her 2026 Halloween Costume

Every year, Heidi Klum—the undisputed queen of Halloween—keeps spooky season fans guessing as to her next big costume reveal. In past years, she’s transformed into E.T., a peacock, a worm, and even Fiona from Shrek. So for her big New York City bash last night, Klum yet again pulled off the art of the unexpected, this time transforming herself into … a giant replica of her own hand. “I always love to do something unexpected,” Klum told Vogue, a few hours before she started this evening’s lengthy getting-ready process. “Every year, I want to surprise people and do something that they haven't seen me—or anyone—do before. Halloween is my favorite time of year because I get to completely transform myself and become something totally different.”

So, where did Klum’s idea for the lifelike (and life-sized) appendage begin? For this Halloween, the German supermodel says she wanted to take something completely normal—and turn it into something that was anything but. “Some of the most interesting ideas come from the most ordinary things,” says Klum. “I love the idea of taking something so common, and that we see every single day, something we probably never even think twice about, and turning it into something larger than life. I thought it would be funny and bizarre to take something so familiar and twist it.”

The star began ideating on the concept about a year ago—even before her 2025 Halloween bash, when she dressed up as Medusa. “Sometimes an idea comes to me very early, and other times I'm still figuring things out closer to Halloween,” says Klum. “I remember trying to explain it to my costume designer, Mike Marino, and he basically told me that he needed to focus on Medusa first! But it stayed in the back of my mind, and I knew I wanted to bring it to life this year.”

As usual, Klum worked her go-to team of special effects artists to bring her delightfully-kooky vision to life. Mike Marino, her right-hand man, led the work with his ProRenFX team. They began by taking a look at Klum’s very own hand for design inspiration. “[Mike] has all of these scans of my body, so he was able to use those to create an exact replica of my hand,” says Klum. “We wanted everything to be as realistic as possible—the anatomy, the veins, the muscles, all the little details that make a hand look like a real hand.”

There were some logistical issues to figure out—like how Klum could actually move and walk around like a hand, for starters. “There is so much planning, sculpting, molding and engineering that goes into these costumes,” says Klum. “The hand had to be large enough to make the impact I wanted, but also constructed in a way that I could actually wear it and move around.”

There were also some special touches added throughout the process—to make it feel undeniably Heidi Klum. “We even recreated my engagement ring and wedding band, as well as the little tattoo on my finger,” says Klum. “Nothing was overlooked! I love that Mike pays attention to things that most people might not even notice at first. The details make these costumes so special. It’s not just any giant hand: It’s my giant hand!”

Klum debuted her latest costume creation at her Heidiween bash in Manhattan last night, held at the Cathédrale restaurant. Turns out, it’s a special anniversary for her star-studded Halloween party. “This year is especially exciting because it’s the 25th anniversary of my Halloween party,” says Klum. “Can you believe it?! Twenty-five years of Halloween, costumes, incredible transformations, and so many amazing memories. It's crazy to think about how much the party has grown over the years.” Her favorite part of hosting it every year? “I always want the party to feel like a place where everyone can be creative and really become someone or something else for the night,” she says. “I love seeing what everyone comes up with. My favorite part is that nobody holds back!”

Ever wonder how someone as committed to a statement look as Heidi ends her Halloween night? Well, usually it involves several hours of shedding her costume. “By the end of the night, I’m usually ready to get out of my costume,” says Klum. “Some of these transformations take so much time to get into, and getting out of them can be an adventure in itself.” And the next morning, she doesn’t call it quits on Halloween just yet. “November 1 is also when I start thinking about next year,” says Klum. “I'm always collecting ideas, so even when Halloween is over, my brain is already working on what I could possibly become next.” And we love her for it.

#6740. 4 Epic New Watches Every Watch Guy Is Salivating Over Right Now

Welcome to Watch Guy Watches, GQ’s monthly curation of high-end timepieces for the true watch nerds among us. This month, Moser goes retro(grade); Lange brings back a beloved bracelet; Biver drops its first hand-wound three-hander; and Breitling puts a pair of vintage-inspired watches in its core catalog.

There are only a few firm absolutes in the horological sphere. One of them is “never bet against H. Moser & Cie.” The high-end independent maker never ceases to amaze with its creativity, wit, and technological prowess. From a mechanical timepiece that bears a suspicious resemblance to a certain famous smartwatch to one the coolest integrated bracelet-bearing luxury sports watches on the market, Moser consistently delivers the Swiss-made goods.

Building upon its Pioneer Retrograde Seconds Midnight Blue release from two years ago, three new models with retrograde seconds join the collection this month in the Pioneer, Endeavour, and Streamliner collections. While all three are beautiful, however, it’s the latter whose aesthetics pair particularly well with this steampunk-esque complication—one in which a small hand tracks the passing seconds in an arc and then jumps back to its starting position at the top of each 30-second period.

Housed in a 40mm brushed stainless steel cushion case with a serpentine integrated bracelet, the Streamliner Retrograde Seconds offers a potent mix of Streamline Moderne and futurism before one even considers its dial. Executed in midnight blue fumé enamel, it features applied indices and the brand’s signature modified syringe handset, with a faint “H. Moser & Cie” signature appearing in white beneath 12 o’clock. The lower half of the face, meanwhile, is given over to the retrograde seconds display. Inspired by instrument gauges such as automotive speedometers, it features smooth action powered by the cal. HMC 252, a product of movement specialists Agenhor. (Flip the watch over and you can view its tungsten rotor whirring away via a sapphire caseback.)

One of the coolest features of the Streamliner collection is that despite the presence of numerous complications; of the use of fumé dials; and of high-end pricing, these watches are meant to be used. With 120m of water resistance, steel constriction, automatic winding, and 72 hours of power reserve, the Streamliner Retrograde Seconds is effectively a high-end tool watch. (Though at a sticker price of 29,900 CHF, maybe take it off if you’re, like, climbing Mt. Everest or whatever?)

While retrograde seconds displays don’t have the same utility as calendar readouts or GMT complications, they do demonstrate horological competence on the part of the watchmaker…and more importantly, they’re wild fun to watch in action. And if you can’t have a little fun in your watch-collecting journey, well—then what the heck are you even doing here, anyway?!

If you’ve been waiting years for the return of platinum bracelet options for A. Lange & Söhne’s Datograph Perpetual watch, we give you permission to rejoice: a new version of the timepiece—made in honor of the model’s 20th anniversary—is equipped not only with a diamond-studded black dial, but with a fresh matching platinum bracelet. Designed with five links rather than the seven of early-2000s models made by German jewelry manufacturer Wellendorff, said bracelet is perhaps more notable than the watch itself, which features the brand’s manually wound manufacture Calibre L952.1 movement and is limited to just 50 pieces.

When watch-world elder statesman Jean-Cladue Biver and his son Pierre co-founded their eponymous firm in 2022, their introductory product was a half-million-dollar automatic tourbillon and minute repeater. Having since added a simple automatic three-hander to their lineup in the form of the Automatique, they’re now expanding their offerings with a hand-wound three-hander in stainless steel. Dubbed the AB, it measures 38mm wide and 9.8mm tall and features a beautiful black multi-level onyx dial with gold accents, plus a cool stainless steel bracelet with an angular five-link design and a patented micro-adjust system. Powered by the new Calibre JCB-004 designed in collaboration with Le Cercle des Horlogers, it’s the brand’s entry-level model…though it’ll still set you back roughly the cost of a BMW M3. (Naturally, it’s already sold out.)

On the slightly less eye-watering—but no less compelling—end of the watch-guy spectrum is the new Breitling Navitimer B09 Chronograph 41. Why does it look so familiar, you might ask? Effectively, it’s a modern version of the famed ref. 806 “Twin Jet”-logo chronograph from the 1960s, only this time, it’s available as a non-limited edition—a fact that will surely excite deep Breitling aficionados. Measuring 41mm in stainless steel, it’s manually wound just like its vintage namesake, and comes paired to a brown leather strap for $7,900 or to a handsome steel bracelet for $8,400. If you fancy something a bit more left-field, there’s also a hand-wound, non-limited version of the Cosmonaute, a riff on the Navitimer equipped with a 24-hour dial that was famously worn by astronaut Scott Carpenter in 1962 ($10,600-$11,000).

#6738. Harry Styles’s Thank-You Note to New York? A Special Issue of The Village Voice

For 70 years now, The Village Voice has been synonymous with what’s happening in New York, whether through its coverage of the downtown arts scene or the writers it has engaged as contributors, from James Baldwin and E.E. Cummings to Tom Stoppard and Colson Whitehead.

So it feels fitting that Harry Styles, a one-man cultural institution if ever there was one, would use a special issue of the Voice—which largely ceased its print operations in 2017—to help him bid farewell to the city; October 31 marked the end of Styles’s 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden during his Together, Together tour.

“It has been an honour to live and work in your city for the past three months,” Styles writes in an opening note addressed to “friends, strangers, citizens of New York.” “The energy of the audiences, the openness, the dancing, the sheer joy, will never leave me; it altered me.”

He continues: “The Village Voice has long been both a creator and unique record of the cultural life of New York City and it is a privilege to collaborate with the iconic arts paper to tell a bit of the story of 30 nights of Together, Together at Madison Square Garden. It’s not the whole story, of course, but it’s a little piece we can share right now. I look forward to hearing your stories in the years to come, and sharing mine.”

The issue includes features on Styles’s opening acts (Tinashe, Jamie xx, Caroline Polachek, Lainey Wilson, and Tears for Fears among them), his band, and members of the crew at MSG; coverage of the tour’s work with Planned Parenthood, Food Bank For NYC, the voting nonprofit HeadCount, and the humanitarian organization Choose Love; and lots of photography from his shows.

If you weren’t able to catch one of Styles’s MSG shows yourself, his special issue of the Village Voice is like paging through a carefully composed time capsule of the experience. Pick one up to see for yourself.

From Harry Styles getting his heart rate up on morning runs over the Williamsburg Bridge to Ethan Hawke turning up for a SAG screening, Glenn Close pulling an absolute grail piece from a film she starred in alongside Robert Redford, and Nicholas Hoult hopping between planes, the celebrity style circuit is showing no signs of slowing down.

Maybe this is the season you’ve been influenced to go all in on corduroy, resurrect those vintage graphic tees gathering dust in your tote bins, or finally dip your dainty toes into the jazz shoe craze. Whatever your sartorial itch, let these celebrities do the legwork for you.

The Hawkester has worn corduroy before, and this look calls to mind Robin Williams in Dead Poets Society, whose affinity for the fabric felt like part of the curriculum. Hawke styles the suit in a way that feels less adjunct professor and more stoner student, thanks to a ratty graphic tee and tinted shades. Rather than dress shoes, he opts for well-worn dark brown Sambas, which contrast nicely with his acorn-colored suit. Carpe diem, and all that.

With his Together, Together tour wrapping up at the end of the month, Harry’s New York stroll fits will likely be inducted into the annals of celeb big fits. He seems to have tapped into the lore of ’90s-era skaters, layering a long-sleeved tee under a T-shirt. Add light-wash jeans, all-white sneakers, and Apple earbuds, and you’ve got a man who feels gloriously analog in a digital world.

Glenn Close shows us how to build an outfit around a statement piece, in this case, a jacket from The Natural, the 1984 film in which she co-starred. Throw on navy slacks, loafers, and a crisp white Oxford shirt, and you’re good to go. Of course, it helps when you have iconic films attached to your name, too.

Example 1,088 of why denim-on-denim is always the answer to the in-flight outfit dilemma. Mr. Hoult opts for a charcoal-hued Canadian tuxedo, offset by black boots and a dad cap. Denim can take a beating. Whether from turbulence-induced coffee spills or an overenthusiastic recline, it provides a welcome layer of warmth on those cold and bone-dry flights.

As the oldest brother in Sweden’s Skarsgård acting dynasty, Alexander proves that an age-old graphic tee and Chuck Taylors will always be a can’t-miss combination. The louche, open trench coat adds a bit of flare to the fit. We also have to note, when you’re 6’4” with a chin chiseled enough to double as an ice luge, it’s hard for anything to look bad on you.

People love to claim that black and brown don’t belong together. I guess they’ve never had a Turtle Pecan Blizzard. The black shirt and blazer flirt with Y2K corporate-core, but the khaki-colored, pleated, baggy chinos and jazz shoes give the whole kit some much-needed attitude.

#6732. At This Manhattan Halloween Party, 250 People Came Dressed as Dolly Parton

On Friday evening, swarms of Dolly Parton lookalikes took over the East Village for The Frankie Shop and Unemployed’s fourth annual Halloween bash. This year, the festivities tipped a rhinestone-covered cowboy hat to the late, great country music icon, with platinum-blonde bouffants, exaggerated bust lines, and plenty of pink as far as the eye could see.

By 10:30 p.m., guests sauntered downstairs to the basement club beneath Ella Funt, the East Village bistro turned late-night hotspot. The subterranean space was as ample as Dolly’s most famous asset—a surprising rarity in downtown Manhattan. Given the theme, it felt like a cross between a Brooklyn warehouse and a Dollywood fever dream, with the wood paneling and hot-pink walls illuminated by a soft rosy glow. At the center of it all was a sunken black-and-white checkered dance floor, though you could barely make out the floor underneath all the dancing Dollys.

Previous editions of the fashion brand and media company’s collaborative party have asked guests to come as Elizabeth Taylor, Princess Diana, and Uma Thurman’s Mia Wallace from Pulp Fiction. For Unemployed’s co-founders Cecile Winkler and Sophie Tabet, the magic lies in seeing how everyone makes the theme their own. “There is nothing more fun than finding yourself in a room where everyone is dressed up as that one thing, but they’re doing it in a different way,” Winkler told Vogue. “It brings you together. And it feels so absurd. You lose your friends because everyone looks the same.”

And with a legacy as celebrated as Dolly’s, there was plenty of room for interpretation. Some, including Rita Ora, opted for classic Tennessee Tuxedoes in the form of double denim, while others channeled her iconic 1978 Playboy cover. Then there were the more imaginative takes, like Salvador ‘Dolly’ and even a pair of sheep brought to life by Saltburn actor Archie Madekwe and Dorian Grinspan. It took a moment for people to realize that the pair were referencing Dolly, the world’s first cloned sheep from back in 1996, famously named after the chart-topper.

No Dolly wig or prosthetic boobs? No problem. Some of the night’s most memorable looks were improvised. One resourceful guest made do with a powdered barrister’s wig, perhaps left over from a previous Halloween costume, while others stuffed balloons of varying sizes down their t-shirts.

As word traveled across the city about the buzzy party, the line outside wrapped around the block well past 1 a.m., while inside, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” sent the dance floor into a frenzy, followed by a string of Dolly’s greatest hits that kept the momentum going. According to The Frankie Shop founder Gaëlle Drevet, her philosophy for the night was simple: “Life is short. Have fun with it.” And judging by the crowd, no one needed to be told twice.

#6727. Ahead of Season 4, The Gilded Age Cast Celebrated in New York and L.A.

Ahead of The Gilded Age’s return to screens on November 1, celebrations on each coast saw the cast reunite for a red carpet outing at The Plaza and an elegant bash at Greystone Mansion in Beverly Hills.

At this week’s lavish season 4 premiere party at The Plaza, Carrie Coon, Cynthia Nixon, Audra McDonald, and their fellow stars left their bustles behind. After three seasons of elaborate period costumes, you’d think slipping into a corset every day would make dressing up for a night out a breeze. Alas, think again.

“It’s so much harder to get ready for a red carpet than it is for work,” Coon, clad in an Acne Studios gown, told Vogue. “My dresser, Amber, helps me get into my costumes and cinch my waist from a 28 to a 24. It takes about six minutes and 30 seconds to take off my costumes and wigs. Red carpets are way more stressful, and sometimes the clothes are just as challenging. For me, it’s the shoes. When you get to 16 hours in three-inch heels, you start to lose your mind!”

For the glamorous premiere and party, Nixon opted for a floor-length white fringe dress by Edeline Lee, while Louisa Jacobson stepped out in a cropped Conner Ives blazer and high-waisted trousers. Kelley Curran embraced a softer palette in a mint set by Lein. Morgan Spector gave formalwear an avant-garde twist in an all-white Maison Margiela look, complete with dramatic coattails. Denée Benton channeled Cher in a 1980s-era Bob Mackie gown, McDonald brought the drama in a sheer Bibhu Mohapatra gown, and Ben Ahlers embraced graphic prints in an optic-patterned Kenzo look.

The Plaza’s storied Grand Ballroom, with its glittering crystal chandeliers and intricate gold detailing, provided a suitably opulent setting for the occasion. Hundreds of hydrangeas and lisianthuses adorned the space, while a dramatic centerpiece of oak foliage anchored the room. And then there was the dessert spread: a decadent affair in its own right, featuring cakes, mousses, spiced chai apple crumble, and fondant top hats.

With season 4 premiering Sunday, November 1, the cast offered hints of the social warfare to come. The eight-episode season picks up roughly six months after season 3, with Bertha Russell (Coon) determined to salvage her fractured marriage to railroad tycoon George Russell (Spector)“Everyone is very invested in what’s going to happen between Bertha and George. I can say, rest assured, Bertha never gives up,” Coon teased. “But that doesn’t mean she always wins. Scary, right?”

Meanwhile, Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) hopes to reclaim her influence among Manhattan’s elite by hosting a dinner for President Grover Cleveland. Bertha counters with a grander affair to advance George’s business interests, setting up another showdown between old money and new. “It’s really fun to spar with her,” Coon said of Baranski. “I respect and admire Christine so much. Her timing is impeccable. You’ll see her character experience an incredible change of fortune, so she’s a bit unhinged.”

Agnes’s sister Ada Forte (Nixon) is stepping into a more independent chapter, trading her role as the family’s steadying influence for a willingness to take risks. She’s now “walking a tightrope and playing with fire,” Nixon said. “I thought, wow, are we really going to go there? I guess we are!”

Love remains complicated for Marian Brook (Jacobson) and Larry Russell (Harry Richardson). Their engagement is over, but feelings remain. “There’s deeper heartbreak than before,” Richardson said. “Larry desperately wants to be with her, but there are so many societal pressures keeping them apart. He’s stumbling and fumbling, and I think that’s quite relatable.”

Marian’s perspective, however, reflects the restrictive social codes of her era. “The expectations for women in 1886, particularly around sexuality and purity, were very, very different,” Jacobson said. “I knew that audiences would have a strong reaction to Marian’s actions, but it made perfect sense to me when I did the research.”

Not every relationship is built on love. Last season, Oscar van Rhijn (Blake Ritson) proposed a marriage of convenience to the newly widowed Enid Winterton (Curran), trading connections and status for her money. Their union promises to challenge society’s conventions further in season 4, fitting for a character who has never been afraid to ruffle feathers. “I’ve been called a hussy in the grocery store!” Curran said with a laugh.

Fan favorite Jack Trotter (Ahlers) is adjusting to life among Manhattan’s elite after selling his clock invention. Having once served the very society he now moves among, Jack must learn its rules. “I had to learn the proper etiquette myself,” Ahlers said. “You see me stepping into this character and Jack stepping into his life in tandem.”

Beyond Manhattan’s old-money dynasties, The Gilded Age shines a light on a thriving Black elite whose stories have rarely been told on television. McDonald, who plays society matriarch Dorothy Scott, is proud that the series showcases more than suffering. “We didn’t just go from slavery to Jim Crow to the ’60s. We’re showing Black excellence, Black joy, and Black love.”

Benton, who plays Peggy Scott, has championed this representation from the start. “It’s been the honor of my career to advocate for that storyline,” she said. “It feels like righting a collective gaslighting in history to really bring the spotlight to people who deserve dignity.”

For one evening at The Plaza, the cast traded their fictional rivalries for a well-deserved moment in the spotlight. But if the series has taught us anything, it’s that no social gathering is complete without a little ambition, a dash of scandal, and a spectacular outfit. After all, on The Gilded Age, the drama never goes out of style. —Paul Chi

Out west, The Gilded Age Cast marked the upcoming season with an outdoor screening at the legendary Greystone Mansion in Beverly Hills.

Commissioned by an oil tycoon in the 1920s, the sprawling Tudor-style estate spans 16 acres of formal English gardens, but this week, all the floral arrangements worth noting were inside the Great Hall.

Upon arrival, over 250 guests were led through Fleurs de Villes’ opulent botanical exhibit inspired by the period drama—which is open to the public through November 4—before congregating on the terrace for a breathtaking view of the city.

While sipping on themed cocktails by the stone balcony, the show’s familiar faces Taissa Farmiga, Kelly Curran, Harry Richardson, and Ben Ahers told Vogue they couldn’t imagine a better spot to celebrate the season premiere in their own backyard.

“It's strange to be so far from New York City,” says Farmiga, who plays heiress-turned-duchess Gladys Russell—daughter of Berta and George. “It makes me think, what would it be like if Gladys would have taken one of Daddy Russell’s trains to come out here?”

After a Champagne toast on the terrace, the cast led guests back up to the gardens to preview the show, marking the first-ever outdoor screening hosted at Greystone. “It’s a piece of history,” said Curran, dressed in a plunging sequined Edeline Lee number befitting the gilded cocktail dress code. “There’s something about the sumptuousness of this show, and to see this in the middle of Los Angeles is so incredibly meta-theatrical.” —Emily Tannenbaum

#6724. Can the Brooklyn Nets Convert a Generation of Newly Minted Knicks Fans?

At the Brooklyn Nets’ home opener against the Charlotte Hornets last week, one longtime fan pointed out the strange dynamic inherent to New York City basketball fandom. He was jealous of places like Boston and Philadelphia, he said, because the entire city organizes itself around one team. Sports franchises, after all, are avatars of civic pride, and the very best organizations come to reflect the values of the cities they represent. (Think the Showtime Lakers or the Grit-and-Grind Memphis Grizzlies.) But in New York, home to both the Nets and the Knicks, fan bases are pitted against each other by fans, media, and sometimes even franchise leaders.

For a long time, the Nets could take solace in their cross rivals' decades-long stretch of ineptitude. That vanished when Jalen Brunson and company lifted the Larry O’Brien in June, leaving Brooklyn with some soul searching to do. “It doesn't make us feel very good,” Nets owner Joe Tsai told NetsDaily over the summer. “It irates our fan base and it is embarrassing.” As The Ringer’s Zach Lowe pointed out on his recently launched Substack, the Knicks’ title cost the Nets “an entire generation of fans.”

I, for one, have never understood why commentators are so obsessed with the size of Brooklyn’s fanbase. I am, obviously, a hugely biased homer, but you don’t hear the same concerns when it comes to other little-brother teams like the Clippers or teams, like Wizards, whose games are sparsely attended. Even as they’ve tanked these past couple of years, the Nets have maintained a 99% attendance rate and are the eighth most-valuable franchise in the entire league. Still, I have to hear talking heads argue that the team should move back to New Jersey? I might be salty, but that’s stupid.

Nevertheless, there is clearly angst about building up a coalition of Nets faithful. On his podcast Curious Mike, where I wish he would be less curious, the team’s star forward Michael Porter Jr. recently said, “When we play Knicks, Celtics, Philly, Lakers, it's mostly their fans. It's crazy.” And he’s not wrong: it's a weird time to be a fan of the Brooklyn Nets—the team’s fallen twice in the lottery and is trying to kickstart a rebuild in the shadow of one of the most storied franchises in the NBA. So I made my way over to the team’s training facility in Sunset Park to see how the Nets are tackling this problem with pillars of the present and future.

“I don't give a shit,” says Julius Randle, tucked into a glass room in the corner of the Nets’ famously photogenic training facility, when I ask him about the invasion of opposing fans at Barclays. “I've been on teams that weren't good and didn’t have the excitement around them. Then you start winning and the whole arena is there to see your team and cheer. So I think that's just part of being a fan. For us as a team, we got to give them something to root for.”

Randle, who played an integral role in the Knicks rebuild before being shipped off to the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2024, has seen New York City basketball fandom from both sides of the river. “It doesn't really matter what team I play for. I was at my son's basketball game yesterday and it was like, Man, I'm a Nets fan. You’re going to kill it this year. Then I get on the other side and it's, Thank you for everything you've done for the Knicks."

Randle, now on his fifth team in 13 seasons, also downplayed the idea that the Nets-Knicks intercity rivalry mattered all that much to players. “From the locker room, basketball is basketball,” he insists. “It's not like college or high school where we play our rival on Friday or whatever. You play 82 games a year. You feel the energy during the game, but I definitely think it's a bigger deal from a fan perspective than it is from a player's perspective.”

I can’t even finish my next question before he cuts me off. Do you see part of your role as growing this next generation of fans or are you just here to—

“No, hell no,” Randle says. “I definitely want to be a part of establishing a culture and giving the city of Brooklyn something to be proud of. I'm not here just to come out and get my numbers or whatever it is. I'm here to win a championship. I'm here to help these young guys excel and speed up their growth process.”

One of those young guys is the anointed prince of the franchise, Mikel Brown Jr., the Orlando-born point guard the Nets took sixth overall in this year’s draft and who fans are already calling “the best prospect in franchise history” (I agree.) Another prominent member of Nets Twitter, moved by preseason action, described him as a mix of CJ McCollum and All-NBA regulars Tyrese Haliburton and Kyrie Irving. (I love that tweet, and I love this fanbase.)

With the Nets, Brown came into a peculiar situation. Not only does the future of the franchise’s success hinge on whether he can reach his star potential—so does the team’s ability to cultivate a new generation of fans. It’s a challenge Brown recognizes and embraces. Many fans, myself included, took note of a phrase he kept repeating on draft night: “I’m home.” It felt like a full-throated endorsement of the franchise and its mission. “Most of the [Nets] fans are there in the arena for a draft night,” Brown says when I ask him what he meant. “So to hear the crowd pop and just to see the energy, it brought me a whole bunch of joy.”

Brown is 20 years old, and looks even younger, but he understands just how much is riding on his rookie season. “I embrace it,” he says. “At the end of the day, we're just kind of focusing on what we can control and then let everything else play on. Whatever happens after that and whoever comes along with us, enjoy the ride because we're going to go to war.”

Everyone I talked to believes Brown has the goods to deliver on both his promises and his potential. Randle, too, told me he’s been texting his friends back home to tell them how gifted Brown is. “I've been thoroughly, thoroughly impressed with not just his talent level, but his maturity and his IQ at such a young age is really, really impressive.” Typically, Randle continues, young players are single-mindedly focused on scoring. But Brown understands that there’s more than one way to contribute. “He just knows how to make the right play every single time. He just knows how to play good basketball.”

Brown is the type of prospect us Nets fans have been waiting to call our own. I loved rooting for every iteration of this team, but what the franchise’s best players—Jason Kidd, Deron Williams, Joe Johnson, Kyrie Irving, and Kevin Durant—have in common is that none of them were drafted by the Nets. Developing a homegrown star is a different task altogether, and the Nets have solid reason to believe they've found one.

On Wednesday night against the Boston Celtics, we caught a glimpse of what Brown can do . The 20 year-old was “not human,” as Nets longtime commentator Ian Eagle likes to say, in the fourth quarter. After pouring in several clutch baskets, he sent the game to overtime with a falling-to-the-side three with just 0.2 seconds left. Brooklyn lost the game, but if Brown’s development keeps trending in this direction, maybe we can win the war.

My Nets fandom is the result of perfect timing. I mostly grew up in California but spent my formative sports-team-choosing years in New Jersey when my family and I moved across the country for my dad’s job. After moving back to the Bay Area halfway through elementary school, I clung even more tightly to the Nets to stay connected with the friends and the place I left behind: the Snoopy fishing rod I used at the local lake, the fireflies in my New Jersey-sized backyard, the cul-de-sac that seemed to have a friend in every neighboring house.

During the Nets home opener, with the team wearing their excellent ABA-inspired red-and-blue jerseys, the game seemed all but decided as the Charlotte Hornets started to pull away at the end of the fourth. But with just over a minute left, the crowd started to pop as Randle bullied his way into an and-one layup and starting center Day'Ron Sharpe blocked a shot at the other end.

I thought back to the simple philosophy both Randle and Brown echoed: just win, and people will show up. The Nets eventually lost that game against Charlotte, and a few other heartbreakers since (against very tough competition, for what it’s worth). It’s unclear whether the Nets will ever convert a generation of fans spellbound by the Knicks, or even win the Finals. But I know I’ll be there.

#6723. Lymphatic Drainage: 4 Simple Habits to Add to Your Daily Routine

Lymphatic drainage has become something of a wellness obsession. From sculpting facial massages to body brushes and compression boots, there are seemingly endless ways to coax away puffiness and encourage a more contoured appearance. But the benefits of a healthy lymphatic system extend well beyond what we can see in the mirror.

The lymphatic system is sometimes described as the “Cinderella of medicine”: “underestimated, yet performing a large part of the essential work,” writes cardiothoracic surgeon Dr. Gerald M. Lemole in his book Lymph & Longevity: The Untapped Secret to Health. While its aesthetic benefits have helped bring lymphatic drainage into the mainstream, this intricate network of vessels, nodes, and fluid is fundamental to everything from immune function to maintaining the body's fluid balance.

And, as it turns out, keeping it functioning properly doesn’t necessarily require a standing appointment with your facialist.

Think of the lymphatic system as the body’s behind-the-scenes maintenance crew. Working alongside the circulatory and immune systems, it helps collect excess fluid from tissues, transports immune cells, and carries certain waste products away from cells.

“Lymph transports various substances—large proteins such as antibodies and enzymes, as well as immune system cells that nourish, protect, and coordinate the body—while removing cellular waste through its collecting ducts,” explains Lemole. He likens the system to a “secret river of health,” a network of vessels through which fluid is continuously transported and returned to the bloodstream. Healthy lymphatic function is essential for maintaining fluid balance and supporting the body’s defenses.

But unlike the cardiovascular system, which relies on the heart to pump blood, the lymphatic system has no central pump of its own. Instead, lymph moves through a combination of muscle contractions, breathing, and the action of valves within lymphatic vessels. “You are the pump,” says Ada Ooi, a traditional Chinese medicine specialist, integrative medicine practitioner, and founder of London’s 001 London Longevity Clinic.

The takeaway? Everyday movement, breathing, and other simple lifestyle habits can help support the body's natural lymphatic circulation. Here are four ways to work them into your routine.

One of the simplest ways to support lymphatic circulation requires nothing more than a few minutes of your time. Deep diaphragmatic breathing—the kind that expands your abdomen rather than lifting your shoulders—creates changes in pressure within the chest and abdomen that help move lymphatic fluid through the body.

“The largest lymphatic vessels and the body's main lymphatic ducts are located in the chest cavity,” explains Lemole. “Every deep breath helps circulate the lymph.”

Whether it’s a few minutes of breathwork upon waking, a gentle yoga session, or simply taking a moment to slow your breathing between meetings, the idea is to make deeper, more deliberate breaths part of your day.

Lemole suggests spending a few minutes each morning and evening practicing slow, diaphragmatic breathing. As a bonus, it can also help counter the shallow, hurried breathing that often accompanies stress.

There’s another reason to get up from your desk. Movement is one of the body’s natural mechanisms for transporting lymph, with each muscle contraction helping to propel fluid through the lymphatic vessels.

And it doesn’t have to involve a strenuous workout. A brisk walk, a few flights of stairs, calf raises, squats, or even ankle rotations can all get your muscles working, according to Cecily Braden, esthetician and creator of The Lymphatic Brush.

For those looking to make their routine a little more playful, there’s rebounding: the mini-trampoline workout that’s found fans in Gwyneth Paltrow, Eva Longoria, and Miranda Kerr. The repeated bouncing combines muscle contractions with changes in gravitational force. Lemole advocates for rebounding as a way to encourage fluid movement, and early NASA research explored the physiological effects of trampoline exercise, although evidence that it offers superior lymphatic benefits to other forms of movement remains limited. Still, bouncing for a few minutes in the morning feels like, if anything, an easy bit of movement and a quick mood-booster. And if trampolines aren’t your thing? Walking, dancing, stretching, and other regular physical activities are equally sensible places to start.

If your morning routine could use a gentler start, consider qigong. The centuries-old Chinese practice combines slow, flowing movements with controlled breathing and focused attention, making it an appealing alternative to more vigorous exercise.

For Ooi, qigong naturally brings together several mechanisms involved in lymphatic circulation. “Slow, rhythmic movements of the limbs, deep and coordinated breathing, gentle rotations of the spine and torso that compress and then release the abdomen, and repeated movements of the arms above the heart… Qigong brings together all the elements that promote lymphatic circulation,” she explains.

The combination of gentle muscle activation, diaphragmatic breathing, and torso movements may help encourage lymphatic flow, while the meditative pace offers an opportunity to unwind. Specific evidence for qigong’s effects on lymphatic circulation is still limited, but its broader benefits as a form of mindful movement make it a worthwhile addition to a daily routine.

And there’s no need to master an elaborate sequence. “Two or three movements performed slowly for ten minutes will be far more beneficial to you than a 20 minute sequence done at full speed,” says Ooi.

What you eat and drink matters, too. Staying adequately hydrated supports the body's normal fluid balance, including the production and circulation of lymphatic fluid.

Beyond drinking enough water, there’s growing interest in the potential role of polyphenols—plant compounds known for their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties—in supporting lymphatic health. Found naturally in berries, beans, vegetables, tea, and a variety of other plant foods, certain polyphenols are being investigated for their effects on lymphatic function. Some have been described as lymphagogues, or substances that may encourage lymph flow, although research in humans remains preliminary.

Rather than reaching for another supplement, the simplest approach is to eat a varied, plant-rich diet and stay well-hydrated. Ultimately, looking after your lymphatic system needn’t become another complicated wellness undertaking. A few deeper breaths, a little more movement, and a balanced diet are all practical ways to support a system that’s already working hard on your behalf.

#6721. Better American Sunscreens Are Here—But We’re Still Way Behind the Best

Anyone who’s applied sunscreen only to be left with a chalky white cast, a greasy finish knows American sun care has long been a frustrating experience. The US is decades behind European and Asian counterparts, which have long been blessed with sunscreens that are lighter, more luxurious, and easier to wear every day. For skincare obsessives (this writer included) trips abroad are also opportunities to stock up on superior sunscreens they can’t find at home.

The root of the problem is regulation. The Food and Drug Administration classifies sunscreen as a drug rather than a cosmetic. Because of that distinction, more time and testing is required to get new sunscreens on the shelves, dramatically reducing innovation in American sun protection. But for the first time since the ‘90s, we’ve had some movement on that front. In June of this year, the FDA approved a new sunscreen filter called bemotrizinol—also known as Tinosorb S or BEMT—after years of lobbying in the states by dermatologists, skincare brands, and Congress members. It’s a meaningful step toward better sun care, but the US is still lagging behind.

Bemotrizinol is prized for its ability to provide both UVA and UVB protection while remaining stable in sunlight. That’s a significant advantage over some existing US-approved filters, which offer protection against one type of UV radiation more effectively than the other. BEMT also has the potential to make sunscreen more pleasant to wear: “And because it’s a large, oil-loving molecule, it mostly stays on the surface of your skin instead of soaking in, and it blends into lightweight, non-greasy formulas with no white cast,” says Dr. Joel Spitz, co-founder, chief medical officer, and board-certified dermatologist at Honeydew, a virtual dermatology platform.

Bemotrizinol might be new for the US market, but it’s already been used in sunscreen formulations abroad for 20 years, Spitz says. That long track record helps explain why consumers in the US have spent years coveting the more cosmetically elegant formulas available in countries like South Korea and France. While most consumers would love if major brands like Neutrogena, La Roche-Posay, or Beauty of Joseon brought their European or Asian formulations to the US, those SPFs still contain filters that the FDA hasn’t approved. As a result, many brands are developing entirely new BEMT-centric formulas for use stateside.

Australian label Ultra Violette was the first brand to release a BEMT sunscreen in the US with its Unblock Screen SPF 50 in August 2026. Neutrogena debuted its Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 in September. Earlier this month French drugstore staple La Roche-Posay put its Anthelios UVDefense Sunscreen SPF 50 up for sale online. Don’t mistake the relatively quick arrival of these products after the FDA’s approval for ease in which brands can develop new formulations. According to Emanuella Louis, La Roche-Posay’s public relations manager, the brand had been working on its new formula for more than two years.

That long lead time reflects the way sunscreen development works: Brands can research and test formulas in anticipation of regulatory changes, then move a product forward when a particular filter gets the green light. Louis says La Roche-Posay has access to filters the FDA may be considering for approval and is “actively working, playing, testing on what possibly those formulas would be.” When a filter is approved, she explains, a formula already in the testing pipeline can be moved up.

Some brands are still tinkering with BEMT formulas for the US. Round Lab, one of South Korea’s most popular sunscreen manufacturers, has sold a version of its SPF in the US since 2024, and is hard at work on a new version of those formulas that contains bemotrizinol.

“Bemotrizinol’s approval in the US is a meaningful change, but it does not mean a Korean formula can simply be brought to the US market as is,” says Koochul Kwon, Round Lab’s chief technology officer. Beyond incorporating the newly approved filter, brands must ensure the ingredients keep the UV filters stably dissolved and working alongside other components, including moisturizing ingredients. The finished product must then meet US requirements for SPF and broad-spectrum testing, product stability, and labeling. With those considerations in mind, Kwon expects Round Lab to release its own bemotrizinol sunscreen sometime in 2027.

A sunscreen is only as useful as a person’s willingness to wear it consistently. Bemotrizinol’s ability to protect against UV damage is important, but its potential to make formulas lighter, less greasy, and more comfortable could be just as consequential to get people to implement it in their everyday skincare routines.

“One of the strengths of Korean sun care is how naturally it has built sun protection into the everyday skincare experience,” Kwon says. “For people to apply enough sunscreen and reapply it when needed, the way it feels matters as much as how well it protects.”

But better filters alone won’t transform American sun care. The real breakthrough will be sunscreens that people actually enjoy wearing—and, as a result, are more likely to apply generously and reapply throughout the day, a key step to ensuring its effectiveness.

Charlotte Palermino, cofounder and chief brand officer of skincare brand Dieux, has been an advocate for easier sunscreen filter approvals ever since she tried her first Japanese sunscreen, Biore UV, a decade ago. She realized sunscreen could stave off skin issues after her dermatologist told her that her hyperpigmentation had been the result of failing to use sun protection. In the years since she has publicly pushed for regulatory reform. She’s hesitant to put an estimated release date on Dieux’s upcoming BEMT-centric sunscreen, simply because the brand is dialed in to ensure its able to deliver a quality, wearable product.

“We’ve gone through this with [Dieux’s] SkinMercy, which is an OTC colloidal oatmeal cream, but for sunscreen, the stability of your sunscreen is so fucking important,” she says. “If my sunscreen separates or if it’s not at that stated SPF 50, if that degrades at all with broad spectrum protection, I would be mortified.”

Palerimo cites brands like Korea’s Beauty of Joseon, which is more popular in the US than in its home country, as evidence that Americans have long been on the hunt for better sunscreen. And though BEMT is a step forward, we still have a way to go. Board-certified dermatologist Jane Yoo has been lobbying Congress to get new sunscreen filters approved for the US and is tracking the FDA’s progress in making those approvals. Currently there are seven other filters—bisoctrizole, drometrizole trisiloxane, octyl triazone, amiloxate, diethylhexyl butamido triazone iscotrizinol, ecamsule, and enzacamene—under the agency’s Time and Extent Application (TEA) pipeline. Those filters are part of the 2014 Sunscreen Innovation Act meant to speed up the process of determining if ingredients are Generally Recognized as Safe and Effective, or GRASE. But here we are 12 years later, and we’re still waiting for their approval.

“A good analogy is we’ve been making sunscreens with both of our hands tied behind our backs,” Palermino says. “We’ve now had one hand released. I would like both hands released.”

#6720. 3-Ingredient Curry Pumpkin Soup

This dead simple three-ingredient soup houses a wealth of flavor with a shockingly trim ingredient list. Made by sizzling curry paste in oil, then adding a can of pumpkin purée and coconut milk, this cozy soup is a celebration of simplicity, creating something that tastes far more complex than it was to make. For the best flavor, I like to use the Maesri brand curry paste, leaning on its warm intensity to lend the soup its depth, but the ubiquitous Thai Kitchen, sold in almost all grocery stores, is also nice, producing a gentle heat.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: The 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Soup You’ll Fall For.

Transfer a couple of spoonfuls or so of one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, stirred well, to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Heat 1 Tbsp. unrefined coconut oil or other oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 2 Tbsp. red curry paste and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, 2–3 minutes. Add one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, remaining coconut milk in can, and 1½ cups water. Increase heat to high and bring soup to a simmer. Remove pot from heat. Taste soup and season with kosher salt if needed. Ladle into bowls and drizzle some reserved coconut milk into each bowl.

#6719. 13 Books That Changed Comedian, Author, and Drag King Murray Hill’s Life

Hollywood is a strange and mysterious place, even for those who have operated within its orbit for decades. But author, comedian, and drag king Murray Hill’s new memoir, Showbiz!: My Life as a Middle-Aged Man (Gallery Books), sheds an alternately moving and hilarious light on “the industry,” charting Hill’s rise from a fraught New England childhood to a career starring in New York and Boston cabaret shows and appearing on television series including Somebody, Somewhere, Life & Beth, and Elsbeth.

In the latest edition of Vogue’s Required Reading series, Hill shares a selection of books that have inspired his own memoir and seen him through the ups and downs of Hollywood life.

Kathleen Hanna is a punk-rock icon, feminist trailblazer, and one of my dearest friends. She’s spent her life making noise, breaking rules, and telling the establishment to beat it. What I love about this book is how she writes about the messy, painful, and hilarious realities behind being a revolutionary. She built her own stage, grabbed the microphone, and started a movement. She is my forever inspiration.

Tina Turner didn’t just make a comeback. She kicked down the door in her red patent leather heels and reclaimed her life while inspiring millions of people all over the world. This book is about surviving abuse, and refusing to let somebody else write your ending. I was drawn to performers like Tina because they showed me that no matter how bad things got, you could get out and start where you are. If I were a religious person (I’m still a recovering Catholic), Tina would be my God.

Etta James had one of the greatest voices in music and one helluva life. Addiction, heartbreak, chaos, and that voice...raw, powerful, and breathtaking. I connected with the struggle behind the spotlight. Etta’s story reminded me that surviving is an accomplishment in itself, even before the curtain goes up.

Jeff Hiller is one of my dearest friends, and one of the funniest people I know. He can make me laugh at a drop of a hat (whatever that means). We both spent decades in show business waiting for the phone to ring. Jeff’s story is proof that there’s no expiration date on making it. Especially for us middle-aged guys who love to improv! And let me tell you, nobody deserves a standing ovation more than this guy.

Viola Davis tells her story with such raw honesty, it practically jumps off the page and grabs you by the collar. Growing up with trauma, feeling invisible, and then fighting to be seen…I know a little something about that. She didn’t just find herself, she fought like hell to become herself. And now the world gets to revel in her talent and strength.

Sammy could sing, dance, act, do impressions, tell jokes—the ultimate entertainer. But what stayed with me was everything he had to overcome just to stand on that stage. He faced racism and rejection and still managed to dazzle the world. Sammy taught me that showbiz magic is making it look easy when nothing about it is and that talent always transcends.

I love Sedaris’s ability to find the absurdity in everyday life, especially the humiliating parts. He writes about family, being an outsider, and all the ridiculous things people do to one another. He reminds me that sometimes you don’t need to make anything up. Just tell people what happened, because just as life is absurd, it is funny, too.

Richard Pryor was a genius, a revolutionary, and such a truthful entertainer. He is by far my favorite comedian of all time. He took his pain, his childhood, his addictions, and everything society told him to keep quiet about and turned it into comedy. He wasn’t just telling jokes. He was telling the truth, and sometimes the truth was ugly as hell. Pryor taught me that comedy can be dangerous, uncomfortable, and still bring down the house.

Steve Martin spent years developing an act nobody understood. Sound familiar? He worked every lousy gig imaginable, refined every little detail, and kept going until the audience finally caught up. This book captures the loneliness, obsession, and sheer stubbornness it takes to be a comedian. Nobody sees the thousands of nights you bomb before they call you an overnight success.

Tina Fey is smart, hilarious, and knows how to run the show. That’s a dangerous combination in a business where people love telling you to sit down and shut up. I love her honesty about ambition, insecurity, and the absurdity of show business. She’s living proof that you can be the boss, get the laugh, and still have absolutely no idea what you’re doing half the time.

Marc Shaiman is a walking, talking, piano-playing encyclopedia of show business. This guy has worked with everybody, and I mean EVERYBODY…even me! What I love is that underneath all the Broadway glamour and Hollywood success is a kid who just wanted to put on a show. I know that kid. I am that kid, too.

This is my kind of history book! Give me the drunks, the nightclub comics, the vaudevillians, the hustlers, and the people doing three shows a night for 20 bucks and a sandwich. Comedy has always been filled with outsiders and oddballs trying to make a living getting laughs. Reading this felt like discovering my family tree.

Hannah Gadsby did something extraordinary. She questioned the very thing that saved my life: comedy. For years, I turned my pain into punchlines because making people laugh was easier than telling them what really happened. Hannah challenged the idea that we always have to make our suffering entertaining. Sometimes the bravest thing a comedian can do is tell a story without giving the audience a way out.

Leslie Jones is a force of nature. She’s loud, fearless, outrageous, and doesn’t give a flying f*ck what anybody thinks. She spent years grinding away in comedy clubs before getting her big break. I love anybody who’s been told they’re too much and responds by turning up the volume. Leslie didn’t change herself to fit into show business. She made show business make room for Leslie F*cking Jones!

#6716. Lasagna-Vibes Zucchini Skillet

For years, one of my go-to dinners in the summer was zucchini lasagna, where zucchini is used in place of noodles. It’s delightful, but it’s also very labor-intensive, requiring you to slice the zucchini into long, thin planks, salt each individual plank, wipe each individual plank, and then layer the zucchini “noodles” with ricotta, sauce, and mozzarella. Now I have far too many children to be salting individual planks of zucchini—so I make this. It’s a dump-and-go skillet meal that has all of those favorite flavors in a way, way quicker and easier format.

Read More: Finding My Way Back to the Kitchen After Giving Birth

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground turkey and cook, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until mostly cooked through with only a little pink remaining, about 4 minutes. Add 3 medium zucchini (about 20 oz.), halved lengthwise, sliced crosswise ⅛" thick, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt; season with freshly ground black pepper. Increase heat to high and cook, stirring often, until meat is cooked through and no longer pink and zucchini is tender, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium and stir in one 14.5-oz. can tomato sauce, 2 tsp. Italian seasoning, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. onion powder, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and half of 1 cup thinly sliced basil leaves. Taste zucchini mixture and season with more salt and pepper if needed. Swirl in spoonfuls of 4 oz. whole-milk ricotta (about ½ cup), then sprinkle 4 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over. Reduce heat to low, cover pan, and cook until mozzarella is melted, about 4 minutes.

Top zucchini mixture with remaining basil and crushed red pepper flakes (if using) to serve.

More often than not, finding the best gifts for dads involves putting your thinking cap on to mentally trawl through all of the very practical things they already own, along with the stuff that they’d just never use. Fortunately, we've got a few good dads on the GQ staff. Opinionated dads. Handsome dads. Great dads. And they've actually got some ideas.

Still no dice? We'd suggest perusing the rest of our gift guides and signing up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

Simple, generously proportioned, and blessed with a great collar, this checked shirt from Japanese label Frizmworks gets all the little things right. And the price? Legendary.

There's a reason a Burberry check scarf costs what it does. The pattern is destined to outlast every passing trend and come back into fashion again and again. And the cashmere? Every bit as luxurious as he'd hope.

A Shaggy Dog for the shaggy ol' dog, y'know. J.Press's sweater is the real deal, made from Shetland wool that's hand-brushed to achieve its signature fuzzy texture. And yes, it's still made in Scotland, where the wool comes from. Tradition is tradition.

#6713. As Midterms Approach, US Consumer Anxiety Is High — But Fashion Is Set to Rally

Ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections, US consumer anxiety is at a high.

Thirty-four percent of respondents to an Economist/YouGov survey conducted in October considered the economy and inflation to be the most important issues facing the US. Sixty-seven percent of respondents said they disapproved of President Trump’s handling of inflation. And, when asked how they felt about their futures compared to 10 years ago, 48% said they were more pessimistic.

As reports of consumer sentiment edging close to all-time lows in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections (it dipped once again in October, falling to 48 from 48.1 in September, according to the University of Michigan’s consumer survey), luxury conglomerates continued referring to North America as a “bright spot” in their most recent quarterly earnings, reaffirming the United States as the boon that it has been for luxury this past year.

“People express frustration and anger and disappointment — and then they go out and shop,” says HSBC US head of retail and apparel Eric Fisch, noting that, despite cost of living increases, this applies to shoppers from mass to luxury. “I’ve consistently seen that, especially since Covid, where consumer spending disconnects from consumer sentiment.”

Though analysts have speculated a US normalization following its growth streak, the country has, for now, remained relatively stable. The Americas led growth at Zegna, up 14%. “In particular, the Americas continued its double-digit trend, despite an increasingly demanding comparison base,” executive chair Ermenegildo “Gildo” Zegna said in a statement. At Hermès, Americas revenues were up 8.8% in the third quarter, also posting the highest growth by region. North America was Kering’s only growth region, up 1% in Q3. It was also up for Moncler and Ferragamo.

Analysts aren’t convinced that the forthcoming midterm elections will have much impact on this still-positive trajectory. If anything, they agree, there might be a slight dip, but not one that will hurt the holidays. “Historically speaking, consumers don’t really let elections influence their spending all that much,” says Neil Saunders, managing director of Globaldata’s retail division. Fisch notes that the ramp up in political ads has crowded exposure for brands, but that should clear up by the holidays.

Brands and analysts alike remain bullish on the US. Fisch, who has just returned from two weeks in Europe, says that many of the brands he spoke with on the ground are hedging their bets on the US shopper. The recent unrest in Europe and continued softness in the Middle East means brands are banking even more — and putting extra pressure — on the US. “The events in Europe are only going to provide more of a cloud over the consumer there, making it more challenging,” Fisch says. “The US continues to be the growth engine and the opportunity.” He adds that many brands are continuing to invest capital in the country.

If the midterms impact on consumer spending will be minor, how is the rest of the year shaping up for the American shopper as we approach the high-stakes holiday season?

It’s now widely accepted that consumer sentiment doesn’t necessarily align with what people are doing with their money. “There has been a growing disconnect between how people say they feel and how they act in terms of spending and buying, including on fashion,” Saunders says. “Despite the gloom, consumers have been spending more on apparel.”

This splintering began after the pandemic, and has been referred to as the “vibecession”, wherein people are downbeat about the economy even if they’re doing financially OK. “Sentiment measures mood and, I would argue, empathy. Consumers may feel personally OK or living comfortably because of their wage gains, but feel others cannot be in a good spot or living comfortably,” Christine Barton, managing director and senior partner at BCG, explains. “Consumers can be trusted about themselves and their households; just not good judges about the economy and real consumption.”

This disjuncture partly stems from the fact that caution and uncertainty are now embedded into the consumer psyche, he adds. Because of this, continued anxiety is unlikely to change the trajectory of the luxury or fashion segments. “What will cause a slowdown is if consumers see a tangible and prolonged compression of their incomes,” Fisch says. “We have seen a bit of these things over recent months thanks to high inflation and slower wage growth, but it is not all that pronounced.”

For fashion retailers and brands, this should be encouraging, says Barton. She points to the firm’s recent holiday research, which found that clothing and shoes are the top planned Black Friday purchase category across every generation in the US, with purchase intent increasing across all age groups compared to last year.

Though US consumers are still spending, they’re doing so in a more researched and considered way, analysts flag. “People are thinking more deeply before they buy and are undertaking more activities like price checking — that’s the area where we’re seeing the shift,” Saunders says. Barton points to a recent BCG survey, whereby 91% of consumers actively research their fashion choices before making a purchase and 53% identify quality for the price as the biggest driver of value.

“Consumers are clearly feeling the pressure of higher prices, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re pulling back on spending,” says Barton. “What we’re seeing instead is a greater emphasis on perceived value, and making sure purchases feel personally worthwhile.”

This, Fisch flags, is why the advanced contemporary category is doing the best of his portfolio. “The consumer is seeing a lot of value for their money. It’s on trend, it’s great product, it’s great quality, and they’re struggling with the price increases that true luxury has gone through over the past few years,” he explains. “You have to look at those two together and say, ‘Oh, the consumer is really quite strong. It’s just the high luxury priced a lot of people out.’” This is evidenced in the success of brands like TWP and Harris Tapper, which are operating at a price point that’s steep, but well below that of luxury brands. Per BCG’s Center for Consumer Insight (CCI) research, 67% of respondents wouldn’t buy a product, even if they could afford it, unless they feel it offers strong value, Barton says.

This attitude will inform US holiday shopping habits, as seasonal deals boost spending further, analysts expect. Eighty-five percent of consumers plan to shop year-end sales events (like Black Friday) this year, up 2 percentage points from 2025, with clothing and shoes leading purchase intentions across every generation, per BCG. “We saw this for the last several holidays, where pent-up demand in the ‘want’ categories and purchases were delayed into holiday spending,” Barton says. “What matters for brands is understanding that consumers can feel anxious about the future while continuing to spend in the present.”

“The US is going to drive growth as it has for the prior three quarters,” Fisch says of Q4’s holiday season, often the most important quarter for brands. And beyond that, into 2027? “I don’t see anything that would lead me to believe that it won’t be a growth year in the US.”

#6712. Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf Cake

Something about having a loaf of lemon poppy seed cake on the counter makes you feel like the star of a sitcom. As if you might drink your coffee from a thick-walled mug and scratch your cat under the chin just before you leave for work, a slice of said cake in your hand as you dash to the bus stop. Whether that rings true or not, know that this is a main character cake, worthy of its own show. Tall and hefty with a gentle tang and the crunchy burst of poppy seeds in every bite, it is completely unfussy yet still elegant. The bright loaf cake sings of sunny lemons thanks to the zest as well as juice. With the addition of oil and the insulating cap of snow-white glaze, it keeps nicely for a couple of days.

Find more cheerful bakes here: Chocolate Guinness Cake; Apple Cider Doughnut Loaf Cake; and Preserved Lemon Tea Cake.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Generously coat a 9x5" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray or unsalted butter, room temperature; line with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Whisk 2¼ cups (281 g) all-purpose flour, 1½ tsp. baking powder, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine.

Beat zest of 3 large lemons, ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, 5 Tbsp. vegetable oil, 2 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract on medium speed in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with paddle attachment until light and creamy, about 5 minutes.

Add 3 large eggs, one at a time, beating after each addition to combine before adding the next one (batter may look curdled at this point). Scrape down sides of bowl with a rubber spatula, add half of dry ingredients, and beat on low speed just to combine. Add ¾ cup whole milk and remaining dry ingredients and mix until batter is smooth and creamy, about 1 minute. Add ¼ cup poppy seeds; scrape down bottom and sides of bowl and fold batter with spatula a few times to ensure it’s evenly mixed.

Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. (If your pan looks more than three quarters full, transfer excess batter to a greased small ovenproof container and bake alongside cake as a cook’s treat). Generously coat the blade of a small paring knife with nonstick spray; run knife lengthwise through center of batter to make a shallow cut (this will help cake split cleanly along line as it bakes rather than cracking randomly).

Bake cake until golden brown all over, it springs back when gently pressed, and a tester inserted into the center comes out with only a few moist crumbs attached, 60–65 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and let cake cool slightly in pan, about 15 minutes.

Run a small offset spatula around edges of cake to loosen, then invert out onto rack. Turn cake right side up and let cool completely.

Stir 1 cup (110 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and a pinch of kosher salt in small bowl, adding up to 1 Tbsp. additional lemon juice as needed, until thick but pourable. Pour glaze over cake, letting it drip down sides. Top with poppy seeds and thin strips of lemon zest if using while glaze is still wet; let sit until glaze is set, at least 45 minutes.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.
