#6694. Salt Bread (Shio Pan)

Welcome to the Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep into why it works. This month we welcome deputy food editor Hana Asbrink to be our guest baker. Come bake and learn with us—and don’t forget to join the Bake Club group chat over on Substack.

The version of this recipe that appeared in our November 2026 print issue has the incorrect bake time listed. The recipe that follows features the correct total bake times of 15–18 minutes (please see step 8).

Salt bread is a wondrous buttery roll known as shio pan in Japanese or sogeum ppang in Korean. It originated in Japan in 2014 and quickly became popularized in Korea soon thereafter, taking off in the post-Covid era around 2021. It’s formed by rolling each ball of dough around a nub of salted butter. As it bakes, the butter melts and oozes out of the bun, “frying” and crisping up the bottom. If you can imagine a warm dinner roll meeting a flaky croissant, you’re getting closer.

You’ll often find a range of salt bread, some leaning closer to sturdy bread with a tighter crumb and others resembling a softer milk bread. In all salt bread cases, there are a few key identifiers: (1) a deeply golden exterior, with the aforementioned crisp bottom; (2) the signature hollow in the middle (where the pat of butter once stood) when you tear the bun in half; and (3) a sprinkle of flaky or coarse salt atop the bun.

In this riff, I use an enriched dough, bringing in qualities of a soft milk bread into the mix. With the bread flour, the end result is a lovely, crowd-pleasing bun that’s great for snacking on its own or enjoying alongside a special holiday meal. If there’s one note to highlight: Ensure you are starting with a fresh pack of instant (or “rapid-rise”) yeast. This will make all the difference in the rise and the eventual yield.

Read More: BA Bake Club’s October Recipe Is the Best Dinner Roll We’ve Ever Made

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 3 hours 30 minutes for resting)

Stir 2 Tbsp. (16 g) flour and ½ cup water in a small skillet, preferably nonstick, over medium heat with a heatproof rubber spatula to combine and cook, stirring constantly, until thickened to the texture of mayonnaise, about 2 minutes; remove from heat. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into small pieces and stir until melted. Transfer tangzhong to the bowl of a stand mixer.

Add 2 large eggs, ½ cup whole milk, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) to tangzhong; stir vigorously by hand with rubber spatula until incorporated. Add remaining 4 cups (500 g) flour, attach bowl to stand mixer fitted with a dough hook or paddle, and mix on low speed until dough is smooth and soft (it may stick to bottom of bowl but should mostly clear sides), 20–25 minutes. Pinch off a small piece of dough and stretch it between your thumbs and index fingers on both hands. The dough should be able to stretch thin enough to let light through without breaking. If it tears, the gluten is not yet developed enough. Keep mixing until it can stretch; it may take up to 30 minutes.

Transfer dough to a work surface (no need to flour) and shape into a ball. Lightly grease stand mixer bowl with vegetable oil. Return dough to bowl, cover tightly with a plate or plastic wrap, and let rise in a warm, draft-free spot until nearly doubled in size, about 2 hours. (For optimal flavor, let dough sit at room temperature 30 minutes, then cover tightly or transfer to an airtight container and chill at least 8 hours and up to 2 days to proof slowly.)

Meanwhile, cut 1 cup (2 sticks) salted butter into 1-Tbsp. pieces and arrange in a single layer on a large plate or small baking sheet. Chill in freezer until ready to use.

Transfer dough to a surface (no need to bring to room temperature before shaping if you chilled it). Using a bench scraper or paring knife, cut dough into 70–75 g portions (you’ll get 12–16 portions depending on how much your dough has risen). Working with 1 portion at a time, cup your hand over dough and drag across surface, moving your hand in a rapid circular motion to form into a tight ball (cold dough is easier to work with; rolling into balls on an unfloured, ungreased counter creates friction and helps the shaping process). Place on a baking sheet and cover with plastic wrap; let sit 15 minutes.

Uncover dough (save plastic wrap) and, working one at a time, carefully roll each ball into a cone shape with your hands (you want them about 4" on the wider end). Return to baking sheet and re-cover with reserved plastic wrap. Let dough rest 15 minutes.

Place a cone in front of you on surface with wider end facing toward you (keep remaining cones covered in plastic wrap). Lightly flatten with your palm, then roll out dough lengthwise to make an isosceles triangle about 12" long with a 3½"–4"-wide base (short side of triangle). Place 1 Tbsp. frozen salted butter at base of dough and roll up (not too tightly) like a croissant. Arrange, seam side down, back on baking sheet. Repeat with remaining cones and salted butter (you may not need all of the butter; save it for another use). Let rolls sit at room temperature until slightly puffed, about 1 hour.

Place a rack in lowest position in oven; preheat to 425°. Remove plastic from rolls. Lightly mist rolls with water from spray bottle; sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Bake 10 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back and continue baking rolls until golden brown on top and bottom, 5–8 minutes more (keep an eye that they don’t burn). Remove from oven (there will be melted butter on baking sheet, so be careful) and, using a heatproof pastry brush, brush butter on baking sheet over rolls. Let rolls cool at least 10 minutes before serving.

Do Ahead: Rolls can be baked 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6693. The Grooms—and Every Single Guest—Wore White to This Wedding at a Virginia Gilded Age Mansion

While visiting their families for the holidays in Northern Virginia, interior designers Cameron Billinghurst and Nolan Beck Rivera went on a Tinder date. As a sweet gesture, Cameron brought Nolan a single calla lily when they met for coffee. The two lost touch until exactly one year later, on December 26, 2019, when the two bumped into each other at the National Museum of African American History and Culture. “We reconnected and started talking every day,” Cameron says. During COVID, the two became even closer and decided to move in together in Richmond, Virginia. “We figured we could just rent a place and leave if we didn’t like it, but we found such an amazing creative community here,” says Cameron. “We’re six years in, and I don’t see us moving.” Not only did they become romantic partners, but they also co-founded a design firm, Studio Tarea, which focuses on bespoke interiors for residential and commercial spaces.

While it wasn’t a proposal, Nolan did have rings made for them both with The Circle Craft just a few months into dating. “I avoided calling them engagement rings for a while, and ‘promise ring’ had a weird ring to it,” he says. “So I just kind of said, ‘Oh here, I made us matching rings,’ and that was it.” In fact, there was no proposal at all when the couple started planning their wedding. “We started talking about what we’d both want out of a wedding and after a few years of that, we decided to just put a date on the calendar,” says Cameron. Adds Nolan, “Not very romantic, but we’re pragmatists. It just kind of felt like it was going to happen from the beginning.”

As they kicked off planning, the hospitality-inclined pair wanted to put guest experience first throughout the day and tap their creative community to bring everything to life. “From the get-go, we knew who we could trust to take our ideas and build something cool on top of them,” says Cameron. “We’ve also been to many weddings and made sure to include the things we loved while skipping some of the expected traditions that didn’t resonate.” Jokes Nolan, “We really streamlined a lot of the romance out of this thing. We just wanted everyone to arrive, have enough to eat and drink, and cut a rug with us.” He adds, “There were no jerks at this wedding. Everyone that was working it and everyone we invited was just the best.”

The to-be-weds set their date for June 6, 2026, at the Branch Museum of Design in Richmond. “It’s an old Gilded Age mansion that is now a design museum in Richmond’s Fan neighborhood,” explains Nolan. As the couple hoped to infuse their cultural backgrounds throughout the affair, this venue decision helped tie in a part of their history. “While the food, music, and much of the entertainment were informed by our respective mothers’ Honduran and African-American cultures, we felt our English-descended dads reflected in the Tudor Revival mansion where the whole thing took place,” says Cameron.

James Beard Award semi-finalist chef Brittany Anderson was a key player in bringing together this ethos of hospitality and culture. “We wanted the experience to be food-centric,” says Nolan. “She was able to weave together Honduran and Black Southern influences into a very unique menu that was very specific to us.” Floral design was also vital to the entire aesthetic of the celebration thanks to the work of Meredith Wheeler of Secret Flowers. “We wanted everything to be minimal and modern in contrast to the Tudor Revival mansion we were in,” explains Cameron. “We’re modernists, and I think the florals really helped keep the wedding in a modernist space.” The final team member who helped execute the celebration was Bryce Carson of Carson Ashby Events, who served as day-of coordinator and helped with last logistical details of the event. “I know that the wedding wouldn’t have gone nearly as smoothly without Bryce,” adds Nolan.

The dress code for the weekend was set with every groom and guest in the same palette. “We decided a long time ago that we wanted to do a dress code of white to beige for all guests,” says Cameron. “We were as excited or more excited to see what friends and family would be wearing than we were about our own looks.” Many friends wore vintage, some designed their own looks, and others even wore their own wedding dresses. “Including my ballet teacher, who wore her original wedding dress from long enough ago that it would be considered vintage today,” adds Nolan.

That said, the couple did put care into their attire. Cameron donned a wool silk suit by Grand Le Mar and black Jacques Solovière loafers. To accessorize, he wore a silver bracelet that belonged to his grandma Eddie Mae and a vintage Seiko tank watch. Nolan’s outfit went through a few trials. “I’d ordered a custom outfit with a matador-style jacket and big, cool design-y pants from a designer on the internet who turned out to be a scammer,” he says. “So I ended up having to go to SuitSupply in Washington, DC only a few weeks before the wedding, and it arrived just before the big day.”

However, the outfit wasn’t perfect just yet. “They had made a mistake with the pants, so we took them to Lida at Roya Alterations here in Richmond—another act of Bryce heroism—and she fixed them the day before the wedding,” Nolan says. He accented the look with silver and pearl calla lily earrings lent by a friend, vintage cufflinks in similar materials, his father’s watch, and Saint Laurent boots. “I bought them when I got one of my first big checks as a self-employed person and walked the heels off of them, so I had them redone before the wedding,” he adds.

Weekend festivities began with a picnic in the park in the gardens of the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts. “More than 80 of our 128 guests were from out of town, and it gave us all an opportunity to spend a little more time together,” says Nolan. That evening, the grooms had an intimate rehearsal dinner at the home of their friends Lucia Zolea and Patrick Inskeep, who are also parents to their flower girl, Jane. “We’d designed their garden a couple of years ago, and it was a really special place to share with our loved ones and have dinner,” says Cameron. Dinner came from the couple’s favorite, Ronnie’s Original BBQ. “Ronnie himself was there, which is kind of a big deal,” adds Nolan.

As the guests arrived on the wedding day, they were treated to cocktails and delicious bites before taking a seat in the ceremony area. On the lawn, the floral team crafted a chapel in-the-round of corn stalks, grasses, and Spanish moss with guests seated in four quadrants around the center. “We had a gospel choir off to one side singing a cappella,” explains Cameron. “My grandmother used to take me to church with her, and this was our way of bringing her into the ceremony. Guests were given white paddle fans, and the result felt romantic and rooted in the South in a non-traditional kind of way.”

The grooms walked down the aisle to “Never Let Me Go” by Florence and the Machine sung by the choir and had the ceremony officiated by their close friend Lanecia Rouse. “Asking Lanecia to officiate was actually one of the first decisions we made for the wedding,” says Cameron. “Lanecia also gave a brief history of jumping the broom and its significance in the Black community, and reminded everyone (in a fun, beautiful way) that the rights that we ourselves were exercising that day (interracial marriage and gay marriage) were both hard-fought and not necessarily secure for future generations, which makes it especially beautiful that we’re able to do this and that everyone showed up for us.” The grooms reflect how the ceremony really made them feel as if they were part of a community.

Next came dinner inside the mansion. “We wanted to keep table arrangements very pared back to accommodate family-style service and guest interaction,” says Cameron. “The final result—stalks of corn on simple chrome bases—was pretty striking when you entered the space, but also incredibly practical at dinner.” Guests were seated based on thoughtful decisions by the grooms. “One of the most fun parts for us of the planning process was creating the seating chart for dinner and imagining all the ways we could connect our loved ones from all over,” explains Cameron. “It felt really special to see it happen in real time. We only invited lovely people that we wanted there, and everyone gelled so perfectly.” Chef Anderson served a menu of grilled chicken, mushroom risotto, veggies, and ticucos, a tamale-like dish native to Honduras. Cheerwine cake from Chef Leah Branch sweetened up the night further.

The grooms broke into a custom disco ball piñata to start the reception. “We filled it with lollipops, chocolate, flavored condoms, poppers, wigs, fake mustaches, candy cigarettes, heart-shaped glasses, and a silver thong,” says Nolan. “I don’t know who got the thong.” The dance party started as a hundred mylar balloons floated down from the choir loft and a kaleidoscopic video of flowers was projected onto the dance floor. Adds Nolan, “Every minute or two a balloon would explode, and everyone would cheer and just keep dancing.” In addition to dancing and mingling, guests could have a tattoo done by Vincent Riquier of The Ceremony Tattoo. “The most popular designs were a drawing of a calla lily that I’ve had tattooed on my shoulder since Cameron and I got together, and the word Amor in my handwriting,” says Nolan.

The grooms did a grand sparkler exit and sped off on Nolan’s 1973 BMW R75/5 with cans tied to the back. Afterward, many guests headed off to Babe’s of Carytown, the oldest lesbian bar on the East Coast. “We hung out there until about 2 a.m., dancing and catching up with all of the people who came into town to celebrate us,” says Cameron. “We closed the night across the street at 7-11 with celebratory Slurpees.” Adds Nolan, “Drinking a bright red Slurpee in a white tux is pretty harrowing, but we just really wanted Slurpees.”

Looking back, the grooms share how wonderful it was to have their community contribute to their celebration and to have so many details feel specific to their story. “It’s the best wedding I’ve ever been to,” says Nolan.

We designed the invitations ourselves and used photos by our friends Lucia Zolea and Kate Jennings. The vintage calla lily brooch was a gift from Lucia, too, and the back of the rehearsal dinner invitation was a photo of her garden, which we designed and is where we had our rehearsal dinner.

Cameron wore a wool silk suit and Nolan wore a tuxedo. Our goal was to look sharp and well-dressed, but we really wanted to create the space for all of our guests’ outfits to shine through as well.

We got married in a 1919 Tudor Revival mansion in Richmond that now houses the Branch Museum of Design.

I borrowed my dad’s vintage Seiko watch, and the bracelet was from a friend’s shop, Na Nin. —Nolan

We decided to get ready together in what was Mr. Branch’s wood-paneled bedroom. Mrs. Branch’s bedroom is where family and close friends got dressed.

It was so special to have so many friends from all over the world in one place.

We loved that, even with the somewhat strict dress code, there were no outfit repeats and everyone was able to bring their own perspective and voice.

My sister’s shoes by Cult Gaia. She wore a dress that was inspired by Greek statuary. Her rings were made by our friends at The Circle Craft. I helped design the rose a few years ago. —Nolan

This patio on the roof was actually a great spot to micromanage everything from.

The couple who built the house had a really robust collection of Renaissance art. We loved the look of modernity in front of a 16th-century Flemish tapestry.

Nolan made our gold bands with The Circle Craft shortly after we started dating. Our wedding rings are from the Mayan city of Copán in Honduras, which we’ve visited a few times. They’re silver with pieces of different semi-precious stones inlaid. —Cameron

We opted for an in-the-round ceremony so we could be surrounded by the people we love.

Meredith at Secret Flowers created this incredible room out of tall grasses and moss.

Cameron brought me a single calla lily on our first date six years ago and they’ve held their importance to us since. —Nolan

Guests were greeted with chilled peanut soup with sunflower chili crisp as they arrived.

Our stylish friend Sam in a J.Crew suit and a shirt by local brand Ledbury. He made the tie himself.

Audra wore a tuxedo and oversized sculptural earrings. She and her seven-year-old daughter came up with the idea of using one of them as a corsage.

Several people made their own outfits. Some people wore their wedding dresses. And the only person who didn’t get the memo blended right in once he took his jacket off.

Our flower girl, Jane, with her mother, Lucia, and our ring bearer, Robby, with his father, Bobby. We’ve been so lucky to be a part of Jane and Robby’s lives since they were born and it was really amazing to have them there on the day.

Jane did an excellent job as the flower girl. She wore the sweetest little dress from Tia Cibani.

Our good friend Lanecia officiated the ceremony.

We walked down the aisle to a gospel choir singing “Never Let Me Go” by Florence + the Machine.

Entering the circle. It was a singular experience.

Lanecia approached the ceremony so thoughtfully and spoke about love, history, and the cultural context of the ceremony.

I grew up going to a Southern Baptist church with my late grandmother, Eddie, and the music was always a really special part of the experience. I knew I wanted that cultural connection to be a part of the day from early on. Four vocalists from Gospel Touch sang selections for guests before and during the ceremony. —Cameron

We had a 12-minute ceremony, then it was off to dinner.

My other love, my 1973 BMW R75/5. I made the heart and tied ribbons around soup cans earlier in the week. —Nolan

My friend Arlene thrifted that shawl about an hour before the wedding. —Nolan

Our cocktails were mignonette martinis and mojitos. The mignonette is a signature drink at Bar Buoy, a restaurant we designed. And we drink a lot of mojitos.

Judson and Quinton having a chat after the ceremony. We made sure everyone had drinks and food from the moment they arrived to the moment they left.

I actually think the seating chart was like a fun puzzle where we got to introduce people we thought would get along. Watching people come together ended up being one of the best parts of the wedding. —Cameron

We asked Meredith to go super minimal with the table decor. We wanted something tall and dramatic but that wouldn’t interfere with cross-table conversations.

All in all, pretty minimalist tables. Each place setting had a scented candle with a special scent that we developed with Na Nin. The place cards were hand-etched by Leah Schmidt.

We have 800 of these matchbooks leftover if you need any.

Dinner was served family style. We had grilled chicken, mushroom risotto, cornbread, and ticucos, a pre-Hispanic sort of tamale from the mountains of Honduras. Everything aside from the chicken was vegan. Chef Brittanny Anderson knocked it out of the park.

Chef Leah Branch came to personally plate and serve the cake. Instead of doing a big central cake, we chose to have individual portions of her Cheerwine cake that she serves at The Roosevelt, one of our favorite restaurants where we signed our marriage certificate last year.

We had a local Latin candy shop, Dulceria Minilandia, make our disco-ball piñata. We filled it with candy cigarettes, wigs, condoms, poppers, fake mustaches, and chocolate... and one silver thong.

Friends, neighbors, and family watching us bash a piñata.

Friends, neighbors, and family watching us bash a piñata.

90 out of 100 of these balloons exploded.

Our neighbors, Michael and Arlinda, looking sharp in their mustaches.

Murilo getting inked. Some of our guests got their first-ever tattoos that night.

Friend and clothing designer Maya Shaw looking incredible.

Jordan and Kael. Jordan wore the first wedding dress she bought for their wedding last year but ended up not wearing. Kael is wearing the shirt that Jordan made for him to wear at their wedding.

We had a projection of a floral kaleidoscope across the dance floor. It looked really stunning and distorted across everyone’s white outfits.

Saoli, Emi, Alisha, and Jacqueline enjoying their skinny European cigarettes. Alisha actually made her own dress for the night.

Driving off on the BMW. We just parked around the corner then got in a friend’s car to hit the gay club. —Nolan

#6691. Texas BBQ in NYC? Bark Takes Brisket on a Caribbean Vacation.

This is Highly Recommend, a column dedicated to what we’re eating, drinking, and buying.

On a Friday night in Brooklyn, the line at Bark BBQ snakes through long communal tables, past a glass-enclosed show pit, and out onto the sidewalk, where the rich scents of oak-smoked beef and pork fill the air. If you didn’t arrive hungry, you certainly are by the time you reach the order counter.

Once you get a taste of pitmaster Ruben Santana’s 14-hour smoked brisket, with its peppery bark and butter-soft interior, you’ll forget the wait. Sour orange-kissed chicharrón—pit-smoked for six hours, chilled, sliced into strips, and fried to order—provides a crackly-chewy counterpart. Smoked carnitas, a play on Dominican carne salada made from brisket trimmings confited in their own fat, are a study in silky-fatty goodness, doused with spicy green aji verde. Each meaty platter arrives with a small mound of bright, house-pickled bell peppers that I wanted to bring home in an extra-large jar.

Cerdo a la Leña goes on low-country smokers.

Perhaps the most unique item, though, is the daily Cerdo a la Leña, a Caribbean-style whole hog that’s marinated in sofrito for two days before it reaches the low-country smokers. Rather than being pulled or shredded, the pork is quartered, its skin rendered crisp in the oven throughout the day, and then chopped to order by weight and dressed with a South Carolina-style vinegar sauce.

Pulling from his Dominican upbringing in Queens, Santana has done what often feels impossible in this oversaturated city — created a fresh culinary mash-up. After studying Central Texas barbecue online and on TV, Santana began infusing his classic Southern meats with the Dominican flavors of oregano, sofrito, adobo, sour orange, molasses, honey, and achiote.

Take a sauce-fueled road trip through the Carolinas, experience the Super Bowl of Swine, plan your next big cookout, and more.

The business began as a pandemic pop-up, which then grew into a Time Out Market stall, which then ballooned into this 8,000-square foot meat emporium in Bushwick. Here, with help from six custom Cen-Tex smokers (four offsets, two low-country) imported from Luling, Texas, Santana’s process begins at 5 o’clock every morning and lasts until the final piece of brisket comes off the smoker at 10 p.m.

The sides, Santana says, offer the most direct connection to his upbringing. Earthy and aromatic arroz congrí follows a recipe from his Cuban uncle. Rich criollo BBQ beans are simmered in adobo and barbecue sauce with a bit of pulled pork. Maduros nail that perfect fried sweet plantain texture: caramelized on the outside, tender on the inside. For dessert, Torta Dominicana reimagines cornbread as a warm, spiced cake soaked in honey butter. Bark also boasts a full bar offering cocktails and meat-specific wine pairings—a rare move for a barbecue joint.

Bark BBQ's colmado displays groceries and snacks that are staples in the Dominican.

Can I tell you this is the best barbecue in New York? I’m not sure I’m qualified to make that statement. But I can tell you, as a born Southerner with a deep interest in such things, that it’s my favorite in New York, not to mention some of the most personal and delicious barbecue I’ve tasted anywhere.

#6690. BA's Best Rice Krispies Treats

Perhaps the most nostalgic of all recipes, a classic Rice Krispies treat is hard to beat. There’s just something about the crisp yet gooey texture that can’t be replicated. While the classic back-of-box recipe is a guaranteed winner, we thought it was high time to give the original a run for its money. Introducing our new favorite way to make Rice Krispies treats, with a few small (but dramatic) tweaks to the original formula. For starters, this version increases the butter and browns it, adding a subtle nutty flavor. From there, the marshmallows are split in two: The first set gets fully melted into the butter along with salt and vanilla, while the remaining set gets folded in along with the cereal so you get pockets of stretchy marshmallow throughout. While seemingly insignificant, these small changes make for a Rice Krispies treat that’s perfectly pullable, delightfully sweet yet salty, and just a touch more exciting than the classic.

Read More: The Only Type of Marshmallows I’ll Use for Rice Krispies Treats

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Lightly coat a 13x9" baking pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray and line with parchment paper, leaving overhang on long sides. Cook ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat, stirring constantly, until butter foams, then darkens to a light amber, about 4 minutes. Remove from heat and immediately add one 10-oz. bag mini marshmallows, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and quickly stir until marshmallows are melted.

Add remaining one 10-oz. bag mini marshmallows and 9 cups Rice Krispies or other puffed rice cereal to pot and mix until cereal is completely coated in melted marshmallow mixture and last addition of marshmallows is melted slightly. Working quickly, transfer mixture to prepared pan and spread into an even layer. (Don’t press too hard.) Let sit at least 1 hour before cutting into squares.

Do Ahead: Rice Krispies treats can be made 2 days ahead. Store tightly covered at room temperature.

#6688. Reckoning With Borat, 20 Years Later

Last month, I sat in a packed-to-the-gills movie theater to experience the latest release from a controversial comedian whose work regularly blurs the line between docu-reality and narrative fiction. I am, of course, referring to Ali G: Who Iz I?—the cinematic return of Sacha Baron Cohen’s once-and-still-somewhat-beloved durag-doffing titular character.

Before the film was unceremoniously dumped on Prime Video last week, I managed to snag a ticket to the only New York City screening that wasn’t totally sold-out, booking a seat—last row, tucked in an alcove of the theater—with the intention of isolated note-taking and (gasp!) the occasional phone-glance should the movie prove tedious. The recliners next to me were eventually claimed by a gentleman decked in a very Ali G-esque skull cap and wraparounds, who unleashed a deafening “BOOYAKASHA!” after Nicole Kidman’s AMC intro.

Cohen’s brand of confrontational cringe comedy continues to attract a level of interest, thanks in part to a certain mustached-and-mankini’d Kazakh journalist. The cultural explosion that was Borat! Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan (has any movie title so padded the word count?) turns 20 years old this week, and it remains a curious artifact of the 2000s: impossibly dated and slightly better than you might remember, even as its creator’s talent has slowly and unmistakably eroded.

If you were just old enough to purchase a ticket to an R-rated movie in 2006, Borat felt like a truly out-of-nowhere phenomenon in terms of mass impact. But the character, armed with little more than a shabby suit and an aggressive cheer, emerged from Cohen’s cult favorite Da Ali G Show, which ran for one season on BBC’s Channel 4 in 2000 before making the leap to HBO in 2003. Alongside Ali G and the gay Austrian fashion correspondent Brüno, Borat Sagdiyev was just one of the many personalities Cohen regularly deployed in the thorny thickets of gotcha-mentary, trading in culturally oblivious and antisemitic observations supposedly inherited from his Kazakh homeland, often to the shock and dismay of his unsuspecting subjects.

These fool-me-once hijinks weren’t necessarily groundbreaking, even for HBO’s then-provocative late-night programming. Several years prior, The Chris Rock Show engaged in similar man-on-the-street shenanigans (once, he polled residents of NYC’s notoriously hate-crime-prone Howard Beach region about renaming a street after Tupac Shakur). But segments in which Ali G addressed Buzz Aldrin as Buzz Lightyear, or the one where Borat led a bar full of Arizonans in a rousing chorus of “Throw the Jew Down the Well,” were practically reverse-engineered for virality in the internet’s pre-social-media infancy, and the appeal of Cohen’s approach—how far will he go, and will ordinary folk follow him?—was easy to understand, regardless of the visceral discomfort it may have generated.

Straying from the sketch-based format of Da Ali G Show, Borat embraced a loose narrative structure, with its titular inquirer setting out for America to make a documentary on the country’s social peccadilloes with the intent of eventually romancing Pamela Anderson. If you want to get highfalutin about it, the plot itself situates Borat within the legacy of films about Europeans attempting to understand America—a small-but-fascinating subgenre that includes Paul Verhoeven’s fairytale-cum-nightmare Showgirls, the post-hippie pessimism of Michaelangelo Antonioni’s Zabriskie Point, and Kristoffer Borgli’s social-mores rom-dramedy The Drama.

Don’t get it twisted, though: Borat was and still is best enjoyed as a showcase of physical comedy and inflammatory non sequiturs. It’s no less funny in 2026 to watch a grown man wash his face in a toilet bowl, or gesture toward a tortoise while sincerely asking, “What type of dog is this?” The scene in which an etiquette coach attempts to guide Borat through the intricacies of comic timing is itself an excellent study in comic timing; the notorious full-frontal hotel chase sequence between Borat and his producer Azamat (portrayed by steadily-working character actor Ken Davitian) is a marvel for its sheer escalation alone. This stuff killed in a massive Northern New Jersey movie theater when I was 19, and it still kills from the confines of my couch 20 years on.

Unlike much of Cohen’s subsequent work, Borat is not an explicitly political film. Nonetheless, a good deal of its “GREAT SUCCESS!”—$262 million in box receipts off an $18 million budget, with a Best Actor Golden Globe for Cohen himself—is undoubtedly owed to a different sort of comic timing. The film came out in the throes of George W. Bush’s second presidential term, with the US mired in two wars abroad and a hell of its own making. Americans were thirsty for easy targets to shoulder the blame and, if possible, provide some cheap laughs in the process.

Their thirst was quenched in the form of Borat’s many unsuspecting subjects. Some of this was low-hanging fruit: Borat telling a group of feminists to smile more, or acting like a literal bull in a china shop amidst Confederate memorabilia. But the film’s more sensational material depicted rough corners of the American psyche long hidden in plain sight. Most memorably, Borat encounters a group of rowdy frat boys who huff about white pride and express dismay at the abolishment of slavery before engaging in a viewing of Anderson’s infamous leaked sex tape with ex-husband Tommy Lee.

Not everyone was displeased at their portrayal, though. Joe and Miriam Behar, the Jewish couple who offered Borat and Azamat room and board, were good-natured in a 2006 interview with the Boston Globe. For her part, Miriam shrugged off Borat’s naked antisemitism. “To me it's an anti-Muslim movie, not anti-Jewish, because Kazakhstan is mostly Muslim,” she offered.

Behar’s observation underlines the casual bigotry that otherwise stains Borat. The film’s portrayal of Kazakh culture is undoubtedly offensive, and provoked mixed reactions from the country’s government for years to come. For what it’s worth, Cohen pushes back—intentionally or not—on anti-Muslim sentiments during the film’s rodeo sequence, in which Borat tells a particularly racist attendee that he is indeed “not Muslim.”

But given the post-9/11 climate into which Borat was launched, the implications of a foreign correspondent from a majority-Muslim country espousing antisemitic and misogynistic viewpoints are crystal-clear, and Cohen himself seems too smart to sincerely profess a lack of awareness as to how this might be received. It doesn’t help that his subsequent projects resulted in exponential escalations of offense: 2012’s more narratively-focused The Dictator spared no quarter when it came to stereotypes of Arab culture, while the astoundingly homophobic Brüno, from 2009, was loaded with gags about anal sex and resulted in an out-of-court settlement with a Palestinian grocer who was falsely credited as a former terrorist in the film itself.

After 2016’s box-office bomb Grimsby, which is most notable for the allegations of on-set sexual harassment co-star Rebel Wilson later brought toward Cohen, his work went in a more explicitly political direction. There was his 2018 docu-satire series Who Is America?—two episodes of which featured writing and directing contributions from Nathan Fielder—and 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm, a second-verse-same-as-the-first sequel which earned several Oscar nominations and brought a truly bizarre “October surprise” to that year’s presidential election involving actress Maria Bakalova, Rudy Giuliani, and the former New York City Mayor’s pants zipper.

Both of those films were more explicitly message-y than they were riotously funny. Cohen’s latest, Ali G: Who Iz I?, is neither, carrying the all-too-familiar stink of a comedian insisting that their capacity to offend amounts to protected speech. At 55, Cohen is clearly not as willing to submit himself to the ragdoll physics he once deployed; in its place is an often-sullen-looking Ali G, his dreads now gray, weighing the merits of cultural appropriation and sparring with a DEI coordinator about the origins of the durag. The entire affair is belabored and depressing.

It made me think of the Who Is America? character Dr. Nira Cain-N'Degeocello, a send-up of Rachel Dolezal-flavored liberals in the form of a Berkeley professor who dons dashikis and keffiyehs. Early in the film, he rages against Ali G’s culturally appropriative ways to a majority-Black community meeting in Oakland. “We don’t care!,” shouts one participant. In hindsight, it’s as much an expression of exhaustion with the dictates of capital-D discourse as it is a referendum on Cohen’s confrontational method, which now yields far less interesting insights about the national psyche than it did when Borat arrived on American soil in 2006.

#6687. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6686. Adria Arjona Has Come Full Circle

Adria Arjona doesn’t like glam that feels like a transformation. A self-described tomboy growing up, Arjona says she avoided makeup at all costs; but through her journey to becoming a Hollywood actor, she’s been fortunate to work with enough pros who’ve helped her define what she likes. “I’ve discovered that with makeup you can enhance yourself without changing the way that you look, and that makes me feel really empowered, beautiful, and sexy because it’s still me,” she tells Vogue. “Now I believe less is more.”

Some might find it ironic, then, that a makeup minimalist would go on to become a face of one of the world’s most known cosmetics brands; Arjona was just announced as the newest L’Oréal Paris global ambassador. For the actor and producer, this partnership hits far closer to home than makeup itself.

Half Puerto Rican, half Guatemalan, Arjona tells me she grew up all over Latin America, where she didn’t have consistent access to TV shows and movies. “Commercials were my most consistent thing,” she says with a laugh. “The L’Oréal Paris commercial is so ingrained in my head. I just remember playing it with my little friends and being like ‘Porque tú lo vales.’ I've been doing that for so long, so to be able to now be an ambassador and be able to say ‘I’m worth it’ to a camera, it’s surreal.”

Arjona was in the middle of filming The Thomas Crown Affair, the romantic heist film set to debut in March 2027, when she got the news. She remembers telling seven of her closest female friends and family members, who happened to be relaxing in her living room with her: “We let out this huge scream.” Fast-forward to Arjona’s campaign shoot, and the excitement hadn’t turned down a notch. “My mom was there [with me], and we both looked at each other like, Oh my God, this is the coolest thing in the world.”

Filming felt like a big, glamorous movie set, she continues, though everyone was incredibly warm and welcoming. I ask her what she hoped to bring to the campaign, and she admits it’s a tricky question. “You’re coming into a company that has empowered women for so long that yes, you want to bring your essence, but I’m Latin American—I want to bring my own sort of spice.” Now, she’s focusing on learning from the other ambassadors and the company itself. She nods specifically to L’Oréal Paris’s ongoing philanthropic work, envisioning how the two can unite to continue uplifting women—a cause the actor champions through her own foundation.

The campaign, directed by Colin Cardo, takes us to the Théâtre du Châtelet in Paris, where Arjona introduces us to the new Volume Liberté mascara. Created for more than 800% more volume in a single application, the formula delivers soft, clump-free lift. The smudge-free, flake-resistant formula is housed inside a sleek click-to-release tube that adds a touch of luxury to your average mascara—so much so that Arjona was shocked when she first tried it. “It almost feels like a piece of jewelry in your bag, or something super high-end and elevated,” she says. “I’m a very big mascara girl. This makes your lashes so beautiful and bold.”

The shape of the brush, she continues, is what takes this formula to the next level. “During the day, I don’t like to look like I have mascara on, but I want my lashes to look a little bit darker and longer,” she says. It’s one product she doesn’t leave the house without.

True to her no-makeup makeup ethos, her daily look is about enhancing her features. Because most days start with working out, she’ll shower and let her curls air-dry with the L’Oréal Paris Elvive mousse: “It’s not crunchy, and it looks really natural.” When it comes to makeup, she’s obsessed with multipurpose products. Along with Volume Liberté, she keeps the shade Worth It Intense of the Blurfiller Lip Liner in her purse; she reaches for it every day to define her lips, yes, but also to contour when she wants to take her daytime look to the next level: “I know it’s not designed to do that, but I’ll just go for it.” For glow, she swears by the Lumi Glotion for face and body radiance, and the Riche Satin Lipstick for special occasions.

“I like makeup to to kind of enhance your own beauty, but not change too much,” she says. “I don’t like looking like I have a lot of makeup on.” As a lifelong L’Oréal Paris fan, this moment means a lot to her. “It’s just so powerful; [being] an ambassador feels really full-circle to me. I definitely don’t take it lightly.”

Last week, Calvin Klein dropped a hint of their next underwear campaign star via Instagram. The clip featured a guy gliding his fingers from his boxers up to his chest. Very suggestive. Very sexy. Instagram, obviously, went wild. A teaser of a teaser, you might say.

#6684. The Artist Behind New York City’s Most Iconic Restaurant Signs

In Person of Interest we talk to the people catching our eye right now about their projects past and present. Next up, we chat with Brooklyn-based sign painter Will Van Zee about the art of hand-painted restaurant signs, how Instagram has helped revive interest in the craft, and why handmade design still matters in the age of AI.

If you've walked past Elbow Bread, S&P Lunch, Levain Bakery, or dozens of other New York restaurants, you've probably seen Will Van Zee's work. Through his Brooklyn-based studio, Van Zee Sign Co., the artist creates hand-painted and gilded signs that have become a fixture of the city's restaurant landscape. While the online discourse around AI-generated food imagery heats up, Van Zee’s most effective tools remain decidedly old-fashioned.

His thriving business is built on centuries-old techniques, yet many of his clients discover him through Instagram, where videos of his work regularly attract millions of views. Van Zee’s specialty is gilded signage for restaurants, bakeries, and shops. Watch his hypnotic Instagram Reels, and you’ll be transfixed by his meticulous brushwork, application of delicate gold leaf, and detailed flourishes. Through Van Zee’s posts, I discover bakeries, restaurants, and shops that immediately earn a spot on my growing list of places to visit. In this age of AI slop, I reason that if a business is thoughtful enough to invest in custom signage, it is probably just as thoughtful about everything else it did.

We spoke with Van Zee about why handmade signs still matter, how social media has helped revive interest in the craft of sign-making, and what he's learned from his unique vantage point as an artist helping define a restaurant's identity.

I moved to New York in 2008 to study product design. Within about a year of graduating, I started sign-painting professionally but my introduction to this work started much earlier. Growing up, I worked as a house painter. My dad would find jobs for me painting fences, trim, and siding around the neighborhood. It was hard work, but it helped me develop brush control at a young age.

I also fell in love with the restaurant industry. Around age 16, I started as a dishwasher and porter, then became a prep cook and eventually worked closely with the chef and owner. There's something special about being part of a team, getting through a busy service, and feeling exhausted but proud at the end of the night.

Part of building this business was creating a career that allowed me to spend more time around restaurants and the people who run them. New York is a city where people come to eat, and it's exciting to play a small role in helping restaurant owners realize their dreams.

What do you enjoy most about being part of restaurant projects?

I've been in this industry for about 13 or 14 years, so it's common to run into people I've worked with before. A contractor, chef, owner, or designer on a new project is often someone connected to a previous one. My business relies heavily on word of mouth, so those relationships are incredibly important.

One of my favorite parts of the job is attending friends-and-family nights. Most of the time, I see restaurants while they're still under construction, so those events are often my first chance to experience the finished space, try the food, and see everything come together. It's rewarding to celebrate alongside everyone who helped bring the restaurant to life and see the project finally open its doors.

How would you describe your design style?

I try to recreate and preserve the visual character of the city. I spend a lot of time looking at historic photographs and documentation, and as a sign painter, I feel a responsibility to help maintain the visual language that makes New York feel like New York. At the same time, every project is a partnership. The goal is to create something I'm proud of while also making sure it properly represents the business.

I encourage clients to look at historic photos of their building and neighborhood. New York has incredible archives that show what these places looked like decades prior, and those images often provide inspiration for signage today. Sometimes the best solution is simply adapting something that already worked fifty years ago and giving it new life.

How do you position your work in the age of AI-generated design and inexpensive digital graphics?

What makes sign painting special is that it's deeply human. Almost everything I do is made by hand, and that creates a natural connection to restaurants, where chefs are also making things by hand everyday. Hand-painted signs have soul. They're not perfect, and that's exactly what makes them special. The same is true of a great meal. You can tell that a real person made it.

Many of my clients want to communicate that they value things made by people. Even if it costs more or takes longer, a hand-painted sign demonstrates care and craftsmanship. That's especially important in fine dining, where every detail matters. Hiring real artisans signals that level of attention to customers

How did you get started on social media? Did you ever expect your audience to grow the way it has?

I was actually pretty resistant to social media when I started. I didn't even have a personal Instagram account. My wife encouraged me to invest energy into documenting and sharing my work, and it's become part of my process. It's made me a better documentarian.

What's exciting is that sign-painting isn't something most people think about every day, even though signs shape how we experience cities and businesses. Getting to share the process has been really rewarding. Social media has been great for my business, but more importantly, it's helped people appreciate the craft.

What have been some of your favorite restaurant projects?

Some of the restaurant clients that stand out include Rezdôra, Sailor, and Levain Bakery, S&P Lunch, and Baby Blues Luncheonette, for which I designed the logo. Sailor was especially meaningful because it's in my neighborhood. I had eaten at the previous restaurant in that space many times, so being involved in its next chapter felt personal.

The projects I'm proudest of are often the ones that stand the test of time. New York restaurants come and go, so when a place is still thriving a decade later, that feels significant. Rezdôra is a great example. The signage itself isn't especially elaborate, but people love that restaurant. Knowing I played a small role in shaping its identity and helping establish a place that has become so beloved is incredibly rewarding.

#6682. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.

#6681. The Vogue Business Funding Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business Funding Tracker, a running list highlighting the most notable and intriguing investment and M&A activity in fashion and beauty. From emerging disruptors to legacy giants undergoing major changes, we spotlight the deals that are shifting the dynamics of the sectors we cover, including fashion, beauty, tech and sustainability.

Company description: Frasers Group has successfully taken control of Hugo Boss. Following a rejected takeover bid of €2 billion (€38 per share) in June, the British retail conglomerate has raised its stake to approximately 50.08% — an additional purchase of 198,666 shares, equating to €7.63 million, according to the stock market filing. The German fashion company will now become a subsidiary of the Mike Ashley-owned business.

Hugo Boss believed the June takeover proposal to be “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Though Frasers continued its efforts, gradually raising its holding once again to 48% in mid-August (up from 30.3% in June, alongside the initial takeover bid). Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray assumed the Hugo Boss chair position last month, after Stephan Sturm stepped down.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4% to 6%. This comes after the growing British retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% last week, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. This marks a potential pullback from its current luxury brand spending spree.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has acquired a 8.78% stake in US-based sports brand Under Armour, continuing a string of cross-category investments in recent months. Earlier this week, Frasers upped its investment in Burberry to 6.3%, having also taken on ownership of esteemed department store Harvey Nichols in August. The Frasers portfolio spans discount retailer Sports Direct through to The Webster, House of Fraser, and Flannels, as well as a strong stake in Hugo Boss — upped to 47.89% in August. Under Armour’s share price has risen since the SEC filing was made on October 1.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct, The Webster)

Company description: Frasers Group has upped its economic interest in Burberry from 4.2% to 6.3%, with the British brand now part of a new luxury division launched in early October. Also part of the luxury portfolio, Hugo Boss — of which Frasers now owns almost 48% — continues to reject the retail group’s takeover bids; it may be looking elsewhere for potential acquisitions.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct).

Company description: Activewear brand 437 was founded in 2016 by co-CEOs Adrien Bettio and Hyla Nayeri. Initially founded as a swimwear brand, 437 moved into activewear in 2023, which is now the core of its business. The Toronto-based brand is the top-selling activewear brand on Revolve, and has fast become a celebrity go-to.

Funding and round: $15 million CAD, minority stake

Investor(s): Revolve (portfolio includes: Alliance Apparel, Alexandre Vauthier)

Investor comments: “437 is still a small player, but is already outselling nearly every activewear brand on our site, including billion dollar brands. The brand is great and the aesthetic and products are great — it’s really just building on their core momentum and continuing to gain awareness. Hyla and Adrien had built something very special, but had also reached a point where they needed additional capital, infrastructure, and a thought partner who had been through the same journey,” said co-founder and co-CEO Michael Karanikolas.

Company description: Founded by former fashion executive Yasmin Sewell, Vyrao launched in 2021 as a fragrance brand blending aromatherapy and neuroscience principles. The brand was ahead of the curve tapping into the cross-section of fragrance and wellness, by offering customers something more than just a scented mist. Following the acquisition, the genderless brand will embark on its next development phase under its new owner.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Company description: Based in LA, Arey launched in 2021 under entrepreneur Allison Conrad and celebrity hairstylist Jay Small, offering vitamin, antioxidant and peptide-infused products to help delay and repigment aging hair. The funding will support Arey’s new product development, ongoing clinical research, and expansion through retail partnerships.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever Ventures (portfolio includes:), Greycroft, Female Founders Fund.

Company description: AI-driven discovery platform Slayd launched in Gurugram, India, in 2025. Targeted at Gen Z, the startup sorts fashion items from more than 300 marketplaces and brands by theme and curates personalized feeds that enable product discovery across multiple sites. Slayd claims to currently have more than 200,000 users, and can identify emerging trends through its proprietary tech software. The investment will help strengthen its team and accelerate the growth of its private-label business, Slayd Originals.

Investor(s): AJVC (portfolio includes: Midcase, Bubble Me, Trufides).

Company description: ISDIN is a product of pharmaceutical company Corporación Químico-Farmacéutica Esteve (CQFE) and beauty group Puig, who partnered to launch the skincare brand in 1975. Since then, both families have supported ISDIN’s evolution into a global dermatological skincare business focused on scientific formulation and innovation. In acquiring CQFE’s 50% stake, Puig will obtain complete ownership of the Spanish brand.

Investor(s): Puig (portfolio includes: Charlotte Tilbury, Byredo, Penhaligon’s, Dr. Baraba Sturm).

Investor comments: “Expanding our presence in dermocosmetics is a strategic priority for Puig. ISDIN is a unique company, with a strong management team, a clear strategy and a distinctive position in dermatology and skincare. Full ownership will give Puig the best platform to support its next phase of growth and continue investing behind the science and innovation that have made ISDIN successful,” Puig CEO Jose Manuel Albesa said.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Talm (“To All the Mamas”) initially focused on bodycare products during pregnancy and postpartum, however the brand has gradually expanded to offer sensitive skincare for all stages of life. It currently offers around a dozen products, operates in roughly a dozen countries, and reports double-digit revenue growth. This marks the first acquisition for Caudalie, which plans to accelerate Talm’s global expansion and product development by leveraging its pharmacy network, sales force and infrastructure.

Company description: Medici Brands, owner of David Protein and newly launched confectionery brand HallPass, will use its Series B funding to enter the next phase of growth. This includes expanding HallPass’s retail presence, alongside the remainder of its product portfolio — extending David into new formats and categories, advancing product innovation, and enabling the launch and scaling of new brands such as Rowdy.

Funding and round: $250 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Greenoaks (portfolio includes: Stripe, Canva, Discord, Robinhood), Valor Equity Partners (portfolio includes: GoPuff, SpaceX, BitGo), Peter Rahal, Iconiq, Imaginary Ventures.

Investor comments: “Two years ago, David Protein showed customers they no longer had to choose between great macros and great taste, and it became one of the fastest-growing CPG brands in America. Now, Medici is bringing that approach to the rest of the store, building a house of brands that delivers the taste consumers adore, without making the compromises they have grown to accept,” said Greenoaks partner Neil Shah.

Company description: Truly Beauty is a plant-based personal care brand founded in 2013 by Maxx Appelman. Known for its viral, Gen Z-focused bodycare and social media marketing, Truly Beauty combines high-performing active ingredients with a luxurious but playful aesthetic. It is headquartered in Los Angeles. For razor company Dollar Shave Club, this marks its first acquisition as it extends beyond grooming.

Investor comments: “By layering Truly’s fast-turn product engine onto our AI-driven inventory planning and backend logistics, we are building a high-velocity innovation model that legacy CPG conglomerates simply cannot replicate,” said Dollar Shave Club CEO Larry Bodner.

Company description: Scottish-born accessible luxury leather goods brand Strathberry has closed its second funding round, consisting of a growth investment from Soho Square Capital’s new Fund II, and marking the fund’s first investment. The funding comes on the heels of a strong year for Strathberry, which delivered 39% year-on-year growth in 2026 at $50.5 million. Soho Square’s investment will support Strathberry founders Guy and Leeanne Hundleby’s ambitions to accelerate the brand’s North America expansion.

Funding and round: Undisclosed minority investment valuing the company at approximately £100 million, second funding round.

Investor(s): Soho Square Capital’s Fund II.

Investor comments: “Strathberry is an exceptional brand with a rare combination of craftsmanship, a distinctive design signature and a genuinely international, loyal customer base. The label’s ‘high-end quality at accessible prices’ ethos is resonating with shoppers disillusioned with top luxury houses. Guy, Leeanne, and the team have created something special, and there is significant scope to grow the business internationally,” Soho Square Capital director David Steel said in a statement.

Company description: Thorne, the science-backed supplements brand founded in 1984, has entered into a definitive acquisition agreement with P&G. Thorne is currently owned by L Catterton’s Flagship Fund. It is now best known in the wellness space for its creatine product, leaning into the rise of the supplement and its various formats. The acquisition helps to further Thorne’s attempt at becoming the market’s most-trusted personalized health brand, as well as P&G’s aim to move its personal health business upmarket. The transaction is expected to close later this year, subject to regulatory approval.

Investor(s): Procter & Gamble (portfolio includes: Seven Seas, Oral-B, Pepto Bismol).

Investor comments: “Consumer interest in selfcare, prevention, wellness, and personalized health continues to grow, and Thorne strengthens our position in premium wellness with a trusted, science-backed brand that complements our existing portfolio,” CEO of P&G Health Care Paul Gama said.

Company description: Frasers Group has taken a 4.2% position in British luxury brand Burberry. Frasers, the company behind House of Fraser, Sports Direct and Flannels, is holding the position through put options, which gives Frasers Group the right to buy shares at a predetermined stock price. The company is also the second largest shareholder in Mulberry PLC.

Frasers Group has been on an investing spree of late, increasing its stake in Hugo Boss to 30.3% and offering a takeover proposal. Frasers Group also bought Matches for £52 million in December 2023, before it announced that it was going into administration; Matches was sold in December 2025 to form part of newly established luxury group Hulcan.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Solomei AI, the company behind the Callimacus platform, has announced that it has entered into an agreement for an investment from Salesforce. The investment will “support Callimacus’s efforts to expand its engineering and AI research capabilities, accelerate product development, and scale commercial operations across Europe and North America.” In January 2026, Callimacus, whose chairman is Brunello Cucinelli, was used to build the new e-commerce experience for the designer’s eponymous luxury brand.

Investor comments: “Brunello has always believed that technology should elevate humanity, and that conviction is at the heart of Callimacus,” said Marc Benioff, chair and CEO of Salesforce. “The team has developed an innovative platform that reimagines AI-powered experiences — bringing together conversational AI, enterprise context, and real-time personalization to create entirely new ways for businesses to engage with their customers.”

“Three years ago, Marc Benioff and I began an endeavor with mathematicians, philosophers, humanists, and technologists, from which Callimacus was born. Our idea was to create a simple, intuitive product capable of speaking the language of human beings; a sort of new web, without pages, categories, or predetermined paths, able to accompany the intent of each individual navigator. I look with great confidence and hope for the path that Callimacus will pursue with Salesforce’s investment,” Brunello Cucinelli, chairman of Solomei AI, added.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Merit is a US-based beauty brand designed as an antidote to using multiple, trend-led products — collapsing everyday cosmetics into a curated, minimal line-up. The investment is led by Vasiliki Petrou, managing partner at Semcap Beauty & Wellness, who also founded the Unilever Prestige division in 2014, spanning Dermalogica, Paula’s Choice, Hourglass, K18, and more.

Investor comments: “Merit is one of the most thoughtfully built brands in beauty, a true icon in the market. I love the timeless brand aesthetic, the simplified and edited approach to beauty, and the focus on the millennial and Gen X consumer, which is a significant white space in our industry. I am thrilled to support the continued global scaling of the brand,” Petrou said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has increased its stake in Hugo Boss to approximately 30.28% (up from 26.06%), which demands an official takeover bid in line with German legislation. The move follows Frasers’s €2 billion (€38 per share) takeover proposal in June, which Hugo Boss believed was “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Frasers, now Hugo Boss’s largest shareholder, said its offer still stands through July 27.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Syntetica is a French startup that transforms textile waste into recycled nylon through a proprietary chemical method that allows the processing of fabrics containing multiple materials. The funding will help Syntetica build its first commercial facility in France, which will be able to transform hundreds of tons of post-consumer textile waste annually. While Syntetica already works with labels such as Victoria’s Secret and Etam, it also plans to scale its recycling efforts and partner with more fashion brands.

Funding and round: $30 million, Series A.

Investor(s): Ecotechnologies 2 (portfolio includes: Standing Ovation, Mantle8), Lululemon (portfolio includes: Epoch Biodesign, Samsara Eco, Zymochem), MAS Holdings (portfolio includes: Victoria’s Secret, Calvin Klein, Gap), Swen Capital Partners, EQT Ventures.

Company description: Founded in 2021 by Abhi Arora and Sanket Agarwal, Fleek is a wholesale vintage fashion marketplace. Fleek connects retailers and resellers with verified, secondhand clothing wholesalers worldwide, enabling them to source vintage inventory in bulk through a digital marketplace with integrated logistics and quality assurance.

Funding and round: $25 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Burda Principal Investments (portfolio includes: Vinted), Ebay Ventures, FJ Labs, H14, Andreessen Horowitz, HV Capital, Y Combinator, and more.

Company description: Whering is a digital wardrobe and styling app founded in 2020 by Bianca Rangecroft. The app enables users to catalogue the clothes they already own, create outfits, track wardrobe usage, and receive styling recommendations, with the aim of encouraging more intentional fashion consumption and reducing unnecessary purchases.

Investor(s): Ebay Ventures, Google AI Futures Fund.

Company description: Hair technology company Halo has developed its first product, HaloBraid. Launching in salons this fall, the device will be the first automated hair braiding tool that works alongside stylists to halve braiding time from as long as 10 hours per appointment. Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian’s VC firm Seven Seven Six is leading the investment into a business that was launched off the back of Yinka Ogunbiyi’s winning Harvard Innovation Labs pitch last year.

Investor(s): Seven Seven Six (portfolio includes: Anthropic, ElevenLabs, Flock Safety), Bling Capital (portfolio includes: Palantir, Gusto, Everlane), AlleyCorp (portfolio includes: ShopMy, Gilt Groupe, Business Insider).

Investor comments: “As an investor, I look for founders that see something broken that everyone else has accepted as fixed. Braiding is a perfect example: it is a process that has not materially changed in thousands of years, despite being one of the most popular hairstyles for millions of Americans and a significant part of the $270 billion salon services industry,” said Ohanian. “Yinka has introduced a novel technology to a traditionally manual and highly specialized professional service.”

Company description: L’Oréal Group has taken a stake in Indian personal care company Innovist. (Vogue Business reported on speculations back in March.) The company has a successful portfolio that includes Indian haircare brand Bare Anatomy, skincare brands Chemist at Play and Sunscoop, and bodycare brand Vinci Botanicals. The company was founded in 2018 by Rohit Chawla, Sifat Khurana, and Vimal Bhola with a focus on science-first formulations, transparent ingredients, and in-house research and development.

Funding and round: Majority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): L’Oréal Group (portfolio includes: Cerave, La Roche-Posay, Vichy, Armani Beauty, SkinCeuticals).

Investor comments: “Our investment in this innovative Indian startup is a clear testament to our unwavering commitment to expanding L’Oréal’s footprint in India,” CEO Nicolas Hieronimus said. “By bringing together the very best of L’Oréal’s global expertise with Innovist’s high-performing, science-led products and deep-rooted understanding of the Indian consumer, I believe we are poised to shape the future of beauty in this dynamic market.”

Company description: Remedy is a dermatologist-developed skincare brand founded by Dr. Muneeb Shah in March 2024. The brand’s products target skin concerns such as dark spots, dryness, fine lines, dullness, keratosis pilaris, and sensitive skin. Remedy is stocked on Amazon, TikTok Shop and Target, the latter of which it partnered with in December 2025. The Series A investment will support the skincare brand with its next phase of growth, including advancing clinical research, expanding its product categories, and improving inventory. Remedy also plans to strengthen its formulation, testing, and consumer education.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): L Catterton (portfolio includes: Merit Beauty, Tula, Kopari, Elemis, Nutrafol, Intercos, Ex Nihilo).

Investor comments: “We seek to partner with exceptional founders building brands that will redefine categories, and we believe Remedy is uniquely modernizing dermatological skincare,” L Catterton partner Tehmina Haider said. “As both a clinician and a consumer educator, Dr. Shah has built a portfolio of simple, effective, and accessibly priced products that leverage advanced ingredient technologies to address real patient needs — and that is what will define the next generation of dermocosmetics. The brand’s rapid growth reflects deep consumer demand for affordable, clinically-grounded skincare, and we are thrilled to partner with the Remedy team on its next chapter.”

Company description: Bacchus is a London-based PR agency founded in 1998 by Anouschka Menzies and Charlotte Lurot, who currently lead the business alongside co-CEO Daize Washbourn. The agency specializes in luxury hospitality and culture, as well as in the prestige VIC and high-net-worth communities. With around 100 employees across seven offices (London, New York, Miami, LA, Dubai, Riyadh, and Doha), Bacchus generates annual sales of approximately $17 million. Its client portfolio includes Red Sea Global Residences, Six Senses, Auberge Resorts, the Victoria & Albert Museum, and Monte-Carlo Société des Bains de Mer.

Funding and round: Acquisition, majority stake.

Investor(s): Mazarine Group (portfolio includes: La Mode en Images, the show producer of Louis Vuitton, Dior, and Gucci).

Investor comments: “There were several objectives [with this investment],” Mazarine founder Paul-Emmanuel Reiffers tells Vogue Business. “First, we needed to add a public relations and influence branch to our group. Second, it had to be large enough for us to develop and accelerate it. With Bacchus, we’re starting from a platform that’s already large enough to consolidate operations, grow further, and open an office in Paris in the short to medium-term. Third, the acquisition gives us seven offices at once, providing an established global network and strengthening our geographic footprint. We already had a presence in Dubai, but now we’re able to establish ourselves in Riyadh, which is important because the Middle East is about to rebound strongly. We’re also strengthening our position in the US by expanding our network from New York to LA and Miami, allowing us to serve clients more effectively.”

He continues: “Finally, the acquisition aligns with what we see as the luxury sectors of tomorrow: hospitality, real estate, and longevity. As luxury brands increasingly move into these areas, we are positioning ourselves to support their expansion. It also creates valuable synergies, allowing us to integrate Bacchus’s expertise and network of personalities, influencers, and guests into our events.”

Company description: Bella Hadid has been slowly growing her fragrance brand Orebella since its launch in 2024. Now, with Series A funding from Silas Capital, which has previously invested in beauty brands including Makeup by Mario, Oak Essentials and Ilia, she can scale the line further across categories and markets.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Silas Capital (portfolio includes: Makeup by Mario, YSE Beauty, Dôen).

Company description: NYC-based startup Vetir is pitching itself as an AI luxury shopping app that goes beyond discovery and transactions to act as “a system of record for the wardrobe” for high-value consumers. In practice, this is something of an AI stylist that learns from the data users share with the app, including existing closet items, shopping preferences, as well as their calendar, travel, and purchasing behavior. It’s also building out a business-to-business, CRM-type system for private stylists and luxury clienteling systems, aiming to bring “structure and continuity to what has traditionally been a fragmented, relationship-driven space”.

Funding and round: $5.5 million, Series A.

Investor(s): A consortium of investors across technology and luxury-adjacent family offices.

Company description: Ruka Hair was founded in 2021 by Tendai Moyo and Ugo Agbai, with the mission of supplying hair extensions that are safe, ethical, and good quality. The brand has now received $4.5 million in funding led by Henkel Ventures, the owner of Olaplex and Schwarzkopf. Ruka will be using the investment to scale its business, starting with the launch of US-based operations later this year. The brand has raised $10 million to date and is stocked at Selfridges.

Investor(s): Henkel Ventures, Freedom Trail Capital, Big Issue Invest, Backed VC, Dina Asher-Smith, Knut Alicke, Sophia Dennis, Didier Morais.

Investor comments: “Ruka Hair exemplifies what we look for: founders solving a real problem with genuine commitment, building through community rather than hype,” said Samyr Laine, co-founder and managing partner of Freedom Trail Capital. “Tendai and Ugo built this brand during one of the most challenging periods for consumer businesses, scaled through an authentic community, and are now pioneering biotech innovation that could reshape an entire category.”

Company description: Since founding Anomaly in 2021, Priyanka Chopra Jonas has scaled her haircare brand across North America, the UK, and the Middle East. In the US, the brand is stocked at Target, while in the UK, Superdrug is one of its biggest retailers. Chopra Jonas launched Anomaly with the aim to bring accessibly priced clean and vegan haircare products to the masses. The investment from Reliance will focus on scaling the brand further in India, alongside growing its international presence.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Reliance Retail (portfolio includes: Pahadi Local and Tira).

Investor comments: “Bringing Anomaly into our portfolio marks a strategic step in expanding our basket of new-age, high-growth beauty brands.
