Company description: Californian premium athleisure brand Vuori was founded in 2015 by Joe Kudla. The brand is known for its unique fabrics and is certified as carbon neutral by Change Climate. Following this investment, the brand’s valuation has reached $5.5 billion, building on a $400 million investment by Softbank Vision Fund 2 in 2021, which brought its valuation to $4 million.

Funding and round: $825 million, secondary tender offer.

Lead investor(s): General Atlantic (portfolio includes: Gymshark, Sézane, Tory Burch), Stripes (portfolio includes: On, Reformation, Khaite) and existing investors.

Investor comments: “Vuori encapsulates everything we look for in a Stripes investment — the products are amazing and beloved by the consumer, the team is fanatical about quality and innovation, and the market for athleisure is global with durable tailwinds,” said Chris Carey, partner at Stripes.

Company description: Secondhand peer-to-peer marketplace founded in 2008 by Milda Mitkutė and Justas Janauskas in Lithuania. The platform is Europe’s largest clothing resale marketplace. The recent investment brings Vinted’s valuation to €5 billion.

Funding and round: €340 million, secondary share sale.

Investor(s): TPG Tech Adjacencies, Hedosophia (portfolio includes: Monzo, Go Puff), Baille Gifford, Invus Opportunities (portfolio includes: Coupang, Chrono 24), FJ Labs (portfolio includes: Farfetch, Uber, Klarna), Manhattan Venture Partners (portfolio includes: Discord, Epic Games, X), Moore Strategic Ventures.

Investor comments: “We’ve seen that consumers are increasingly choosing secondhand as a core part of their wardrobe, as sustainability and flexibility become top of mind for many people. Vinted’s customer focus, leading product experience, and sophisticated approach to logistics have made this market accessible to an even broader population,” said TPG partner Andrew Doyle.

Company description: Biotech-powered prestige skincare brand Reome was founded by beauty editor and acupuncturist Joanna Ellner in 2023. The UK-based brand is known for its sensorial products and is stocked in Space NK, Liberty and Moda Operandi among others.

Investor(s): Rianta Capital (portfolio includes: El Rayo, Home Cooks).

Company description: UK-based women’s shirt brand launched in 2017 by a former Vogue stylist and Tatler editor Pip Durell. The B Corp-certified brand, which is known for timeless designs inspired by men’s tailoring and British heritage, launched its first pair of trousers earlier this year and plans to expand further with blazers and knitwear at the start of 2025. With Nothing Underneath was named one of Walpole’s Brands of Tomorrow in 2022.

Lead investor(s): Pembroke VCT (portfolio includes: Tala, Me+Em, Bella Freud) and JamJar Investments (portfolio includes: Deliveroo, Oatly, Spoke).

Investor comments: “With Nothing Underneath (WNU) holds a unique position in the womenswear market. Pip and her team have built a fantastic brand around one staple item, the shirt — an essential in most women’s wardrobes. It has become a standout in the fashion industry and early growth metrics have given us conviction in the brand. This investment will enable this emerging British heritage brand to enhance its product range, assist with growth and support WNU’s international reach,” said Andrew Wolfson, CEO of Pembroke Investment Managers.

Company description: UK-based luxury retail platform that stocks a curation of independent brands. The retailer is known for its selection of vibrant eveningwear. Founded in 2019 by Nina Briance, Cult Mia initially received $3 million in seed funding in November 2023 led by Fuel Ventures, with participation from Morgan Stanley and David Wertheimer of the Chanel family.

Funding and round: $2 million, seed (bringing total seed funding to $5 million).

Investor(s): H&M Group Ventures (portfolio includes: Goop, Klarna) and existing investors.

Investor comments: “We are delighted to invest in Cult Mia on their mission to launch independent and diverse designers from around the world. We have been incredibly impressed by all that Cult Mia has achieved in such a short space of time,” said Nanna Andersen, chief of new growth and ventures at H&M Group.

#6679. Moussaka With Roasted Eggplant and Lamb

Moussaka is a weekend project with a golden, bubbling payoff: layers of tender eggplant and cinnamon-spiced lamb under a thick cap of cheesy béchamel. Fresh mint, oregano, and Fresno chiles give this take on the Greek casserole a little extra punch.

One task we won’t ask of you: frying all that eggplant in batches. Instead, brush the slices with garlic-herb oil and roast them, hands-off. Get the lamb-and-tomato sauce going while the eggplant’s in the oven, or spread the prep over a couple of days.

Choose a baking dish you’ll be happy to plop on the table—this one deserves to be seen. Resist the urge to dig in right away: The moussaka needs a 30-minute rest after baking, just enough time to toss together a crunchy Greek salad.

Yes—and you don’t have to make every component on the same day. You can refrigerate the lamb-and-tomato sauce and roasted eggplant separately for up to 3 days, and the béchamel for up to 2 days. You can also bake the whole casserole 1 day ahead; let it cool, then cover and chill.

Yes. Bake the casserole first, let it cool, then cover and freeze for up to 3 months. Thaw before reheating in a 250° oven until warmed through, about 1 hour.

How do I keep moussaka from turning watery?

Give the meat sauce time to thicken: Most of the liquid should cook off before you start layering. The béchamel should be as thick as pudding before the cheese and egg yolks go in. And don’t rush the 30-minute rest after baking—it’s part of the recipe, not a serving suggestion.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 475°. Whisk 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, ½ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 1 Tbsp. chopped mint, and 1 Tbsp. chopped oregano in a small bowl to combine. Brush both sides of 3 large eggplants (about 3½ lb. total), sliced into ½"-thick rounds, with herb oil, making sure to get all of the herbs and garlic onto eggplants; season with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Transfer eggplants to a rimmed baking sheet (it’s okay to pile rounds on top of each other) and roast until browned and tender, 35–45 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 400°.

Meanwhile, heat remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large wide pot over high. Cook 2 lb. ground lamb, stirring and breaking it up with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through and liquid from meat has evaporated (there will be a lot of fat in the pot), 12–16 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer lamb to a medium bowl. Strain fat in pot through a fine-mesh sieve into a small bowl. Pour off all but 3 Tbsp. lamb fat and discard.

Heat 2 Tbsp. lamb fat in same pot over medium-high. Set remaining 1 Tbsp. lamb fat aside for assembling moussaka. Add 2 medium onions, finely chopped, one 3" cinnamon stick, 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and softened, 8–10 minutes. Add 2 Fresno chiles, finely chopped, and remaining 4 garlic cloves, finely grated; cook, stirring and scraping up browned bits from bottom of pot occasionally, until onion is golden brown, about 5 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. paprika and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring, until combined and mixture is brick red, about 1 minute. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until slightly reduced and alcohol smell has dissipated, about 3 minutes. Add one 28-oz. can whole peeled tomatoes and break up with a wooden spoon into small pieces (the seeds can shoot out at you if you’re too aggressive, so start carefully). Add reserved lamb and remaining 1 Tbsp. chopped mint and 1 Tbsp. chopped oregano and cook, stirring occasionally, until most of the liquid has evaporated and mixture looks like a thick meat sauce, 5–7 minutes. Fish out cinnamon stick and discard.

Heat 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium saucepan over medium until foaming. Add ½ cup (63 g) all-purpose flour and cook, whisking constantly, until combined, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 2½ cups whole milk, warmed, whisking constantly until combined. Bring to a boil and cook, whisking often, until very thick (it should be the consistency of pudding), about 5 minutes. Whisk in ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Remove pan from heat and whisk 4 oz. farmer’s cheese, crumbled (about 1 cup) and 1 oz. Pecorino Romano or Parmesan, finely grated (about ¾ cup) into sauce. Let sit 10 minutes to allow cheese to melt, then add 3 large egg yolks, beaten to blend, and vigorously whisk until combined and mornay sauce is golden yellow.

Brush a 13x9" baking pan with reserved 1 Tbsp. lamb fat. Layer half of eggplants in pan to cover bottom entirely. Evenly spread half of lamb mixture over eggplants. Repeat with remaining eggplants and lamb mixture to make another layer of each. Spoon mornay sauce over and smooth surface; scatter remaining 1 oz. Pecorino Romano or Parmesan, finely grated (about ¾ cup) over.

Bake moussaka until bubbling vigorously and mornay sauce is browned in spots, 30–45 minutes. Let cool 30 minutes before serving.

Do Ahead: Moussaka can be baked 1 day ahead. Let cool, then cover and chill, or freeze up to 3 months. Thaw before reheating in a 250° oven until warmed through, about 1 hour.

Editor’s note: This recipe was originally published in September 2017. Head this way for more of our favorite casserole dishes →

#6678. Pumpkin Enchiladas With Black Beans

Homemade enchiladas might sound like a laborious weekend project, but with a few clever tricks, this version made with black beans and pumpkin can be whipped up on even the most hurried of work nights. For starters, canned pumpkin creates the base of a quick sauce that requires no precooking. And because they are vegetarian, the filling—a combination of canned black beans, onion, and bell pepper flecked with cilantro—comes together in a flash. In lieu of baking the enchiladas, this version opts for broiling in order to brown the tops while also heating the enchiladas through in the same skillet you cook the beans in. A flourish of pumpkin seeds, sliced onion, cilantro, and fresh lime brightens up everything, although serving them straight from the oven would be just as delicious.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large broilerproof skillet over medium-high. Add 1 large white onion, finely chopped, and 1 medium green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, and cook, stirring often, until browned in spots and fragrant, 7–9 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, two 15-oz. cans black beans, rinsed, and 2 Tbsp. chili powder and cook, stirring occasionally, just until combined and beans are warmed through, about 3 minutes. Transfer bean mixture to a large bowl; reserve pan.

Smash bean mixture with a spoon or potato masher until about half of the beans are mashed. Mix in juice of 1 lime and ¼ cup coarsely chopped cilantro; season with kosher salt. Set bean mixture aside.

Whisk together one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 1 tsp. Tabasco, and 1¼ cups water in a large bowl; season pumpkin sauce with salt.

Place 1 of twelve 6" flour tortillas on a surface. Scoop out ¼ cup (heaping) reserved bean mixture and arrange in center down length of tortilla. Scatter some of 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over, then roll up tortilla into a cylinder. Place, seam side down, in reserved skillet. Repeat process with remaining tortillas. Brush tops with oil.

Place a rack in upper third of oven; heat broiler. Broil enchiladas until tops are deeply toasted and charred in spots, 4–7 minutes (depending on your broiler; watch carefully as they can go from browned to burnt very quickly). Pour pumpkin sauce over enchiladas and spread into an even layer. Top with remaining 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup) and raw pumpkin seeds (pepitas; if using). Broil until cheese is melted and deeply browned in spots, 4–7 minutes (watch carefully). Remove enchiladas from broiler and top with thinly sliced white onion and cilantro leaves with tender stems. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

The Nazca Lines are sprawling geoglyphs that were constructed on Peru's ground and hillsides around 2,000 years ago. But why were they built?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Nazca Lines are the most famous geoglyphs in the world. Dating back around 2,000 years and reaching a combined length of more than 800 miles (1,300 kilometers), they depict a variety of motifs, including humans, animals, geometric shapes, plants and flowers. These designs were constructed on the arid hills and valleys of coastal Peru by the Nazca people between 200 B.C. and A.D. 500, long before writing was used in the region.

It's not clear exactly how many Nazca Lines there are, but they number in the thousands, with new geoglyphs continuing to be discovered with the help of AI.

Scientists have been debating this question since the lines were first formally investigated in the early 20th century. Although the definite answer remains unknown, experts have proposed various reasons for the famous geoglyphs.

There "are many ideas out there about their function and meaning," Ana Nieves, a professor of art history at Northeastern Illinois University, told Live Science in an email. "If you look at the area's geoglyphs closely, though, there are different styles of geoglyphs, some are relatively larger and some smaller, some are on hillsides while some are on the pampas. It is not likely that a single explanation would apply to all."

More Nazca Lines, including one that looks a bit like a person.

A vast array of theories for the lines' uses have been proposed over the years, with the most outlandish of these suggesting that they were sites for aliens to land spaceships.

More grounded theories link the lines to cultural and religious practices.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

"The question of why the geoglyphs exist is difficult to answer, given that we lack any type of preserved oral or written testimony," Karsten Lambers, an art history professor at the University of Augsburg in Germany, wrote in an essay published in the book "Los geoglifos: imágenes y escenarios en el desierto de Nazca y Palpa [The Geoglyphs: images and settings in the desert of Nazca and Palpa]" (University of Augsburg, 2017). It's possible that the uses for the geoglyphs changed over time, he added.

One suggestion is that they were initially used to mark routes for travelers and caravans and later became places for gathering and feasting.

In a 2026 study, researchers noted that some of the earlier Nazca geoglyphs were constructed on hillsides, seem to be located on trails, and "were visible from considerable distances." This means the geoglyphs may have been used to mark travel routes and indicate areas that were good for temporary camps. The team suggested that the markings became places for gathering and feasting.

A geometric-shaped geoglyph from Nazca; the geoglyphs vary in size and shape and may have had different purposes.

Another idea is that the geoglyphs were used to match astronomical alignments to serve as a kind of calendar. In December 1941, historian Paul Kosok examined the lines and determined that they had astronomical alignments. Mathematician Maria Reiche followed up on Kosok's work, examining the Nazca Lines for more than 40 years to identify many geoglyphs she believed have an astronomical relationship to various celestial bodies, a research team noted in a 2021 paper. Yet after analyzing the geoglyphs, the modern-day team found that only a relatively small number had a possible alignment to a star or solar event such as a solstice.

"The results suggest that the geoglyphs, as a whole, certainly cannot be interpreted as a calendar system," the team wrote. However, this doesn't discredit the idea that the Nazca Lines had an astronomical significance, Christiane Richter, a researcher at the University of Applied Sciences in Germany and first author of the 2021 paper, told Live Science in an email.

Since the paper's publication, Richter and her team's research has indicated that around 8% of the geoglyphs have some form of lunar alignment. It is "highly probable that celestial bodies played a role in the creation of the drawings," Richter said in an email.

Offerings such as ceramics, crabs, corn and earrings made from Spondylus shells (a genus of bivalves known as thorny oysters) were also placed on low rock platforms near some of the geoglyphs, especially those shaped like trapezoids, Lambers noted in his paper. Spondylus shells are normally found farther north, in Ecuador, but during El Niño events, they can appear farther south, in Peru. These shells, alongside crabs and corn, tend to be associated with water and fertility, Lambers noted.

Another idea is that the geoglyphs themselves may have been used for ritual processions. Some of the geoglyphs are made with a single, uninterrupted line," Nieves said. "Those are the ones that would lend themselves for processions since people could walk them in a single file."

Some of the activities at the Nazca Lines may have helped foster a sense of community and equality, said Darryl Wilkinson, a professor of religion at Dartmouth University who has written about the geoglyphs. For instance, "walking the lines was a group activity, and participating in such processions would have likely created a feeling of community among those involved," Wilkinson told Live Science in an email. "I interpret the Nasca lines as geared towards the realization of a relatively more equal expression of community."

Whatever the reasons for their construction the Nazca Lines are awe inspiring today. Lambers wrote in his essay that the Nazca people who built them "succeeded in transforming one of the driest deserts in the world, over the course of many centuries, to serve the region’s inhabitants as an expression of their cultural ideas and a setting for their social activities."

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6676. Daniel Roseberry Ran the New York City Marathon … And Only Started Training Two Months Ago

Marathon Sunday was a blur, but Schiaparelli creative director Daniel Roseberry does remember a few things vividly: the dappled light across the 26.2-mile route; the rhythmic sounds of sneakers against pavement as he strode onto a bridge and the crowds faded away; the absolutely perfect weather; and the overwhelming feeling of love he felt as he saw his friends and family on the sidelines, cheering him on.

“There are no words to describe it,” Roseberry tells Vogue of running the New York City Marathon, his first. “This day will stay with me … for a long time.”

The funny thing is, this time last year Roseberry had no intention of taking on the arduous course. But last Christmas, the designer went out on an impulsive—and what would prove to be fateful—run through Paris along the Seine, the city’s famous central waterway. While he was no stranger to the magic and romance of the city where he has lived and worked since 2019, the run opened his eyes to his surroundings in new and profound ways. Something awoke in him, and, ten months later, he found himself among the nearly 60,000 participants of the New York City Marathon, which he completed in 4 hours and 24 minutes.

“It was just the perfect day,” Roseberry says a few hours after finishing, his medal still draped around his shoulders. He’d just enjoyed some post-race pizza and pasta (a “second dinner” of Shake Shack was also on its way), and he was looking ahead to some much-deserved time in Therabody recovery boots. “It really reconnected me to my love of this city.”

Roseberry started the day early, at 3:30 a.m., before taking a 5:00 a.m. bus to Staten Island, where the race begins before winding its way through the remaining four boroughs and ending in Central Park. “It was pin-drop silent on the bus,” he recalls. “But you can sense everyone’s energy. It’s like this pent-up anticipation.” He was part of the last wave, which set off at 11:30 a.m., meaning that after he arrived he had to wait five hours before starting his journey.

After scaling the route’s opening gambit—the four-mile-long Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, with a two-mile, 174-foot elevation gain, the race’s highest climb—the infamous crowds that line the route started to materialize. “The city really shows up, and it’s beautiful. All these people cheering for you… and they don’t know you. They’re cheering your name, telling you you can do it. It really carries you and is a beautiful representation of humanity at its best. It transcended every expectation I had.”

Roseberry completed this feat with just two months of training, starting in September, as he was preparing his spring 2027 ready-to-wear collection. He worked with Jonathan Fins, his trainer of two years, to structure a program that built on his existing fitness foundation, rooted in strength training, mobility, and calisthenics. (Roseberry can not only design a shockingly glamorous dress but also do a deeply impressive 24 pull-ups.) It was truncated and intense: In September, the pair added a weekly run that increased in mileage, peaking at 33 kilometers (around 20 miles) before tapering, so as not to exhaust the body in the lead-up to the main event. (It’s common practice for first-time marathoners not to run the full 26.2 until the actual race.)

The training process allowed him a break from his usual responsibilities, in which he’s the one calling the shots. “Most days, everyone’s looking to me for answers,” he says. “With this, I was able to put myself into the care of another person.”

Roseberry had no specific finish time in mind. “I just want to finish, and be able to walk,” he half-joked during a FaceTime call the day before the race. He did later note, however, that he’d acheived one objective: he went through the entire course without walking.

The designer chose New York as the location for his first race because he was already scheduled to be in town to accept the Leader in the Arts Award at the Hirshhorn Gala award on Monday. With Halloween rolling into Marathon Day, however, he also realized that it was one of the best weekends to be in the city. “It just had to be New York,” he says.

During training, Roseberry would spend the first half of his run talking (and sometimes bickering) with Fins, only to reward himself with a pop-heavy playlist for the second half (Olivia Rodrigo, Taylor Swift, and Rosalía were in heavy rotation). And while he cued up an epic song cycle for the actual marathon, he ended up only listening to it for 15 minutes. “It didn’t feel like it was in the spirit of the day,” he says. “I wanted to be in the moment, honor it, and take it all in. I wanted to be present with the other runners, and with the people who came to watch.”

Roseberry’s $15 sunglasses, found at Dick’s Sporting Goods in Maine.

As one would imagine, Roseberry was very particular about his training attire: Asics Gel-Kayano running shoes, Nike socks, open-weave cotton tank tops from Sunspel, and cheap, sporty wraparound sunglasses that he bought in multiple colors from Dick’s Sporting Goods in Maine over the summer.

And training for and then completing the marathon gave him great insight into his own work as a designer. “It had me thinking about the body in different ways,” he says. “How could it not? And I like that the marathon is this thing with a defined beginning and end; it’s a closed loop. There are so many things always going on in fashion, but I’d like to take that mentality into my work.”

Post-marathon glow. The T-shirt features an image of Roseberry’s head superimposed onto Julie Andrews’s in The Sound of Music, an inside joke between him and his friends.

Roseberry poses with his friends and family after finishing.

On the morning of the race, Roseberry sent a voice note, reflecting on what the two-month, intensive program had meant to him. “The thing I keep coming back to is this physical transformation is so important to me. It feels so vital because it’s a physical manifestation of an inner transformation that’s been happening over the past year,” he said. “I think for four decades I had been completely, in many ways, living for the approval of other people and living in total abandonment of myself, and my body, for sure. I think this marathon has significance because it’s the first real thing to be envisioned, worked and trained for, and completed in a a really radical, new way of thinking. The transformation isn’t transforming into somebody different or somebody new or something better. It’s about remembering what my body was always capable of in the first place. I feel like I met this body, like it’s a person, that I re-met a year ago. And the last eight weeks of training have been a way of honoring that relationship going back into my life.”

At one point during our call after the race, Roseberry mentions something about next year, which begged the question: will he be back? “Oh, yeah,” he says. “Early on in the race, like mile four or five, I called my friend and told her, ‘We’re so doing this next year.’”

#6674. Of All the Cookware, BA Editors Keep Coming Back to These Made In Products

We've all heard the old adage “If it ain't broke, don''t fix it" and that rings particularly true in the kitchen. Because when you're scrambling on a Tuesday night to get dinner on the stove, or ambitiously experimenting with a dessert recipe to show off at your annual Friendsgiving, you need your favorite cookware to show up. These are not the moments to be re-inventing the cookware-wheel.

Perhaps this is why BA staffers keep coming back these Made In pieces. They just work. When so much else can go sideways mid food-project (was that cup of sugar a few grams off? Did that bread dough proof all the way??), having tools that do what they're supposed to do gives us one less thing to worry about.

As much as we love testing new gear (it’s literally our job), Made In has earned a permanent spot in our the rotation of our writers and editors.

What our writers and editors say: “It’s the only pan I reach for when I want to make eggs and quesadillas." - Emily Farris, contributing writer

The CeramiClad Non-stick frying pan was my first “grown-up” piece of cookware I ever invested in, and years later, it's still one of my most reached for pans in my cabinet. Other editors love it too; in her review, contributor Emily Farris claims it got her to break up with Teflon for good. She said the slick, ceramic coating made quick work of eggs and quesadillas, while the five-ply base gives it a sturdier feel and even heat distribution. It’s also impressively easy to clean with nothing more than a soft sponge and soapy water. Just stick to low or medium heat, skip the metal utensils, and wash it by hand to help preserve that nonstick surface.

What our writers and editors say: "Made In’s baking slab has brought some much needed crunch in my life." - Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor

Why we love it: If you’re someone who fights for as much of the crispy top of a baked pasta as you can get, then you will love this baking slab. In his review, Noah Kaufman found that Made In’s shallow, 9-by-13-inch porcelain slab delivers more of the hard, crispy edges that make baked dishes so satisfying. Its low sides also make it much easier to slide a spatula underneath desserts like blondies and bars without mangling the whole thing. Kaufman put it to work on everything from fudgy brownies to baked mac n' cheese with excellent results. It won’t replace a deep casserole dish for every recipe, but for the shallower bakes where you want a satisfying crunch on top, this slab slays.

What our writers and editors say: “I’m officially retiring my traditional saucepan in favor of this saucier.” - Olivia Tarantino, senior reviews editor

A saucier might just look like an uppity saucepan, but its rounded bottom really does make it especially useful for whisking, stirring, and tossing. Last November, our senior commerce editor Olivia Tarantino got her hands on this 5-quart version and fell in love. The five-ply stainless steel has excellent heat transfer and retention, which helped delicate scrambled eggs cook without sticking. She also loved it for pasta, where its curved sides made it easy to toss noodles with sauce until every strand is coated in a silky finish. It was so impressive that she ditched her old saucepan in favor of it—which is about as strong an endorsement as a piece can get.

Round Enameled Cast-Iron Dutch Oven, 5.5-qt.

What our writers and editors say: “I wasn’t shocked at how much I enjoyed using the Made In Dutch oven—I just didn’t expect to reach for it as often as I do.” - EF

Le Creuset and Staub have long dominated the Dutch oven game, but Made In makes a compelling case for spending less on an heirloom piece without sacrificing quality. In her side-by-side review, Farris found that the brand’s enameled cast-iron pot held its own against both legacy favorites, with a similarly sturdy build and smooth interior. Its wide, flat side handles are a particular standout, offering plenty of surface area for lifting the heavy pot off the stove or out of the oven. Available in a 5.5-quart size, you can use it for braises, soups, and even sourdough—and it won't completely drain your wallet like the other brands might.

What our writers and editors say: “I can't get over how well this thing sears food from edge to edge. And the fact that you can transform just about any cooking surface into a griddle makes it even better.” - Francesca Krempa, contributor

I yearn for a giant Blackstone but don't have the space, which is why I love Made In's carbon steel griddle set. It delivers that flat-top experience on a much smaller footprint, with even heating and a seasoned cooking surface that’s prime for searing smash burgers, fried rice, and more. It’s also lighter than cast iron, so it’s easier to lift and shift around, and comes pre-seasoned (hallelujah). Best of all, you can turn a compatible stovetop or cooking surface into a griddle without dedicating precious patio real estate to a massive piece of equipment. Just measure your stovetop before buying, since the integrated handles may not fit every range.

Made In x Tom Colicchio Carbon Steel Frying Pan

What our writers and editors say: "I love the way the handle feels: It gives good leverage for tossing and keeps your hands far from any splattering oil if you’re moving it into the oven." - NK

Limited-edition cookware can sometimes feel more like a collector’s item than something you’d actually want to cook with, but this collab has the performance to back up its celebrity partnership. In BA’s October editor-favorites roundup, Kaufman praised this pre-seasoned black steel pan for its striking brass handle and thicker construction that makes it easier to get a deep, even sear.

What our writers and editors say: “They're a splurge but if you love to grill, they're worth it." - FK

I’m a sucker for kitchen tools that balance function with good design, and Made In’s stainless steel grill tools hit that sweet spot. The sturdy stainless steel heads can handle the usual cookout lineup, from flipping burgers to turning vegetables, while the composite handles add a warm, classic touch that looks right at home next to the grill. The handles, which are made from a material called Micarta, a composite that looks like wood but is as maintenance-heavy. Plus they're more comfortable in-hand than all-metal tools. They're a splurge, but if you love to grill, they're worth it.

What our writers and editors say: “More than two years in, my Made In flatware has taken hundreds of trips through the dishwasher and my kids have slammed it onto our granite countertop more times than I’d like to admit—and it still looks great.” - EF

Farris dubbed this her “forever flatware” and it's easy to see why. Made In’s 18/10 stainless steel (read: very durable) set struck the right balance between substantial weight and comfy handling. The mirror-polished finish and understated curves look polished enough for a dinner party without feeling too precious for everyday meals. It's not cheap, but its timeless design and impressive durability make it a smart long-term investment for anyone ready to retire their mismatched drawer of utensils.

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

You'll have two chances to see October's full Hunter's Moon rise dramatically this week. Here's when to get the best views.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

October's full "Hunter's Moon" is about to rise, and skywatchers will get two great chances to see it appear on the eastern horizon around sunset.

Although it officially turns full at 12:11 a.m. EDT on Monday (Oct. 26), the Hunter's Moon will appear almost perfectly full as it rises on both Sunday (Oct. 25) and Monday evenings, giving skywatchers two opportunities to observe it.

October's full moon is nicknamed the Hunter's Moon because it was traditionally a signal for hunters to prepare for the coming cold winter by hunting, slaughtering and preserving meat, according to Time and Date. That's an Anglo-Saxon name; Native American names for October's full moon include the Drying Rice Moon, the Falling Leaves Moon and the Freezing Moon.

The first chance to see the Hunter's Moon comes just before sunset on Sunday, when the almost-full moon will rise in the east. The second opportunity comes on Monday, when the moon — still essentially 100% illuminated — will again rise just after sunset. Because it will be in a slightly darker sky, Monday's moonrise will likely be more dramatic.

As it rises Sunday, the moon will appear in the constellation Aries, and Saturn will be to its upper right. On Monday, it will rise above the Pleiades open cluster (M45).

For the best view on either evening, find somewhere with a clear view low to the eastern horizon and be in position shortly before moonrise where you are. An elevated viewpoint, open field or coastline is ideal because buildings, trees and hills can delay the moment the moon becomes visible.

Although the full moon will look magnificent with the naked eye, a backyard telescope or good stargazing binoculars can help you zoom in on various lunar features.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Hunter's Moon may appear unusually large thanks to the "moon illusion," which makes the moon seem bigger when it's seen beside familiar objects, such as trees and buildings, near the horizon. The illusion stems from the fallacies of how our brains use distance to perceive size.

October's Hunter's Moon isn't a supermoon, but it comes immediately before a notable sequence of four consecutive supermoons. The first will be the next full moon, the Beaver Moon, on Nov. 24, followed by full moons in December, January and February. A supermoon occurs when a full moon happens while the moon is relatively close to Earth in its slightly elliptical orbit, making it appear somewhat larger and brighter than average.

His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.

#6670. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6669. 37 Thanksgiving Appetizers, Including Make-Ahead Ideas

Making a tray of Thanksgiving appetizers should not feel like cooking a second dinner. This is the moment for a salty snack, a swoosh of dip, or a flaky, cheesy bite you can eat while shaping the rolls. They should keep everyone happy—especially the cook!—while dinner comes together.

The recipes below include a smoky (cheap!) carrot dip you can make up to a week ahead and a feta and sun-dried tomato dip you can blitz up in about five minutes. For a manageable spread, pick one rich option (like a retro cheese ball because it’ll make your aunt happy) and one crisp, crunchy counterpart. Add a third snack if you have time or the guest list calls for it—or, better yet, mix yourself a Thanksgiving cocktail to sip while you nibble.

Five minutes, a food processor, and you’re in business. Sun-dried tomatoes, feta, and Calabrian chile paste make a salty, tangy dip that needs no cooking and can be refrigerated two days ahead.

Save the oven for the turkey: This creamy spinach-artichoke dip comes together on the stove. You don’t have to serve it in a bread bowl, but don’t you kinda want to?

Blend roasted carrots, chickpeas, and almonds into this dairy-free dip up to a week before Thanksgiving. Try not to eat it all on sandwiches and egg-topped toast before the big day.

The secret to this exceptionally creamy hummus? Blend a couple of ice cubes in with the canned chickpeas and tahini. Serve with crunchy vegetables and olives.

French onion dip gets a tangy Greek yogurt base and a generous helping of jammy shallots. Salt-and-vinegar chips make a very welcome accompaniment.

Pomegranate molasses gives this roasted red pepper and walnut dip its sweet-tart edge. Put out toasted pita and crunchy vegetables, and let everyone scoop.

Give a can of white beans the holiday treatment with toasted pine nuts and garlicky oil. The dip keeps in the fridge for up to two days; bring it to room temperature before serving.

Give the beige snacks some competition. Beets, toasted hazelnuts, and lemon make a vivid, nutty dip you can refrigerate up to a week ahead—one less thing to tackle on Thursday.

Roasted parsnips give this garlicky feta dip a sweet backbone. Top it with hazelnuts and dill oil, and serve with plenty of crackers for scooping.

Put the whole bunch of chard to work: Both stems and leaves go into this lemony, tahini-rich dip. It’s dairy-free and can be refrigerated three days ahead, ready for a platter of hearty crackers.

Garlic and citrus make the olive oil here just as enticing as the olives and feta. Keep good bread nearby for soaking up every last drop.

A cheese ball makes an entrance, especially one with cheddar, cream cheese, and a retro coating of toasted pecans. Bring on the Ritz.

Soft goat cheese gets a bath in citrus-and-spice-infused olive oil. Spoon some of that fragrant oil over each serving, and keep crusty bread nearby—this isn’t the moment for a timid little cracker.

Give your Thanksgiving charcuterie board a head start. Manchego takes on garlic, orange, and rosemary as it marinates overnight; prepare it up to three days ahead and keep it refrigerated until you’re ready to serve.

A wheel of brie, a few herbs, and olive oil are the main event here. The oven softens the cheese, making it scoopable; crackers and sliced pears make excellent vehicles.

Crisped-up salami coins, dates, and pecans bring salty, sweet, chewy, and crunchy textures to the same bowl, with rosemary tying it all together.

Ina Garten’s smoky cheddar crackers are a strong argument for keeping cocktail-hour-ready dough in the freezer. The log can stay there up to four months, ready to slice and bake when company is coming.

A bag of kettle chips is already a respectable contribution. Add Pecorino and black pepper, then give it four minutes in a hot oven, and suddenly everyone wants to know what you did.

Fresh curry leaves, golden onions, and a good hit of chile turn cashews into a salty, spicy snack worth hovering over. You make it all on the stovetop, leaving the oven for the turkey.

A little honey, plenty of garlic, and a mix of fennel, coriander, and paprika make these pecans sweet, salty, and decidedly savory. Save a handful to scatter over a salad.

Tomato powder, garlic, and cayenne give popcorn a tangy, spicy kick. Mix the seasoning up to three weeks ahead, then pop a batch when guests start getting peckish.

A cornichon tucked beside each cocktail sausage gives these Windy City pigs their snap. Store-bought crescent dough, mustard, celery salt, and poppy seeds do the rest. Set out napkins; expect repeat visitors.

All the appeal of pastry-wrapped brie, with considerably less wrapping. Thawed puff pastry, jam, and cheese take about five minutes to assemble.

Homemade breadcrumbs, Parmesan, garlic, and herbs fill these mushroom caps, which bake up tender underneath and crisp on top. They’re decidedly old-school, and all the better for it.

Store-bought puff pastry does the heavy lifting for these crisp, cheesy twists. Shape and freeze them up to a month ahead, then bake straight from frozen, adding a few minutes to the baking time.

No need to wrap dozens of individual pastries: Bake one big, flaky ham-and-cheese slab, then cut it into 60 little squares. Assemble up to 12 hours ahead, then refrigerate until ready to bake.

Sharp cheddar and green curry paste make these flaky little spirals anything but shy. A spoonful of mayo helps the filling spread easily over store-bought puff pastry; folding and slicing create the fancy shape.

Roasted garlic gets mashed into ricotta, broccoli turns crisp at the edges, and hot honey ties the whole toast together. Use the broccoli stems too; they’re part of the appeal, not scraps.

Sweet tomato jam, tangy white anchovies, and lemon oil make a toast worth taking your time over. The jam needs a long cook, so make it up to five days ahead and refrigerate it until you’re ready to assemble.

These crisp little beet-and-potato fritters come with beet-green yogurt for dipping. They require last-minute frying, so put someone else on turkey duty.

Sharp cheddar, dill, and scallions give these airy cheese puffs plenty of bite. Pipe and freeze them up to a week ahead, then bake straight from frozen.

The trick to these generously filled deviled eggs is to add more eggs: Blend a few whole, cooked eggs into the yolk mixture to make the generous filling especially smooth and creamy.

Give the turkey a little seafood competition. Poach and peel the shrimp, and make the cocktail sauce a day ahead; refrigerate separately, then arrange the shrimp over cracked ice when guests arrive.

Crunchy vegetables, punchy pickles, mortadella, olives, breadsticks: This is a platter for grazers. Tuck in the dips, pour the drinks, and let everyone help themselves.

Not a creamy dip—a tangy, savory powder for dunking vegetables. Pistachios, nutritional yeast, and dill give this vegan snack its ranch-like appeal. Make the powder two weeks ahead, then store it in an airtight container at room temperature.

Skip the forks. Crisp romaine leaves are perfect for dunking in garlicky lemon-yogurt dressing and provide a crisp, cool, no-cook counterpoint to all that cheese and pastry.

A cold, crunchy pickle belongs beside the rich stuff. These cucumbers need 1–6 hours in the refrigerator to soak up the seasoning; add the dill and lemon juice just before serving.

#6667. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

AI companies know they are being held hostage by each other, and that they need to take action to self-regulate before they suffer major reputational and legal consequences. There is a blueprint on how they can do it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The largest artificial intelligence (AI) firms increasingly understand that they are hostages of one another. If one firm pushes ahead recklessly, others may feel compelled to follow. If one deploys a dangerous model without adequate safeguards, others may see it as a green light to do the same.

The debate over AI has centered on what governments should do to regulate this frontier technology. That remains essential. But a more immediate question is emerging: Can the companies building these powerful systems take action independently before they lose credibility and suffer legal consequences?

That question no longer looks theoretical and is being recognized as an urgent challenge. We've already seen AI firms lose control of their models — for example, in Australia, a rogue AI hacked a government healthcare website. If we are not careful, it's only a matter of time before one of these incidents causes large-scale, real-world harm, like shutting down an electricity grid or municipal water system, or a mass misdiagnosis in a health system. If this trend continues, the entire industry could become tarnished.

But there is a blueprint for self-regulation in a risky business: the nuclear industry, which has built up layers of oversight, controls and self-scrutiny over decades.

Frontier AI may require something similar: private regulation among competitors that do not trust one another but have a mutual interest in preventing outcomes that could damage them all. This does not appeal to the better angels of human nature — it's self-preservation for the industry itself.

There is a historical precedent for this kind of arrangement. The nuclear sector did not become safe because every actor suddenly became benevolent. It became safer through a layered system of peer scrutiny, technical standards, information-sharing and external oversight. International organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which was established in 1957, emerged to coordinate monitoring and verification, while national regulators and industry bodies gradually built professional norms around catastrophic risk.

The result was not perfect safety, as the Chernobyl disaster in 1986 clearly attests. But nuclear governance architecture is designed around the recognition that in high-risk technological systems, one actor's failure can become everyone's problem. This was seen following Chernobyl: global nuclear safety increased significantly after the disaster, with upgrades to reactor designs, improved training and international monitoring networks.

In the aftermath of the Chernobyl disaster, safety and regulation in the global nuclear industry increased.

And this movement to self-regulation also occurred in the U.S. nuclear sector, following the Three-Mile Island nuclear accident near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, in 1979. The reactor suffered a partial meltdown after a relatively minor cooling malfunction. Investigations later revealed design flaws in instruments and alarms, along with inadequate emergency response training, were the root cause of the incident.

The event nearly killed the nuclear energy industry in the U.S., causing public support to fall from a record high of 69% in 1977 to 46%t in 1979. The entire industry suffered because of failures at one facility. In response, the U.S. nuclear industry established the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations (INPO) in December 1979 to improve operational safety.

The analogy to AI should not be overstated. Nuclear materials are easier to count than algorithms, and nuclear facilities are harder to hide than model weights. The outcomes of a catastrophic AI blunder are also less existential, although its use in weapon systems is not without risk. In September, an AI hallucination almost led to the U.S. intercepting a Chinese ship suspected of carrying nuclear material to Iran.

Yet the comparison remains useful because the core governance problem is similar. In both cases, competitors operate in an environment where the downside risk of unchecked rivalry is borne by society while the upside is private gain for these firms. The challenge is to create institutions that make restraint the rational default — even when no actor fully trusts the others, and the inner workings of the industry are not readily visible to outsiders.

For AI, that could mean reciprocal evaluation of frontier models before deployment, secure mechanisms for sharing safety information, agreed red lines around certain capabilities, and independent third parties empowered to audit compliance. Such mechanisms would not replace government regulation. They would instead serve as an intermediate layer: stronger than voluntary ethics statements but more adaptive and technically informed than legislation alone can often be in fast-moving domains. The state would act as a background enforcer.

AI governance is often discussed as if the only choices were laissez-faire innovation or heavy-handed state control. History suggests a third path.

AI executives appear willing to look for solutions too, with Elon Musk recently suggesting a peer-review system before advanced model release, and Demis Hassabis, co-founder and chair of Google DeepMind, putting forward a framework for an AI Standards Body, similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

Skeptics will object, with reason, that industry-led governance can become cartel behavior or public-relations theater. Companies may use "safety" language to entrench incumbency, slow rivals or deflect binding regulation. Those are real dangers. The lesson from nuclear history is not that private coordination works automatically. It is that private coordination works only when nested inside a broader system of transparency, verification and public authority. Without those elements, private regulation becomes little more than trust-me rhetoric.

Still, dismissing private regulation altogether would be a mistake. Governments do not yet possess the technical capacity, speed or international alignment needed to oversee frontier AI on their own. And if the leading labs already see themselves as bound together by shared exposure to catastrophic risk, that recognition can become the basis for institutional design. The question is how to turn mutual fear into durable rules.

That is where the nuclear analogy is most powerful. It reminds us that industries facing existential hazards do not need perfect trust in order to cooperate. They need mechanisms that make cooperation preferable to defection. In practice, that means inspections, peer review, incident reporting, professional norms and a state-backed enforcement perimeter. AI governance is often discussed as if the only choices were laissez-faire innovation or heavy-handed state control. History suggests a third path: structured private coordination under public shadow.

The real opportunity, then, is not to celebrate the newfound (apparent) prudence of technology executives, it is to recognize what their comments reveal. When even fierce rivals begin to argue for mutual scrutiny, they are admitting that competition alone cannot govern the frontier. That admission should be treated not as reassurance but as evidence that the risk has become collective.

The policy task now is to build institutions that fit that reality. Governments should push for mandatory reporting, independent evaluation and legal backstops. But they should also encourage enforceable forms of peer oversight among the handful of firms whose systems may shape the trajectory of the technology. Frontier AI is becoming an industry in which the leading actors are hostages of one another. The nuclear age showed that such conditions can produce serious governance. The hope is that AI firms learn that lesson before they learn the cost of ignoring it at the peril of the public at large.

Akhil Bhardwaj is an Associate Professor of Strategy and Organization at the University of Bath, UK. He studies extreme events, which range from organizational disasters to radical innovation. Akhil is interested in the epistemological problem of understanding the underlying dynamics that lead up to these events. He also studies how thinking can be improved as well as the implications of AI adoption in the context of strategic management, entrepreneurship, and high-risk systems. His work is philosophically grounded in pragmatism. Prior to joining academia, Akhil has worked as an engineer and manager at CAT., Inc and consulted as a SOX compliance analyst in the U.S.

Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6662. What Is Swedish Mys? And Where to Experience It

The brutal cold of Sweden’s winters is well documented, but Stockholm has a knack for bringing some special magic even to its gloomiest season. The city, located just 500 miles south of the Arctic Circle, enjoys as little as six hours of daylight during the bleakest months, with the peak of darkness occurring at the winter solstice on December 21—and it’s no coincidence that this is when Stockholm fills with fairy-lit streets and cozy dining rooms illuminated with candles and roaring fireplaces. Add a whole host of invigorating winter activities, from ice-skating on frozen lakes to plunging through holes drilled in the frozen Baltic Sea, and you’ll see why many Swedes claim this as their favorite time of year.

“Winter is a time to hunker down, cook and play vinyl records; to wear something cozy and breathe the crisp outdoor air; to heat up the sauna, cut a hole in the ice, and—well, don't even get me started on how much I love cold-water plunges!” exclaims Hanna Oscarsson, the creative director at Stockholm’s most celebrated cocktail bar, Röda Huset.

“Cooling off on a hot summer day is wonderful too, of course,” she continues. “But winter dips are like a deep breath to reset the constant, hectic pace of modern life.”

Nowhere does cozy like Sweden—so much so that they even have a special word for it. Mys is Swedish for that feeling you get when you curl up under a soft blanket on a deep-cushioned sofa next to a fireplace, your hands wrapped around a giant cup of hot chocolate, or when you wrap up in your thickest knits and mittens and head out for a bracing walk along winter-lit streets, a soft dusting of snow creaking under your boots. It’s not entirely unrelated to what the Danes call hygge—but where hygge has hardened into an international lifestyle aesthetic, mys remains purely a state of mind.

I grew up in Sweden and toughed it out for 20-or-so years until the darkness got the better of me, prompting me to move to Barcelona and never look back. So imagine my surprise earlier this year, when my feed suddenly filled with Swedish “coolcations”, as the whole of southern Europe fled north to escape the stifling heat. “That’s cool,” I thought to myself, but you don’t really know Sweden until you’ve tasted the cold. So grab your furriest coat and woolliest hat, because when it comes to winter wonderlands, nowhere does it quite like Stockholm.

Imagine jetting off to Stockholm to visit your art collector pals in their private waterfront residence. If an invite from said friends doesn’t come through, a stay at Lydmar Hotel is the next best thing. Part hotel, part gallery, the 46-room property is home to one of the largest, privately owned fine-art photographic collections in the Swedish capital. Each of the plushly upholstered rooms—some of which enjoy unobstructed views of the Stockholm waterfront all the way to the Royal Palace—has its own vibe, brought to life through a curated blend of photography, artworks and bespoke furniture. Expect plenty of mys-filled nooks designed for curling up with a book while gazing at your favorite artwork.

When a hotel set in a former bank names its main dining room Bonnie’s (a tribute to legendary outlaw Bonnie Parker), you know you’re in for a good time. Guests at Bank can warm their cockles at nearby Sturebadet, a beautiful Moorish-inspired Art Nouveau bathhouse and sauna complex (access is included for suite guests while others enjoy preferential rates), before whiling away their evenings in the hotel’s Papillon cocktail lounge, a sultry, wood-paneled affair serving warming Old Fashioneds and Negronis. Spacious rooms come with soft slippers for keeping cozy on icy nights.

Set on the easternmost tip of the well-to-do island of Lidingö (one of the 14 islands that make up the city of Stockholm), Ellery Beach House is a former IBM conference center-turned-Palm-Springs-inspired seaside fun palace. If toasty saunas and invigorating sea dunks are your poison, you’ll be in your element in the hotel’s four heated pools and two saunas, one of which is set right on the edge of the Baltic Sea—ideal for defrosting after a glacial plunge. There are countless other activities on offer, from padel to cornhole or boules, to sipping cocktails under a blanket in the firepit-heated relaxation room.

Swedish chef Niklas Ekstedt uses only natural heat, soot, ash, smoke, and fire to prepare the tasting menu at his eponymous Michelin-starred restaurant. This is a meal that will stay with you long after you’ve trudged home through the snowy streets, frost-nipped gloved fingertips in pockets and earlobes tucked under woolly hats. You’ll sample the first courses, such as the Swedish caviar, or vendace roe, topped with crown dill, and be served a cast-iron flatbread in the snug, flame-heated kitchen, before being led to a table for the mains, which include a sublime confit North Sea langoustine, like a smaller, firmer lobster, infused with rose and lingonberries.

Nowhere does mys like this comfy café set in a castle-like structure built for the 1897 Stockholm World’s Fair. It makes a perfect stop for oversized cups of tea and fresh-baked cinnamon rolls in front of the crackling fireplace after a bracing walk along the Djurgården shoreline, past the Kärleksudden (Lovers’ Point) observation deck with its breathtaking views.

Where better to sample a Swedish classic than this low-lit space tucked alongside the Stockholm Opera House? Bakfickan (the back pocket) is an intimate, 28-seater restaurant that serves Swedish comfort food, or husmanskost, including their best-selling meatballs with all the customary accoutrements: creamy gravy, potato purée, lingonberries, and pickled cucumber.

The name Röda Huset (red house) conjures images of a red-painted cottage deep in the Swedish countryside, but this particular house is as urban as it gets, with its bright crimson façade overlooking Sergels Torg, Stockholm’s most central square. The moodily lit top floor is home to an award-winning cocktail lounge, where drinks are laced with hyperlocal Scandinavian produce. Think a Manhattan infused with heather honey from the Baltic island of Gotland or a tart, green tomato-flavored Dry Martini.

Stockholm’s southside, or Södermalm (Söder for short), was once an impoverished district where affordable homes were built for factory workers. These days, it’s best known for its laid-back, unbothered vibe, lively bars, and hip stores. It’s where Swedish actor Alexander Skarsgård grew up and where you’ll often spot him casually hanging out with friends when he’s in town. Start at Nytorget and wander through the trendy SoFo district, where you can marvel at the Christmas lights and the elegant Nordic Classicism buildings. Once you reach Mariatorget, climb the hill to Monteliusgatan Street where you’ll be treated to one of the most magnificent aerial views across the frozen waters of Riddarfjärden to the snow-dusted rooftops of Stockholm City Hall.

Staying in Söder, the area around Nytorget is full of chic boutiques like the 6/5/4 clothing and concept store and menswear brand A Day’s March (to help you perfect that effortlessly cool Skarsgård look). Don’t miss interior design mecca Tambur, where you can invest in some mys of your own, like cozy wool throws and charcoal-scented candles. Meanwhile, Hornsgatan is home to the Slow Fashion District, a collection of some 20 stores selling vintage, second-hand, upcycled and sustainable fashions, as well as skincare and homewares.

Swedes love to tell you “there’s no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing”—and winter is the time to prove them right as you bundle up and get your outdoor mys on. It takes a cold winter for Stockholm’s waterways to freeze over, but when they do, they fill with ice skaters from families teaching their little ones to stay upright to hardcore long-distance skaters. If open water ice-skating is too adventurous, there’s also a public rink in central Stockholm at Kungsträdgården. Meanwhile, winter kayaking is an exhilarating option for milder winters.

Saunas are as beloved here as they are in Finland, but scoring a membership at one of Stockholm’s private sauna clubs is like getting an audience with His Majesty King Carl XVI Gustaf. This year saw the launch of Stockholm’s first-ever public sauna, Bastun Tanto: a photogenic, verdigris-green floating pontoon set on the fashionable Hornstull waterfront that offers icy plunges and steamy warm-ups all winter long (with slots bookable 30 days in advance).

#6661. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

Gigantopithecus was the largest primate that ever lived. What would have happened when human ancestors encountered it?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At nearly 10 feet (3 meters) tall and around 500 pounds (230 kilograms), Gigantopithecus was the largest primate that ever lived.

Foraging across the dense tropical forests of Southeast Asia between 2 million and 200,000 years ago, the giant ape may have shared the habitat with new arrivals — hominins such as Homo erectus. (Hominins are members of the group that includes modern humans, their ancestors and closely related species, after the evolutionary split from great apes.)

Despite their immense size Gigantopithecus mainly consumed plants and is closely related to modern-day orangutans.

So what would have happened when Gigantopithecus encountered these human ancestors?

Experts suggested a variety of possible scenarios, including that Gigantopithecus and human ancestors didn't encounter each other at all.

It's "very difficult to say with any certainty, as we have no direct evidence documenting interactions between Gigantopithecus and human ancestors," Renaud Joannes-Boyau, director of higher-degree research training at Southern Cross University in Australia and an archaeologist who has conducted extensive research into human evolution, told Live Science in an email.

What would have happened if hominins encountered Gigantopithecus?

"That said, if we look at the broader pattern of human evolution, our lineage [Homo] has consistently behaved as an apex predator," Joannes-Boyau said. "Humans and our ancestors have shown a remarkable tendency to explore, exploit and, at times, eliminate large animals that shared their environment. I think it is reasonable to imagine that those interactions may have involved a mixture of indifference, curiosity and violence, depending on the circumstances."

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Friedemann Schrenk, a professor of paleobiology at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz in Germany, thinks Gigantopithecus would have likely tried to avoid humans. "Humans were and are the most aggressive primates ever on earth using tools and weapons and were probably encroaching on Gigantopithecus habitats," he told Live Science in an email. Homo erectus made use of hand axes and possibly hafted spears.

Schrenk envisions the hypothetical interactions as similar to those between modern-day humans and orangutans, which has resulted in humans encroaching on orangutan habitats and the apes' populations declining. "After all, Gigantopithecus was a gigantic orangutan," he said, noting that if there was hostility in a direct encounter, early humans would have been the aggressors.

Yet it's also possible that Gigantopithecus and hominins lived in different environments in Southeast Asia, which would have minimized the number of interactions they had, said Hervé Bocherens, a professor of biogeology at the University of Tübingen in Germany.

Fossilized Gigantopithecus jawbones suggest that the giant ape's diet was plant-based.

The "carbon stable isotopic ratios measured on some teeth of both taxa suggest a different habitat, closed forests for Gigantopithecus and open savannah for Homo erectus," Bocherens told Live Science in an email. However, because of limited data, "we cannot exclude that some hominins were also present in more forested environments," he added. Grinding patterns in their teeth suggest that Gigantopithecus' diet was essentially plant-based and may have included bamboo.

In a 2024 study, scientists investigated the demise of Gigantopithecus and found no evidence that hominins contributed to Gigantopithecus' extinction. Instead, they determined that the main cause was environmental change that resulted in a reduction in the forested environment where Gigantopithecus lived and foraged. In fact, hominins and Gigantopithecus may not have encountered each other at all, Yingqi Zhang, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and first author of the paper, told Live Science in an email.

We can only imagine what hominins would have thought when they glimpsed these gigantic creatures. It’s not clear how hominins and Gigantopithecus would have interacted, if they ever did, said Frido Welker, a professor of biomolecular paleoanthropology at the University of Copenhagen. He thinks they would have avoided each other but they may have "been in awe when they did happen to run into each other."
